I had been called away from town for a few days, and on my return
found Poirot in the act of strapping up his small valise.

“_A la bonne heure_, Hastings. I feared you would not have returned
in time to accompany me.”

“You are called away on a case, then?”

“Yes, though I am bound to admit that, on the face of it, the
affair does not seem promising. The Northern Union Insurance
Company have asked me to investigate the death of a Mr. Maltravers
who a few weeks ago insured his life with them for the large sum
of fifty thousand pounds.”

“Yes?” I said, much interested.

“There was, of course, the usual suicide clause in the policy. In
the event of his committing suicide within a year the premiums
would be forfeited. Mr. Maltravers was duly examined by the
Company’s own doctor, and although he was a man slightly past the
prime of life was passed as being in quite sound health. However,
on Wednesday last—the day before yesterday—the body of Mr.
Maltravers was found in the grounds of his house in Essex, Marsdon
Manor, and the cause of his death is described as some kind of
internal hæmorrhage. That in itself would be nothing remarkable,
but sinister rumours as to Mr. Maltravers’ financial position have
been in the air of late, and the Northern Union have ascertained
beyond any possible doubt that the deceased gentleman stood upon
the verge of bankruptcy. Now that alters matters considerably.
Maltravers had a beautiful young wife, and it is suggested that he
got together all the ready money he could for the purpose of paying
the premiums on a life insurance for his wife’s benefit, and then
committed suicide. Such a thing is not uncommon. In any case, my
friend Alfred Wright, who is a director of the Northern Union, has
asked me to investigate the facts of the case, but, as I told him,
I am not very hopeful of success. If the cause of the death had
been heart failure, I should have been more sanguine. Heart failure
may always be translated as the inability of the local G.P. to
discover what his patient really did die of, but a hæmorrhage seems
fairly definite. Still, we can but make some necessary inquiries.
Five minutes to pack your bag, Hastings, and we will take a taxi
to Liverpool Street.”

About an hour later, we alighted from a Great Eastern train at the
little station of Marsdon Leigh. Inquiries at the station yielded
the information that Marsdon Manor was about a mile distant. Poirot
decided to walk, and we betook ourselves along the main street.

“What is our plan of campaign?” I asked.

“First I will call upon the doctor. I have ascertained that there
is only one doctor in Marsdon Leigh, Dr. Ralph Bernard. Ah, here
we are at his house.”

The house in question was a kind of superior cottage, standing back
a little from the road. A brass plate on the gate bore the doctor’s
name. We passed up the path and rang the bell.

We proved to be fortunate in our call. It was the doctor’s
consulting hour, and for the moment there were no patients waiting
for him. Dr. Bernard was an elderly man, high-shouldered and
stooping, with a pleasant vagueness of manner.

Poirot introduced himself and explained the purpose of our visit,
adding that Insurance Companies were bound to investigate fully in
a case of this kind.

“Of course, of course,” said Dr. Bernard vaguely. “I suppose, as
he was such a rich man, his life was insured for a big sum?”

“You consider him a rich man, doctor?”

The doctor looked rather surprised.

“Was he not? He kept two cars, you know, and Marsdon Manor is a
pretty big place to keep up, although I believe he bought it very
cheap.”

“I understand that he had had considerable losses of late,” said
Poirot, watching the doctor narrowly.

The latter, however, merely shook his head sadly.

“Is that so? Indeed. It is fortunate for his wife, then, that there
is this life insurance. A very beautiful and charming young
creature, but terribly unstrung by this sad catastrophe. A mass of
nerves, poor thing. I have tried to spare her all I can, but of
course the shock was bound to be considerable.”

“You had been attending Mr. Maltravers recently?”

“My dear sir, I never attended him.”

“What?”

“I understand Mr. Maltravers was a Christian Scientist—or something
of that kind.”

“But you examined the body?”

“Certainly. I was fetched by one of the under-gardeners.”

“And the cause of death was clear?”

“Absolutely. There was blood on the lips, but most of the bleeding
must have been internal.”

“Was he still lying where he had been found?”

“Yes, the body had not been touched. He was lying at the edge of
a small plantation. He had evidently been out shooting rooks, a
small rook rifle lay beside him. The hæmorrhage must have occurred
quite suddenly. Gastric ulcer, without a doubt.”

“No question of his having been shot, eh?”

“My dear sir!”

“I demand pardon,” said Poirot humbly. “But, if my memory is not
at fault, in the case of a recent murder, the doctor first gave a
verdict of heart failure—altering it when the local constable
pointed out that there was a bullet wound through the head!”

“You will not find any bullet wounds on the body of Mr. Maltravers,”
said Dr. Bernard dryly. “Now, gentlemen, if there is nothing
further——”

We took the hint.

“Good morning, and many thanks to you, doctor, for so kindly
answering our questions. By the way, you saw no need for an
autopsy?”

“Certainly not.” The doctor became quite apoplectic. “The cause of
death was clear, and in my profession we see no need to distress
unduly the relatives of a dead patient.”

And, turning, the doctor slammed the door sharply in our faces.

“And what do you think of Dr. Bernard, Hastings?” inquired Poirot,
as we proceeded on our way to the Manor.

“Rather an old ass.”

“Exactly. Your judgments of character are always profound, my
friend.”

I glanced at him uneasily, but he seemed perfectly serious. A
twinkle, however, came into his eye, and he added slyly:

“That is to say, when there is no question of a beautiful woman!”

I looked at him coldly.

On our arrival at the manor-house, the door was opened to us by a
middle-aged parlourmaid. Poirot handed her his card, and a letter
from the Insurance Company for Mrs. Maltravers. She showed us into
a small morning-room, and retired to tell her mistress. About ten
minutes elapsed, and then the door opened, and a slender figure in
widow’s weeds stood upon the threshold.

“Monsieur Poirot?” she faltered.

“Madame!” Poirot sprang gallantly to his feet and hastened towards
her. “I cannot tell you how I regret to derange you in this way.
But what will you? _Les affaires_—they know no mercy.”

Mrs. Maltravers permitted him to lead her to a chair. Her eyes were
red with weeping, but the temporary disfigurement could not conceal
her extraordinary beauty. She was about twenty-seven or eight, and
very fair, with large blue eyes and a pretty pouting mouth.

“It is something about my husband’s insurance, is it? But must I
be bothered _now_—so soon?”

“Courage, my dear Madame. Courage! You see, your late husband
insured his life for rather a large sum, and in such a case the
Company always has to satisfy itself as to a few details. They have
empowered me to act for them. You can rest assured that I will do
all in my power to render the matter not too unpleasant for you.
Will you recount to me briefly the sad events of Wednesday?”

“I was changing for tea when my maid came up—one of the gardeners
had just run to the house. He had found——”

Her voice trailed away. Poirot pressed her hand sympathetically.

“I comprehend. Enough! You had seen your husband earlier in the
afternoon?”

“Not since lunch. I had walked down to the village for some stamps,
and I believe he was out pottering round the grounds.”

“Shooting rooks, eh?”

“Yes, he usually took his little rook rifle with him, and I heard
one or two shots in the distance.”

“Where is this little rook rifle now?”

“In the hall, I think.”

She led the way out of the room and found and handed the little
weapon to Poirot, who examined it cursorily.

“Two shots fired, I see,” he observed, as he handed it back. “And
now, madame, if I might see——”

He paused delicately.

“The servant shall take you,” she murmured, averting her head.

The parlourmaid, summoned, led Poirot upstairs. I remained with
the lovely and unfortunate woman. It was hard to know whether to
speak or remain silent. I essayed one or two general reflections
to which she responded absently, and in a very few minutes Poirot
rejoined us.

“I thank you for all your courtesy, madame. I do not think you need
be troubled any further with this matter. By the way, do you know
anything of your husband’s financial position?”

She shook her head.

“Nothing whatever. I am very stupid over business things.”

“I see. Then you can give us no clue as to why he suddenly decided
to insure his life? He had not done so previously, I understand.”

“Well, we had only been married a little over a year. But, as to
why he insured his life, it was because he had absolutely made up
his mind that he would not live long. He had a strong premonition
of his own death. I gather that he had had one hæmorrhage already,
and that he knew that another one would prove fatal. I tried to
dispel these gloomy fears of his, but without avail. Alas, he was
only too right!”

Tears in her eyes, she bade us a dignified farewell. Poirot made
a characteristic gesture as we walked down the drive together.

“_Eh bien_, that is that! Back to London, my friend, there appears
to be no mouse in this mouse-hole. And yet——”

“Yet what?”

“A slight discrepancy, that is all! You noticed it? You did not?
Still, life is full of discrepancies, and assuredly the man cannot
have taken his own life—there is no poison that would fill his
mouth with blood. No, no, I must resign myself to the fact that
all here is clear and above-board—but who is this?”

A tall young man was striding up the drive towards us. He passed
us without making any sign, but I noted that he was not ill-looking,
with a lean, deeply bronzed face that spoke of life in a tropic
clime. A gardener who was sweeping up leaves had paused for a
minute in his task, and Poirot ran quickly up to him.

“Tell me, I pray you, who is that gentleman? Do you know him?”

“I don’t remember his name, sir, though I did hear it. He was
staying down here last week for a night. Tuesday, it was.”

“Quick, _mon ami_, let us follow him.”

We hastened up the drive after the retreating figure. A glimpse of
a black-robed figure on the terrace at the side of the house, and
our quarry swerved and we after him, so that we were witnesses of
the meeting.

Mrs. Maltravers almost staggered where she stood, and her face
blanched noticeably.

“You,” she gasped. “I thought you were on the sea—on your way to
East Africa?”

“I got some news from my lawyers that detained me,” explained the
young man. “My old uncle in Scotland died unexpectedly and left me
some money. Under the circumstances I thought it better to cancel
my passage. Then I saw this bad news in the paper and I came down
to see if there was anything I could do. You’ll want some one to
look after things for you a bit perhaps.”

At that moment they became aware of our presence. Poirot stepped
forward, and with many apologies explained that he had left his
stick in the hall. Rather reluctantly, it seemed to me, Mrs.
Maltravers made the necessary introduction.

“Monsieur Poirot, Captain Black.”

A few minutes’ chat ensued, in the course of which Poirot elicited
the fact that Captain Black was putting up at the Anchor Inn. The
missing stick not having been discovered (which was not surprising),
Poirot uttered more apologies and we withdrew.

We returned to the village at a great pace, and Poirot made a bee
line for the Anchor Inn.

“Here we establish ourselves until our friend the Captain returns,”
he explained. “You notice that I emphasized the point that we were
returning to London by the first train? Possibly you thought I
meant it. But no—you observed Mrs. Maltravers’ face when she caught
sight of this young Black? She was clearly taken aback, and he—_eh
bien_, he was very devoted, did you not think so? And he was here
on Tuesday night—the day before Mr. Maltravers died. We must
investigate the doings of Captain Black, Hastings.”

In about half an hour we espied our quarry approaching the inn.
Poirot went out and accosted him and presently brought him up to
the room we had engaged.

“I have been telling Captain Black of the mission which brings us
here,” he explained. “You can understand, _monsieur le capitaine_,
that I am anxious to arrive at Mr. Maltravers’ state of mind
immediately before his death, and that at the same time I do not
wish to distress Mrs. Maltravers unduly by asking her painful
questions. Now, you were here just before the occurrence, and can
give us equally valuable information.”

“I’ll do anything I can to help you, I’m sure,” replied the young
soldier; “but I’m afraid I didn’t notice anything out of the
ordinary. You see, although Maltravers was an old friend of my
people’s, I didn’t know him very well myself.”

“You came down—when?”

“Tuesday afternoon. I went up to town early Wednesday morning, as
my boat sailed from Tilbury about twelve o’clock. But some news I
got made me alter my plans, as I dare say you heard me explain to
Mrs. Maltravers.”

“You were returning to East Africa, I understand?”

“Yes. I’ve been out there ever since the War—a great country.”

“Exactly. Now what was the talk about at dinner on Tuesday night?”

“Oh, I don’t know. The usual odd topics. Maltravers asked after my
people, and then we discussed the question of German reparations,
and then Mrs. Maltravers asked a lot of questions about East
Africa, and I told them one or two yarns, that’s about all, I
think.”

“Thank you.”

Poirot was silent for a moment, then he said gently: “With your
permission, I should like to try a little experiment. You have told
us all that your conscious self knows, I want now to question your
subconscious self.”

“Psychoanalysis, what?” said Black, with visible alarm.

“Oh, no,” said Poirot reassuringly. “You see, it is like this, I
give you a word, you answer with another, and so on. Any word, the
first one you think of. Shall we begin?”

“All right,” said Black slowly, but he looked uneasy.

“Note down the words, please, Hastings,” said Poirot. Then he took
from his pocket his big turnip-faced watch and laid it on the table
beside him. “We will commence. Day.”

There was a moment’s pause, and then Black replied:

“_Night_.”

As Poirot proceeded, his answers came quicker.

“Name,” said Poirot.

“_Place_.”

“Bernard.”

“_Shaw_.”

“Tuesday.”

“_Dinner_.”

“Journey.”

“_Ship_.”

“Country.”

“_Uganda_.”

“Story.”

“_Lions_.”

“Rook Rifle.”

“_Farm_.”

“Shot.”

“_Suicide_.”

“Elephant.”

“_Tusks_.”

“Money.”

“_Lawyers_.”

“Thank you, Captain Black. Perhaps you could spare me a few minutes
in about half an hour’s time?”

“Certainly.” The young soldier looked at him curiously and wiped
his brow as he got up.

“And now, Hastings,” said Poirot, smiling at me as the door closed
behind him. “You see it all, do you not?”

“I don’t know what you mean.”

“Does that list of words tell you nothing?”

I scrutinized it, but was forced to shake my head.

“I will assist you. To begin with, Black answered well within the
normal time limit, with no pauses, so we can take it that he
himself has no guilty knowledge to conceal. ‘Day’ to ‘Night’ and
‘Place’ to ‘Name’ are normal associations. I began work with
‘Bernard’ which might have suggested the local doctor had he come
across him at all. Evidently he had not. After our recent
conversation, he gave ‘Dinner’ to my ‘Tuesday,’ but ‘Journey’ and
‘Country’ were answered by ‘Ship’ and ‘Uganda,’ showing clearly
that it was his journey abroad that was important to him and not
the one which brought him down here. ‘Story’ recalls to him one of
the ‘Lion’ stories he told at dinner. I proceed to ‘Rook Rifle’
and he answered with the totally unexpected word ‘Farm.’ When I
say ‘Shot,’ he answers at once ‘Suicide.’ The association seems
clear. A man he knows committed suicide with a rook rifle on a farm
somewhere. Remember, too, that his mind is still on the stories he
told at dinner, and I think you will agree that I shall not be far
from the truth if I recall Captain Black and ask him to repeat the
particular suicide story which he told at the dinner-table on
Tuesday evening.”

Black was straightforward enough over the matter.

“Yes, I did tell them that story now that I come to think of it.
Chap shot himself on a farm out there. Did it with a rook rifle
through the roof of the mouth, bullet lodged in the brain. Doctors
were no end puzzled over it—there was nothing to show except a
little blood on the lips. But what——”

“What has it got to do with Mr. Maltravers? You did not know, I
see, that he was found with a rook rifle by his side.”

“You mean my story suggested to him—oh, but that is awful!”

“Do not distress yourself—it would have been one way or another.
Well, I must get on the telephone to London.”

Poirot had a lengthy conversation over the wire, and came back
thoughtful. He went off by himself in the afternoon, and it was
not till seven o’clock that he announced that he could put it off
no longer, but must break the news to the young widow. My sympathy
had already gone out to her unreservedly. To be left penniless,
and with the knowledge that her husband had killed himself to
assure her future was a hard burden for any woman to bear. I
cherished a secret hope, however, that young Black might prove
capable of consoling her after her first grief had passed. He
evidently admired her enormously.

Our interview with the lady was painful. She refused vehemently to
believe the facts that Poirot advanced, and when she was at last
convinced broke down into bitter weeping. An examination of the
body turned our suspicions into certainty. Poirot was very sorry
for the poor lady, but, after all, he was employed by the Insurance
Company, and what could he do? As he was preparing to leave he said
gently to Mrs. Maltravers:

“Madame, you of all people should know that there are no dead!”

“What do you mean?” she faltered, her eyes growing wide.

“Have you never taken part in any spiritualistic séances? You are
mediumistic, you know.”

“I have been told so. But you do not believe in Spiritualism,
surely?”

“Madame, I have seen some strange things. You know that they say
in the village that this house is haunted?”

She nodded, and at that moment the parlourmaid announced that
dinner was ready.

“Won’t you just stay and have something to eat?”

We accepted gratefully, and I felt that our presence could not but
help distract her a little from her own griefs.

We had just finished our soup, when there was a scream outside the
door, and the sound of breaking crockery. We jumped up. The
parlourmaid appeared, her hand to her heart.

“It was a man—standing in the passage.”

Poirot rushed out, returning quickly.

“There is no one there.”

“Isn’t there, sir?” said the parlourmaid weakly. “Oh, it did give
me a start!”

“But why?”

She dropped her voice to a whisper.

“I thought—I thought it was the master—it looked like ’im.”

I saw Mrs. Maltravers give a terrified start, and my mind flew to
the old superstition that a suicide cannot rest. She thought of it
too, I am sure, for a minute later, she caught Poirot’s arm with
a scream.

“Didn’t you hear that? Those three taps on the window? That’s how
_he_ always used to tap when he passed round the house.”

“The ivy,” I cried. “It was the ivy against the pane.”

But a sort of terror was gaining on us all. The parlourmaid was
obviously unstrung, and when the meal was over Mrs. Maltravers
besought Poirot not to go at once. She was clearly terrified to be
left alone. We sat in the little morning-room. The wind was getting
up, and moaning round the house in an eerie fashion. Twice the door
of the room came unlatched and the door slowly opened, and each
time she clung to me with a terrified gasp.

“Ah, but this door, it is bewitched!” cried

Poirot angrily at last. He got up and shut it once more, then
turned the key in the lock. “I shall lock it, so!”

“Don’t do that,” she gasped, “if it should come open now——”

And even as she spoke the impossible happened. The locked door
slowly swung open. I could not see into the passage from where I
sat, but she and Poirot were facing it. She gave one long shriek
as she turned to him.

“You saw him—there in the passage?” she cried.

He was staring down at her with a puzzled face, then shook his
head.

“I saw him—my husband—you must have seen him too?”

“Madame, I saw nothing. You are not well—unstrung——”

“I am perfectly well, I——Oh, God!”

Suddenly, without any warning, the lights quivered and went out.
Out of the darkness came three loud raps. I could hear Mrs.
Maltravers moaning.

And then—I saw!

The man I had seen on the bed upstairs stood there facing us,
gleaming with a faint ghostly light. There was blood on his lips,
and he held his right hand out, pointing. Suddenly a brilliant
light seemed to proceed from it. It passed over Poirot and me, and
fell on Mrs. Maltravers. I saw her white terrified face, and
something else!

“My God, Poirot!” I cried. “Look at her hand, her right hand. It’s
all red!”

Her own eyes fell on it, and she collapsed in a heap on the floor.

“Blood,” she cried hysterically. “Yes, it’s blood. I killed him.
I did it. He was showing me, and then I put my hand on the trigger
and pressed. Save me from him—save me! he’s come back!”

Her voice died away in a gurgle.

“Lights,” said Poirot briskly.

The lights went on as if by magic.

“That’s it,” he continued. “You heard, Hastings? And you, Everett?
Oh, by the way, this is Mr. Everett, rather a fine member of the
theatrical profession. I ’phoned to him this afternoon. His make-up
is good, isn’t it? Quite like the dead man, and with a pocket torch
and the necessary phosphorescence he made the proper impression.
I shouldn’t touch her right hand if I were you, Hastings. Red paint
marks so. When the lights went out I clasped her hand, you see. By
the way, we mustn’t miss our train. Inspector Japp is outside the
window. A bad night—but he has been able to while away the time by
tapping on the window every now and then.”

“You see,” continued Poirot, as we walked briskly through the wind
and rain, “there was a little discrepancy. The doctor seemed to
think the deceased was a Christian Scientist, and who could have
given him that impression but Mrs. Maltravers? But to us she
represented him as being in a grave state of apprehension about
his own health. Again, why was she so taken aback by the reappearance
of young Black? And lastly, although I know that convention decrees
that a woman must make a decent pretence of mourning for her
husband, I do not care for such heavily-rouged eyelids! You did
not observe them, Hastings? No? As I always tell you, you see
nothing!”

“Well, there it was. There were the two possibilities. Did Black’s
story suggest an ingenious method of committing suicide to Mr.
Maltravers, or did his other listener, the wife, see an equally
ingenious method of committing murder? I inclined to the latter
view. To shoot himself in the way indicated, he would probably have
had to pull the trigger with his toe—or at least so I imagine.
Now if Maltravers had been found with one boot off, we should
almost certainly have heard of it from some one. An odd detail like
that would have been remembered.

“No, as I say, I inclined to the view that it was a case of murder,
not suicide, but I realized that I had not a shadow of proof in
support of my theory. Hence the elaborate little comedy you saw
played to-night.”

“Even now I don’t quite see all the details of the crime?” I said.

“Let us start from the beginning. Here is a shrewd and scheming
woman who, knowing of her husband’s financial _débâcle_ and tired
of the elderly mate she has only married for his money, induces
him to insure his life for a large sum, and then seeks for the
means to accomplish her purpose. An accident gives her that—the
young soldier’s strange story. The next afternoon when _monsieur
le capitaine_, as she thinks, is on the high seas, she and her
husband are strolling round the grounds. ‘What a curious story that
was last night!’ she observes. ‘Could a man shoot himself in such
a way? Do show me if it is possible!’ The poor fool—he shows her.
He places the end of the rifle in his mouth. She stoops down, and
puts her finger on the trigger, laughing up at him. ‘And now, sir,’
she says saucily, ‘supposing I pull the trigger?’

“And then—and then, Hastings—she pulls it!”

“Yes, though I am bound to admit that, on the face of it, the
affair does not seem promising. The Northern Union Insurance
Company have asked me to investigate the death of a Mr. Maltravers
who a few weeks ago insured his life with them for the large sum
of fifty thousand pounds.”

“Yes?” I said, much interested.

An hour later, we alighted from our train at the small station of Marsdon Leigh, and a short drive in a somewhat rickety fly brought us to the gates of Marsdon Manor. It was a somber-looking house, dating perhaps from the Tudor period, and its dark stone walls seemed to absorb the waning light of the afternoon. As we walked up the drive, Poirot paused for a moment, his eyes sweeping over the well-kept flowerbeds and the thick shrubbery that bordered the path. “A peaceful spot, Hastings,” he remarked softly, “but where there is great peace, there is often a great deal to hide. Let us see what the widow, this beautiful Mrs. Maltravers, has to say to us.”

The journey into Essex was relatively brief. Poirot spent most of it in silence, his head tilted slightly to one side as he contemplated the facts already in his possession. Upon our arrival at the small station of Marsdon Leigh, we took a trap to the manor itself. It was a somber, grey-stone building, surrounded by dense trees that seemed to press inward with a certain foreboding. As we stepped into the hallway, we were met by a middle-aged man with a professional air and a somewhat harassed expression, whom Poirot greeted with a polite inclination of the head.

The journey to Essex was uneventful, and as the train pulled into the small, grey station of Marsdon Leigh, the atmosphere of the place struck me as singularly depressing. A fine drizzle was falling, veiling the flat landscape in a shroud of mist. Poirot, his collar turned up to protect his precious throat, hailed a dilapidated fly, and we were driven to the village. Our first destination was the residence of Dr. Ralph Bernard, the physician who had attended the late Mr. Maltravers and signed the death certificate. The doctor was a tall, thin man with a restless manner and eyes that seemed perpetually to avoid one's own, a trait I found instantly suspicious, though Poirot merely greeted him with his customary exquisite politeness.

The journey to Essex was a somewhat silent one. Poirot appeared lost in thought, his eyes fixed on the flying landscape with a peculiar expression of concentration. We were met at the station of Marsdon Leigh by a small, high dog-cart which conveyed us to the manor. It was a somber house, surrounded by trees that sighed mournfully in the wind. Mrs. Maltravers received us in the library. She was a woman of singular beauty, though her face was now marred by the ravages of grief. She was dressed in deep mourning, which served to accentuate the ivory pallor of her skin. With her was a tall, bronzed man whom she introduced as Captain Black, a friend of her late husband's who had arrived from East Africa only a few days before the catastrophe.

About an hour’s journey brought us to the small station of Marsdon Leigh, and a further ten minutes in a somewhat antique vehicle saw us drawing up before the door of the manor. It was a fine old house, but it wore an air of neglect that spoke of its owner’s recent financial straits. We were received by a man of about fifty, with a professional manner and a sharp, searching eye. This was Dr. Ralph Bernard, who, as Poirot had informed me, was the first person to reach Mr. Maltravers after his collapse. He looked at Poirot with a curiosity that he did not attempt to hide, his fingers nervously drumming against his medical bag.

About an hour later, we alighted from a Great Eastern train at the
little station of Marsdon Leigh. Inquiries at the station yielded
the information that Marsdon Manor was about a mile distant. Poirot
decided to walk, and we betook ourselves along the main street.

“What is our plan of campaign?” I asked.

“First I will call upon the doctor. I have ascertained that there
is only one doctor in Marsdon Leigh, Dr. Ralph Bernard. Ah, here
we are at his house.”

The house in question was a kind of superior cottage, standing back
a little from the road. A brass plate on the gate bore the doctor’s
name. We passed up the path and rang the bell.

“Is that so? Well, well,” said the doctor. “It is a world of trouble. As to the death of Mr. Maltravers, there was nothing to suggest anything but natural causes. He was found by one of the gardeners near the edge of the small plantation, quite dead, with a great quantity of blood about the mouth. I should say a large vessel had given way in the lungs. He was an older man, as you know, and the heat—it was a very hot day—might easily have brought on the catastrophe. He had been out for a stroll with a friend who was staying with him, a Captain Black, but the Captain had left him to return to the house for some tobacco.”

"It was a most distressing case," the doctor continued, oblivious to Poirot’s scrutiny. "I was called to the Manor just after nine o’clock on Wednesday evening. Mr. Maltravers had been walking in the grounds—near the edge of the spinney—when he was apparently seized with a sudden seizure. He was dead by the time I arrived. A very clear case of internal hemorrhage, as I stated in the certificate. There was a considerable amount of blood, you understand—most unpleasant." Poirot leaned forward, his eyes shining with that peculiar green light that always betokened his interest. "And you are quite certain, Doctor, that there was no other possible cause? No sign of—shall we say—a struggle, or perhaps a weapon?" The doctor looked positively scandalized at the suggestion. "Good heavens, no! The idea is preposterous. The man was in evening dress, and there was not a mark on him—save for the blood, of course."

“That is the misfortune of the thing,” said Dr. Bernard. “He had always seemed a man of robust health. In my opinion, it was a sudden lesion of a large vessel—most likely gastric. He was found by his wife, you know, just by the edge of the plantation. A very sad business. She is quite prostrate with grief, poor thing.” Poirot nodded sympathetically. “And there were no other witnesses to this—unfortunate occurrence?” “None. Except perhaps for a Captain Black, a guest at the house, who arrived just as the end came. But there was nothing to be done—nothing at all.”

"That is the way of the world," said Dr. Bernard. "But I cannot say I saw any sign of financial strain. As for his death, it was a sudden thing—a very sudden thing. He was out in the grounds with a small rook rifle, intending to shoot some of the rooks that have become a nuisance lately. His wife was near him at the time. Suddenly he gave a cry, the rifle fell from his hand, and he collapsed. By the time I arrived, life was extinct. It was, as I stated on the certificate, an internal hemorrhage, the result of a small gastric ulcer of which I had previously suspected the existence."

“Is that so? And what did he die of, actually?”

“Internal hemorrhage,” said the doctor. “It was quite clear. He must have had a gastric ulcer for some time. I had attended him once or twice for what he called ‘acute indigestion,’ but he was not a man who liked doctors. He was found near the edge of the small plantation on the estate. He had been out with his gun, it seems—though he hadn’t fired it. The shock of the hemorrhage must have been almost instantaneous. Captain Black, a guest staying at the Manor, found him.”

“Is that so? Indeed. It is fortunate for his wife, then, that there
is this life insurance. A very beautiful and charming young
creature, but terribly unstrung by this sad catastrophe. A mass of
nerves, poor thing. I have tried to spare her all I can, but of
course the shock was bound to be considerable.”

“You had been attending Mr. Maltravers recently?”

“My dear sir, I never attended him.”

“What?”

“I understand Mr. Maltravers was a Christian Scientist—or something
of that kind.”

“But you examined the body?”

“Certainly. I was fetched by one of the under-gardeners.”

“And the cause of death was clear?”

“Absolutely. There was blood on the lips, but most of the bleeding
must have been internal.”

“Was he still lying where he had been found?”

“I am a layman,” said Poirot. “But is it not unusual for a gastric ulcer to kill so suddenly, without any previous symptoms?”

“It is rare, I admit,” replied Dr. Bernard, “but by no means impossible. The excitement of the sport, the slight exertion—any of these might have been the predisposing cause. As for the rifle, it had been fired once, but as I have already told you, there was no wound upon the body. The death was due to natural causes, and I have had no hesitation in giving a certificate to that effect.”

“I examined the body very carefully,” the doctor continued, a trifle stiffly. “There was no trace of any wound. One barrel of the rook rifle had been discharged, but that is easily accounted for. He must have been in the very act of firing when the seizure took place. As I say, the cause of death was perfectly clear—a sudden and violent hemorrhage. The man’s mouth was full of blood.”

“And there were no other guests at the Manor?” inquired Poirot.

“I believe there was one gentleman—a Captain Black. It was he, in fact, who found the body.”

“I apologize,” said Poirot, with a little bow. “But in my profession, one must consider every possibility—even that of a self-inflicted wound. However, you are certain there was no injury of that nature?”
“The rifle had not even been fired, Monsieur Poirot,” the doctor replied with a touch of professional indignation. “And there was no wound of any kind upon the body. As I have told you, the blood came from the mouth, and the physical evidence of a gastric ulcer was unmistakable. I have issued the death certificate accordingly.”
“I see,” said Poirot, his eyes following the flight of a bird through the window. “And at what time did this occur?”
“The body was found at approximately six o'clock in the evening,” Dr. Bernard answered. “Death had probably occurred some two hours earlier. He had been dead a considerable time when I arrived.”
Poirot thanked the doctor for his courtesy, and we took our leave, heading once more towards the open road that led to the Manor.

“I examined the body most carefully,” continued the doctor, a trifle stiffly. “There was no wound of any kind—except, of course, the evidence of the internal rupture. As for the rifle, it had been fired once, but there was no sign of a struggle, no footprint other than his own. It was a clear case of a physical breakdown under strain. The man was not young, and if, as you say, he was in financial difficulties, the worry would naturally affect his health.” Poirot leaned forward, his eyes shining with that peculiar green light that always betokened his interest. “And at what time, doctor, did you estimate that death took place?” “It was seven o’clock when I arrived,” replied Dr. Bernard. “I should say he had been dead at least six hours. That would place the time of death at about one o’clock, shortly after lunch.”

“I apologize,” said Poirot with a little bow. “But you see, in my profession, one must consider all possibilities—even the most improbable ones. As a man of science, you will appreciate that we must exhaust the evidence.”

“There was no wound,” said Dr. Bernard stiffly. “Except, of course, for the traces of the hemorrhage. The idea of a gunshot is quite out of the question. I have already signed the death certificate to that effect.”

“And the time of death?”

“I reached him at approximately six o'clock. He had been dead, I should say, for at least two hours. In my opinion, the exertion of the walk or perhaps the excitement of the sport triggered the internal rupture.”

“I see,” said Poirot thoughtfully. “And there were no other visitors at the house that afternoon? No guests staying there?”

“I believe a young man, a Captain Black, had arrived that morning. I saw him for a moment when I went to the Manor to inform Mrs. Maltravers of the tragedy.”

“I demand pardon,” said Poirot humbly. “But, if my memory is not
at fault, in the case of a recent murder, the doctor first gave a
verdict of heart failure—altering it when the local constable
pointed out that there was a bullet wound through the head!”

“You will not find any bullet wounds on the body of Mr. Maltravers,”
said Dr. Bernard dryly. “Now, gentlemen, if there is nothing
further——”

We took the hint.

“Good morning, and many thanks to you, doctor, for so kindly
answering our questions. By the way, you saw no need for an
autopsy?”

“Certainly not.” The doctor became quite apoplectic. “The cause of
death was clear, and in my profession we see no need to distress
unduly the relatives of a dead patient.”

And, turning, the doctor slammed the door sharply in our faces.

“And what do you think of Dr. Bernard, Hastings?” inquired Poirot,
as we proceeded on our way to the Manor.

“Rather an old ass.”

“Exactly. Your judgments of character are always profound, my
friend.”

I glanced at him uneasily, but he seemed perfectly serious. A
twinkle, however, came into his eye, and he added slyly:

“That is to say, when there is no question of a beautiful woman!”

I looked at him coldly.

Mrs. Maltravers was indeed a very beautiful woman. Her face was of a transparent pallor, and her large, dark eyes were heavy with weeping. She sank into a low chair, her hands twitching nervously at her black-edged handkerchief. “It is about the insurance, is it not?” she murmured. “I suppose it is necessary, but it is very painful. Must I answer many questions?”

The lady sank into a chair and looked at Poirot with wide, appealing eyes. She was indeed, as the doctor had said, a very beautiful woman. Her golden hair was massed under her widow’s cap, and her face was of a transparent pallor. “It is of no consequence,” she murmured. “I understand. You represent the insurance company. It is natural, I suppose, that they should make inquiries. But it is very painful. To have to talk of these things while my heart is so heavy. My husband was a good man, Monsieur Poirot. A good and kind husband. I cannot believe even now that he has been taken from me.”

Mrs. Maltravers sank into a low chair, her hands nervously pleating a fold of her black dress. She was indeed a beautiful woman, with a pale, ethereal face and large, haunting eyes. “I do not understand,” she murmured. “My husband—he is dead. What more can there be? The doctor has said it was an accident—a sudden illness.” She looked from one to the other of us with a bewildered, appealing gaze that would have melted the heart of a stone.

Mrs. Maltravers took the letter from Poirot’s hand with a slight tremor. She sank into a low chair and motioned us to be seated. “It is about the insurance, is it not?” she murmured. “Mr. Wright, who I believe is a director of the company, warned me that there might be certain—formalities. But it is so hard, Monsieur Poirot. My husband's death was such a terrible shock. We were so very happy together, and now, to have his name associated with... with what they are suggesting... it is more than I can bear.” She applied a small lace handkerchief to her eyes, her voice trailing off into a sob.

Mrs. Maltravers sank into a chair with a heavy sigh. Her face was pale, and her eyes showed signs of recent weeping. "I understand, Monsieur Poirot," she said in a low, musical voice. "The Northern Union must be satisfied. It is all so cruel—so terribly sudden. To think that only Wednesday morning Daniel was so full of life, and now..." She broke off, dabbing her eyes with a lace handkerchief. "It was the shock of it, you see. Finding him there—in the plantation—with that horrible rifle beside him. I cannot bear to think of it."

Mrs. Maltravers permitted him to lead her to a chair. Her eyes were
red with weeping, but the temporary disfigurement could not conceal
her extraordinary beauty. She was about twenty-seven or eight, and
very fair, with large blue eyes and a pretty pouting mouth.

“It is something about my husband’s insurance, is it? But must I
be bothered _now_—so soon?”

The parlourmaid was summoned, and she conducted us up the stairs to a darkened bedroom. There, on the bed, lay the body of the master of the house. Poirot, with a practiced air of solemnity, approached the deceased. He studied the face of the dead man for some minutes, his eyes resting particularly on the lips, and then he turned his attention to the surrounding furniture. On a small table by the bed, there was a glass half-filled with water and a small bottle of medicine. Poirot picked up the bottle, studied the label, and then, with a sharp intake of breath, replaced it exactly where it had been.

The parlourmaid was summoned, and she conducted us up the stairs to a large, somber bedroom. On the bed lay the body of the master of the house. Mr. Maltravers was a man of about fifty, with a face that even in death looked harassed and careworn. Poirot, with a word of apology to the girl, moved to the bed and began a swift but thorough examination. He paid particular attention to the mouth and the staining upon the lips, his eyes sharp and bird-like as they darted from one feature to another. After a few minutes, he straightened himself with a sigh and motioned for us to leave the room.

The parlourmaid was summoned, and she conducted us up the wide oak staircase to a room on the first floor. The blinds were drawn, but as Poirot pulled them aside, a shaft of afternoon sunlight fell across the bed where lay the mortal remains of Mr. Maltravers. He was a man of some sixty years, with a thin, refined face, now set in the finality of death. Poirot stood for a moment in silence, his eyes darting here and there with bird-like rapidity. He leaned over the body, scrutinising the face with a singular intentness, then, with a small grunt of dissatisfaction, he replaced the sheet and indicated that we should withdraw.

She rang the bell, and the parlourmaid who had admitted us appeared. At a word from her mistress, she led us out of the house and across the sweeping lawns toward a small plantation of larch and fir trees. “It was just here, sir,” she said, indicating a spot at the very edge of the trees where the grass was somewhat trampled. “The master was lying with his head towards the house, and the little gun was just beside him.”

The parlourmaid was summoned, and she conducted us up the stairs to a large, darkened bedroom where the curtains were drawn. On the bed, beneath a white sheet, lay the body of the late Mr. Maltravers. He appeared to have been a man of some fifty odd years, with a thin, ascetic face that still bore the traces of a recent struggle or perhaps merely the weariness of a man who had found life a heavy burden. Poirot stepped softly to the bedside, his eyes keen and searching. He turned back the sheet for a moment, his fingers moving with a bird-like quickness as he examined the dead man’s face and hands. I noticed him sniff the air slightly, and then his eyes rested for a long second on the dead man’s lips before he replaced the covering with a meticulous touch. We withdrew from the room in silence.

The parlourmaid, summoned, led Poirot upstairs. I remained with
the lovely and unfortunate woman. It was hard to know whether to
speak or remain silent. I essayed one or two general reflections
to which she responded absently, and in a very few minutes Poirot
rejoined us.

“I thank you for all your courtesy, madame. I do not think you need
be troubled any further with this matter. By the way, do you know
anything of your husband’s financial position?”

She shook her head.

“Nothing whatever. I am very stupid over business things.”

“I see. Then you can give us no clue as to why he suddenly decided
to insure his life? He had not done so previously, I understand.”

I paused as Poirot came to a sudden halt by the lodge gates. He was looking back at the gabled roof of the Manor with a look of profound abstraction. “The premonition of death,” he murmured. “It is a very useful thing to have in one’s pocket, is it not, Hastings? It explains so much. It accounts for the insurance, it accounts for the suddenness of the end. It is, in fact, almost too convenient. And then, there is the little matter of the two shots from the rook rifle. Why two, I ask myself? If he were shooting rooks, where are the dead rooks? I saw none. Did you?” Before I could reply, a tall, bronzed man with a military carriage came striding down the path toward us, his face set in a look of grim determination.

“Yet I am not entirely satisfied. This ‘premonition’ of which the
beautiful lady spoke—it is very convenient, is it not? A man who
thinks he is about to die of a hemorrhage does not usually go out
to shoot rooks. It is a sport for the vigorous. And the two shots...
where were the birds? We saw none. No, Hastings, we will not return
to London by the next train. We will go to the ‘Anchor’ and engage
rooms. I wish to see the spot where the body was found, and I wish
to speak with the under-gardener who discovered it.”

“And yet I do not like it, Hastings. It is all too simple, too—how do you say?—cut and dried. The premonition of death, the convenient hæmorrhage, the bankruptcy... it fits together like the pieces of a puzzle, but the picture it forms is not to my liking. And there is one thing that I do not understand. Why did he fire *two* shots with the rook rifle? To kill a rook, one shot is usually sufficient. To miss, one might fire again—but would a man on the point of death from a sudden hæmorrhage have the time or the inclination to fire a second time? Let us go and see the spot where he was found.”

“And yet—it is all so very neat, is it not? The premonition, the gastric ulcer, the little rook rifle. It is a stage beautifully set. But one thing does not please me, Hastings. The doctor, he was too anxious to be rid of us. And the beautiful Madame Maltravers, she is a very good actress. But see, who is this gentleman approaching us? He has the air of the military, does he not?”

“It is too perfect, Hastings. The gastric ulcer, the premonition, the convenient insurance. It is a little like a drama on the stage where the actors have learned their parts too well. And did you observe the rook rifle? It had been fired twice. Why two shots? To kill a rook, one shot should suffice. If you miss, the bird does not wait for a second invitation. No, there is something here that does not ring true. It offends the little grey cells. Let us return to the village. I wish to make one or two small inquiries at the local hostelry, the ‘Anchor Inn.’ I noticed a gentleman there when we passed who looked as though he might be a guest—a military-looking man with a very tanned face.”

“A slight discrepancy, that is all! You noticed it? You did not?
Still, life is full of discrepancies, and assuredly the man cannot
have taken his own life—there is no poison that would fill his
mouth with blood. No, no, I must resign myself to the fact that
all here is clear and above-board—but who is this?”

We turned and followed the stranger. He had already reached the front door and was about to ring when Poirot’s voice arrested him.

“Pardon, monsieur, but I believe I address Captain Black?”

The young man turned, looking surprised.

“That is my name. But I’m afraid I haven’t the pleasure——”

“My name is Hercule Poirot. I am staying in the neighborhood, and I was told you were a friend of the late Mr. Maltravers. A most shocking affair, was it not?”

Captain Black’s face clouded.

“Terrible,” he said briefly. “I only heard the news this morning and came down at once to see if I could be of any assistance to Mrs. Maltravers.”

We followed the stranger at a cautious distance, watching as he skirted the main entrance and made his way toward the side of the house where a terrace overlooked the gardens. As he approached, the French windows of the morning-room opened, and Mrs. Maltravers stepped out. The change in her demeanor was startling; the mask of quiet grief had vanished, replaced by a look of sharp anxiety. They began to speak in hushed, urgent tones, and though we were too far off to catch their words, the intimacy of their manner was unmistakable. Poirot’s eyes kindled with a sudden green light, a sure sign that his interest was thoroughly piqued. “_Aha!_” he whispered. “The plot, it begins to thicken. Who is this traveler from the tropics, and what is his business with the beautiful widow?”

We turned and followed the stranger at a discreet distance. He did not go to the front door, but skirted the house and disappeared through a side entrance. Poirot quickened his pace, and we arrived just in time to see the parlourmaid who had previously admitted us. In response to Poirot’s urgent inquiry, she looked somewhat surprised. “That is Captain Black, sir,” she explained. “A friend of the late Mr. Maltravers. He had been staying here for a night or two earlier in the week, and has just returned from town on hearing the sad news.”

We turned and followed the stranger. He had reached the front door and was about to ring when Poirot reached his side.

“Pardon, monsieur,” said Poirot, bowing with his accustomed grace. “I believe I have the honour of addressing a friend of the late Mr. Maltravers?”

The young man turned, looking somewhat surprised. “Yes, I was a friend of his. My name is Black—Captain Black. But I’m afraid I’ve come at a bad time. I only just heard the news of his death in the papers.”

“You were staying here recently, were you not, Captain?”

“Yes, I spent Tuesday night here. I’m on my way back to East Africa, and I came down to say goodbye to old Maltravers. Why do you ask? And who are you, anyway?”

We retraced our steps and reached the front door just as the young man was being admitted. Poirot, with his usual effrontery, followed him closely, murmuring to the maid about a cane he had purportedly left behind. Inside the hall, the stranger turned, eyeing us with a certain amount of bewilderment. Poirot did not give him time to speak. “I beg your pardon, Monsieur,” he said with a flourish. “I believe I address the gentleman who was a guest here on Tuesday? My name is Hercule Poirot.” The young man started, his hand going instinctively to his moustache. “How did you know that? Yes, my name is Black—Captain Black. I’ve just come back from East Africa, and I ran down to see Maltravers for a night. I only heard the news of his death this morning in the papers.”

We hastened up the drive after the retreating figure. A glimpse of
a black-robed figure on the terrace at the side of the house, and
our quarry swerved and we after him, so that we were witnesses of
the meeting.

Mrs. Maltravers almost staggered where she stood, and her face
blanched noticeably.

“You,” she gasped. “I thought you were on the sea—on your way to
East Africa?”

“That is very good of you, Captain Black,” said Mrs. Maltravers
with a becoming modesty. “I expect there will be a great deal to
see to.”

“Well, you know I’m your man if you want me. If you’ve anything
difficult to deal with, don’t hesitate to let me know.”

We then moved on, Poirot leading the way.

“Well, Hastings, what did you think of Captain Black? I noticed
you looked at him very closely. Do you think he would be a likely
person to commit a murder?”

“He certainly has a very determined face,” I answered. “A man who
had once made up his mind would be likely to go through with it.”

“Exactly,” Poirot replied. “I was thinking the same myself. But
now we must find out something about this Captain Black.”

We accordingly made inquiries at the village inn. We were told that
the Captain had arrived on Tuesday and stayed the night. He had
gone off again on Wednesday morning.

“That would give him plenty of time to commit a murder,” I
remarked. “But I cannot see that there is any evidence against him.
Still, we can but go on with our inquiries.”

“_Mais oui_,” agreed Poirot. “And now I have a little commission
for you, Hastings. I want you to go to London and find out all you
can about Captain Black. I have a friend at the Colonial Office
who will be able to help you. And I want you to find out if he was
in any way connected with the deceased Mr. Maltravers.”

“And what are you going to do?”

“I shall remain here for the present. I have one or two little
matters to attend to.”

“This gentleman is Captain Black,” said Mrs. Maltravers, turning
to us with some embarrassment. “He was staying here for a night
on Tuesday, and he has just come down again on hearing of our
terrible trouble.”

“Captain Black, I have much pleasure in making your acquaintance,”
replied Poirot, with his usual flourish. “_Au revoir_, Madame!
I have changed my mind—I will not return to town just yet. I must
see Dr. Bernard once more—I think I left my umbrella there.”

We left the house.

“And you think, Poirot, that the Captain’s appearance was a
surprise to her?”

“Decidedly. It was a surprise, but—not an unpleasant one.”

I could not help thinking that it was a very odd kind of coincidence
that brought this young man back to the place just at the very
time when his presence might be most desired.

“There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio,” I murmured,
as we went our way to the village. “The coincidence of the Captain
receiving news that kept him in England on the very day that poor
Maltravers met with such a tragic end!”

“Yes, indeed,” said Poirot dryly. “It is a truly remarkable
coincidence, is it not?”

Mrs. Maltravers was about to answer when she caught sight of us.
The young man too had turned, and was looking at us inquiringly.

“Will you excuse me, Mr. Black? These gentlemen have come from my
late husband’s Insurance Company.”

“I see,” said Captain Black, as he was introduced. “Well, I will
wait inside if you will allow me, and we will talk later.”

“Captain Black, did you say?” asked Poirot.

“Yes, I have been out in Africa for some time, and happened to be
down here for a night on Tuesday last. Sad thing about poor
Maltravers, wasn’t it? I saw the doctor as I came through the
village, and he told me all about it.”

“One moment, Captain Black,” said Poirot. “You knew Mr. Maltravers
well?”

“Oh, fairly well. I had met him once or twice in London, and when
I came down here we had a long talk. He was interested in my tales
of the East, and we got on very well together. He seemed a bit
depressed, I thought, and as if he had some trouble on his mind.”

“He had, indeed,” murmured Poirot. “But we must be getting along.
Good-bye, Captain Black. Good-bye, Mrs. Maltravers.”

And we set off towards the station.

“You seemed very interested in Captain Black, Poirot,” I remarked.

“Yes, he is an interesting young man. But I was more interested in
something else.”

“What was that?”

“In Mrs. Maltravers’ face when she saw him. She was startled,
undeniably. And more—she was afraid.”

“Afraid! Why should she be?”

“Ah, that is what I intend to find out!”

Mrs. Maltravers was visibly moved.

“This is so kind of you, Captain Black. It was really a very sudden
death, and quite a shock. My husband, as you know, had been
indisposed of late.”

“Oh, quite so, quite so. Still, it was a very great shock.”

Poirot had now stepped forward.

“Pardon me, madame, but as we are leaving, may I just ask one
thing? I understand that your late husband’s secretary, Mr. Alfred
Wright, is not at the house at present?”

“No, I sent him to London on some business of my own. I did not
feel equal to it. He will be back this evening.”

“I see. Thank you. Good-bye, then, madame. Good-bye, Captain
Black.”

And we were once more on our way to the station.

“Who is Captain Black, Poirot? Is it possible that he——”

“My dear Hastings, I have already told you that if a man dies of
a hæmorrhage he cannot have been murdered. He may have committed
suicide, it is true, but that would be a very difficult matter.
No, I think we have found a mare’s nest. Still, I should like a
word with Mr. Wright, if he would be so kind as to come and see me
at my rooms this evening.”

“It is very kind of you, Captain Black,” murmured Mrs. Maltravers
faintly.

“But who is Captain Black?” Poirot inquired of me as we walked
rapidly away from the scene of the encounter.

“He is a friend of hers—a very old friend, by the look of it. An
officer in the Merchant Service, perhaps.”

“Well, we must make sure of that. It is worth while looking up the
passenger-list of the ship on which he was to sail. In the meantime,
I must find out more about this young man. Let us inquire at the
village inn.”

A visit to the “Black Bull” provided the necessary information.
Captain Black had arrived on Tuesday morning and had left for
London the next day. He was a cousin of Mrs. Maltravers, and had
spent most of his time at the Manor during his visit.

“_Bien_,” commented Poirot as we walked back to the station. “And
now, Hastings, we will go and see your friend Alfred Wright.”

“My friend?”

“He is a director of the Northern Union, you told me. I will find
out from him what he knows about the financial position of Mr.
Maltravers.”

At that moment they became aware of our presence. Poirot stepped
forward, and with many apologies explained that he had left his
stick in the hall. Rather reluctantly, it seemed to me, Mrs.
Maltravers made the necessary introduction.

“Monsieur Poirot, Captain Black.”

We found the landlord of the “Anchor” in the tap-room. Poirot
ordered two glasses of a local cider and began to converse with
the air of a man who has all the time in the world. It appeared
that Captain Black had indeed stayed there on Tuesday night. He
had arrived in the afternoon and had gone up to the Manor for
dinner, returning shortly after eleven. The landlord spoke of him
with respect. “A fine, seafaring gentleman, sir. Very much shocked
he was to see the news in the papers. He’d only just got back from
town when he heard it.”

We found the Captain in the low-ceilinged parlour of the "Anchor," contemplating a glass of whisky with a somewhat gloomy expression. Poirot, with the easy camaraderie he could assume at will, soon drew him into conversation. It appeared that Captain Black had been an acquaintance of long standing, and had run down to Essex to bid his friend farewell before departing for Africa. He confirmed that he had stayed the night of Tuesday, leaving early the following morning.

"And Mr. Maltravers, was he in good spirits when you saw him?" inquired Poirot.

We found the Captain in the small coffee-room, staring gloomily out of the window. He seemed surprised to see us again, but Poirot’s easy manner soon put him at his ease. Before long, they were deep in a discussion of the African continent, from which the Captain had recently returned. It appeared he had spent several years in the interior, and he spoke of the superstitions of the natives with a certain grim fascination.

“It is a strange world, is it not?” remarked Poirot. “And Mr. Maltravers, did he find your tales of the wild interesting when you visited him on Tuesday?”

Black nodded slowly. “He was a nervous man, Monsieur Poirot. Highly strung. He seemed particularly struck by a story I told of a man who died of sheer fright—seeing what he believed to be a ghost.”

We found Captain Black in the small, low-ceilinged coffee-room of the “Anchor.” He was alone, and looked up with some surprise as we entered. Poirot, with his usual easy grace, soon had the young man talking. It appeared that he had indeed been a guest at the Manor on the Tuesday night, leaving early on Wednesday morning to catch his boat—a journey he had subsequently abandoned upon receiving the news of his legacy.

We found the Captain in the small, low-ceilinged bar-parlour, staring into a glass of whiskey with a look of profound abstraction. He started as Poirot greeted him, but accepted our company with a sort of gruff politeness. Poirot, with his usual dexterity, soon had the conversation turning towards the late Mr. Maltravers. He mentioned the tragedy and his own role as an investigator for the insurance company, watching the Captain’s face for any sign of discomfort as he alluded to the guest who had stayed at the Manor the night before the death.

“Here we establish ourselves until our friend the Captain returns,”
he explained. “You notice that I emphasized the point that we were
returning to London by the first train? Possibly you thought I
meant it. But no—you observed Mrs. Maltravers’ face when she caught
sight of this young Black? She was clearly taken aback, and he—_eh
bien_, he was very devoted, did you not think so? And he was here
on Tuesday night—the day before Mr. Maltravers died. We must
investigate the doings of Captain Black, Hastings.”

In about half an hour we espied our quarry approaching the inn.
Poirot went out and accosted him and presently brought him up to
the room we had engaged.

Poirot offered the Captain a cigarette, which was declined. “You find this part of the country attractive, Captain Black?” he began, settling himself into a chair with precise care. The Captain shrugged his broad shoulders. “Not particularly. I came down to see Maltravers on a matter of business—some East African ventures we were discussing.” “Aha! And he was in good spirits when you saw him on Tuesday?” “He seemed a bit edgy,” Black admitted, leaning back and crossing his legs. “Talked a lot about death and such. He had a theory that one could be frightened to death—literally. He’d been reading some book on the subject, and he even told me a story about a man in India who died because he thought he saw a phantom. It was a weird conversation to have over dinner, I can tell you.”

“A drink, Captain?” Poirot suggested. “The sun, it is over the yardarm, as you say in the Navy—though you are of the Army, I perceive.” Black accepted a whisky and soda, and Poirot skilfully led the conversation toward his previous visit to Marsdon Manor. “You were there on the Tuesday, were you not? Was the poor Mr. Maltravers in good spirits?” The Captain frowned. “He was a bit odd, if you ask me. At dinner he was quiet enough, but later, when we were alone, he started talking in a very queer way. He seemed obsessed with the idea of sudden death. He told me a story about a Chinese merchant who died just because a ‘spirit’ touched him. He was quite worked up about it. To tell you the truth, I thought the poor old chap was a bit ‘touched’ in the upper story.”

“A little glass of something, Captain?” suggested Poirot. “The sun, it is hot for the time of year.”

Captain Black accepted the offer. He seemed a straightforward sort of fellow, if a bit blunt.

“You were a friend of the late Mr. Maltravers?” Poirot inquired, as he poured out the drinks.

“Hardly that. I knew him in town, and he invited me down for a night. Met him at the club, you know. To tell you the truth, I think he wanted to talk to me about East Africa. He had some idea of investing out there, I fancy.”

“He was in good spirits then?”

“Well, he seemed a bit jumpy—nervous, you know. Kept looking over his shoulder. But he was a good host.”

Captain Black appeared somewhat defensive at first, but Poirot’s easy manner and a well-timed offer of refreshment soon loosened his tongue. He had known the Maltravers for some time, it seemed, and had come down to say goodbye before his intended departure for Africa.
“A strange business, Maltravers’ death,” he remarked, leaning back. “The man was a nervous wreck when I saw him on Tuesday. He was obsessed with the idea that he hadn't long to live. He told me a most extraordinary story—or rather, I told him one—about a man in East Africa who had died in exactly the same way—an internal hemorrhage, following a vision of some kind. It’s almost as though he’d been frightened to death by the mere thought of it.”

“A sad business,” said Poirot, as he offered the Captain a cigarette. “A very sad business indeed. To die so suddenly, and so soon after ensuring the future of one’s wife. It is almost—how do you say?—a coincidence too great?” Captain Black took the cigarette, his eyes narrowing slightly. “I suppose it is. I only saw the news in the papers this morning. I was shocked, naturally. Maltravers seemed in the best of health when I spent the night here on Tuesday.” “You stayed the night, then?” Poirot’s tone was one of polite interest. “And you talked, perhaps? A man who knows he is to die often speaks of it.” “Not a word of it,” replied Black. “We talked mostly of East Africa. He was interested in the prospects there. In fact, he seemed quite keen on a scheme I mentioned. He didn't look like a man at death's door to me.”

“I have been telling Captain Black of the mission which brings us
here,” he explained. “You can understand, _monsieur le capitaine_,
that I am anxious to arrive at Mr. Maltravers’ state of mind
immediately before his death, and that at the same time I do not
wish to distress Mrs. Maltravers unduly by asking her painful
questions. Now, you were here just before the occurrence, and can
give us equally valuable information.”

“I’m afraid I didn’t see very much of him,” answered the young
officer, a little stiffly. “I only came on Tuesday afternoon and
went back on Wednesday morning.”

“Exactly. You were then the last person to see him before he went
out with his gun on Wednesday?”

“No, I don’t think so. I left about eleven o’clock. But I did see
him on Tuesday evening, and he seemed then to be in quite good
spirits.”

“He did not mention his health to you?”

“No. He mentioned his losses in the city, but didn’t seem to
consider them very serious.”

“I see. He was not a Christian Scientist, I presume?”

“A what? Good heavens, no! Why on earth should you think that?”

“Mrs. Maltravers mentioned it,” said Poirot mildly.

“Oh, she did, did she?”

A look of surprise crossed Captain Black’s face.

“Now, about that evening?” continued Poirot. “How did you pass
it?”

“Oh, we had a very quiet evening. Just a little music and a chat
after dinner. And then, about nine, Mrs. Maltravers went up to bed,
and her husband and I had a drink together in the library.”

“And what did you talk about?”

“Oh, nothing in particular. He told me a few stories of his early
days in the East. He was in China, you know, for some years.”

“Yes?”

“And then—let me see—oh, yes, we got on to the subject of ghosts.”

“Ghosts?”

“Yes. Maltravers told me a most gruesome story he’d heard out in
the East. It seems there is a particular kind of ghost that haunts
certain houses, and its appearance is always followed by a
hæmorrhage. Very queer, wasn’t it?”

“Very. And what happened after that?”

“Oh, nothing. I went to bed soon after. And I left the house, as
I told you, at eleven the next morning.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Many thanks to you, Captain Black.”

The young man took his departure.

“_Eh bien_, Hastings,” said Poirot. “What do you think of that?”

“It is a most extraordinary story,” I said.

“Is it not? A ghost whose appearance is followed by a hæmorrhage!
_Vraiment_, it is most remarkable.”

“You think he was telling the truth?”

“I am sure of it. But why did Mr. Maltravers tell him that
particular story? And why did Mrs. Maltravers say her husband was
a Christian Scientist? It is a discrepancy, is it not?”

“One of many,” I said. “But what are we going to do now?”

“We are going to have a little dinner,” said Poirot. “And then
we are going back to the Manor.”

“But it will be dark!”

“The better for our purpose, my friend.”

“What is our purpose?”

“I am going to see a ghost!”

“Poirot!”

“Do not be afraid, Hastings. I shall not ask you to see it too.
I have a little plan—a very little plan.”

And with that he would say no more.

“Really, I’m afraid I can’t help you much,” said Black. “I only
spent a night here, you see. I was on my way to catch my boat at
Southampton, when I thought I’d just run down and say good-bye to
my old friend, Maltravers.”

“And how did you find him? In good spirits?”

“Well, no—rather the reverse. He seemed a bit depressed, I thought.
In fact, he told me that he was quite convinced he was going to
die soon.”

“Indeed. He told you that?”

“Yes, and what’s more, he seemed to have some idea that he might
die at any moment.”

“_Tiens!_ How very remarkable.”

“He had had some trouble with his heart or something, I believe.
I didn’t pay much attention, you know. I thought he’d been moping
too much in the house—no life, you know.”

“He did not suggest that he might take his own life?”

“Lord, no!” Captain Black laughed. “He wasn’t that sort of man.”

“You did not happen to see him on the Wednesday morning?”

“No, I left early.”

“I see. Well, many thanks, Captain Black.”

We shook hands and the Captain took his departure.

“And what do you think of Captain Black, Hastings?” asked Poirot.

“A very straightforward, honest young fellow,” I replied with
conviction.

“Really? I was thinking he was a very poor liar.”

“My dear Poirot, what on earth makes you say that?”

“Because he has a very bad memory, _mon ami_. He told us just now
that he only saw Maltravers on Tuesday evening—and that he thought
he had been moping too much in the house—no life. Yet when he was
at the Manor just now he said to Mrs. Maltravers: ‘I see he’s
still at his old game of shooting rooks!’ Now, how did he know
that? He must have seen him at it, and he couldn’t have seen him
on Tuesday, because it was pouring with rain all day.”

“He might have seen him on Wednesday morning,” I suggested.

“He told us he left early.”

“How early?”

“The first train is at 7.30. It is possible, of course. But there
is another point. Why did he cancel his passage?”

“He told us. His uncle died and left him some money.”

“_Précisément!_ The uncle who dies so opportunely! I should like
to see that uncle’s death in the _Times_—and I should like to know
how much he left his nephew. No, no, Hastings, it will not do.
Captain Black is lying—and lying very badly. And why is he lying?
Because he and Mrs. Maltravers are—what do you call it?—in
collusion? Perhaps.”

I was about to protest when there came a sharp knock at the door.
A tall, thin man stood there, whom I recognized at once as the
director of the Northern Union.

“Ah, Alfred Wright!” cried Poirot. “What a surprise!”

Captain Black, though still slightly suspicious, gave us all the
information we required. He had arrived at the Manor on Tuesday
night, and had left on Wednesday morning. He had seen Mr. Maltravers
but briefly, and had not found him changed in any way. He said
nothing to us of any change in his plans, but after lunch had
made an appointment with his lawyers and had spent the night in
London.

Poirot thanked him and we took our leave.

“You have noticed something, I can see,” I remarked, when we were
safely on our way back to London.

“_Certainement!_” He looked at me with some amusement. “A most
interesting point, my friend. Captain Black is a very observant
young man.”

“Then you don’t think he is the murderer?”

“The murderer? My dear Hastings, I have never said there was a
murderer. But there is a mystery, and I intend to get to the bottom
of it. Now, as I told you, I am going to London to see our friend
Alfred Wright. He may be able to throw some light on the subject.”

“I don’t know that I have much to tell,” said the Captain, somewhat
surprised. “The house was full of guests, it being a shooting party,
and I was there but one night. I had just come down to say
good-bye. I should think you would find it far more useful to
interrogate some of the other guests—Captain and Mrs. Marvell, and
a Mr. and Mrs. Smith. There were quite a number of people there.”

Poirot’s eyes widened, and I could see that he was as much taken
aback as I was.

“A large party?”

“Oh, yes. There were six or seven people there, at least.”

“Indeed. I had no idea. Then why did Mrs. Maltravers say her
husband had been alone when he died?”

“I don’t think she did,” said Captain Black, looking rather
puzzled. “She only said she had not seen him since lunch.”

Poirot sat silent for a minute or two. Then he began to ask
questions of Captain Black as to his impressions of Mr. Maltravers’
mental state on that Tuesday evening. Captain Black was emphatic
on one point—namely, that he had never seen a man in better
spirits. Mr. Maltravers had been the life and soul of the party,
and apparently had not a care in the world.

“And did he seem to have any premonition of his death?”

“None whatever. On the contrary, he was full of plans for the
future.”

“_Tiens!_ That is very strange. And you did not notice anything
else that was at all—remarkable?”

Captain Black hesitated.

“Well, there was one thing. I don’t suppose it has anything to do
with it, but it was rather a curious coincidence. We were playing
at some game or other in the evening—one of those things where you
have to go out of the room and people ask you questions. I was
sitting next to Mr. Maltravers, and I happened to tell him a story
I had heard about a man who was very much in the same position
as he was. It was a story about a man in East Africa who was
supposed to have died of a hæmorrhage, but who had really been
murdered by his wife. She had managed to—well, I won’t go into
all the details, but it was a very ingenious story.”

“And what did Mr. Maltravers say?”

“He didn’t say anything. He just sat there looking—well, I can’t
describe it, but he looked as though he had seen a ghost. It was
very odd. Of course, it was only a story, but it seemed to have
a most extraordinary effect upon him. I’m afraid I didn’t think
much about it at the time.”

Poirot leaned forward, his eyes shining.

“And this story—can you remember it? It might be of the utmost
importance.”

Captain Black shook his head.

“I’m afraid I can’t. It was just a yarn I’d heard—something about
a man who was killed by a woman who managed to make it look like
a natural death.”

“And you told this story to Mr. Maltravers on the very night before
he died?”

“Yes, on the Tuesday evening.”

“_Merci_, monsieur. You have given me much to think about.”

When Captain Black had left us, Poirot turned to me with a look of
triumph.

“You see, Hastings? The plot thickens. We have a beautiful widow,
a devoted admirer, a large insurance policy, and a mysterious
story told on the eve of the tragedy. It is all very interesting.”

“But what does it mean?” I asked.

“That is what we have to find out. And now, my friend, I think we
will pay another visit to Marsdon Manor.”

“I’ll do anything I can,” Captain Black responded heartily. “But
I don’t know anything about it. I wasn’t even in the house. I was
putting up here.”

“I see. And had you seen Mr. Maltravers recently?”

“I hadn’t seen him for years. I knew him in the East, you know.
But we’d lost touch with each other.”

“And you were down here on Tuesday?”

“Yes, I came down for the night. I wanted to see him about a
matter of business. But I didn’t see him.”

“How was that?”

“Well, I’d better tell you the whole story. I’d been in town for
a few days, and I thought I’d run down and see Maltravers. I’d heard
of him from a man in the club. So I came down on the Tuesday and
put up here. I went up to the house in the evening, and as I was
walking up the drive I met Mrs. Maltravers. She told me her husband
was away, and wouldn’t be back until the following morning. So
I went back to the inn and spent the night, and then I thought it
wasn’t worth while staying on, so I took the first train back to
London.”

“I see. Then you didn’t see Mr. Maltravers at all?”

“No.”

“And what was this business you wanted to see him about?”

Captain Black hesitated.

“It was—well, a private matter.”

“I see,” said Poirot, with a smile. “Well, I think that is all.”

Captain Black rose and took his leave.

“A very interesting young man,” said Poirot, as the door closed
behind him. “Now, Hastings, for a little more investigation. We
will go back to the Manor.”

“But we have only just come from there!”

“Wait, my friend. I wish to see the gardener who was sweeping
leaves.”

We found the man without difficulty. Poirot went up to him.

“A little question, my friend. On the night that this gentleman—the
one who has just passed—was here, did you see him?”

“No, sir, I can’t say I did. I was away on Tuesday, it being my
day off.”

“_Dommage!_ But perhaps you can tell me who was in the house that
night?”

“Only the mistress and the servants, sir, as far as I know. Mr.
Maltravers was away in London.”

“I see. And you have no idea what time he returned on Wednesday?”

“He came by the 12:15, sir. I saw him myself.”

“I thank you. Now we will go and see the parlourmaid.”

The parlourmaid was even more communicative.

“Mr. Maltravers came back on Wednesday morning, sir. He seemed
very much upset—quite unlike himself. He went into his study and
stayed there all the afternoon. Mrs. Maltravers went out after
lunch, as she told you. About four o’clock the master came out of
his study and went into the garden. He had his little rifle with
him. A few minutes later we heard a shot, and then another. Then
one of the under-gardeners came running to the house to say he’d
found the master dead.”

“I see. And you say he was very much upset when he came back from
London?”

“Yes, sir, he looked quite ill. He didn’t even have any lunch.”

“Thank you. That will be all.”

As we walked away, Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? There is something here that is not quite
right. Mrs. Maltravers tells us her husband had a premonition of
death, and yet he goes and insures his life for fifty thousand
pounds! Captain Black says he didn’t see Mr. Maltravers on Tuesday
night, and yet the gardener says Mr. Maltravers was away in London!
Now, why should Captain Black say he didn’t see him if he did? And
why should Mrs. Maltravers say her husband was away if he wasn’t?
There is something very fishy about all this.”

“You think they were in it together?” I suggested.

“It is possible. But we must not jump to conclusions. We must
investigate further.”

We returned to the Anchor Inn and had some tea. Afterwards Poirot
suggested a stroll. We wandered through the village and presently
found ourselves near the church. It was a beautiful old building,
and we went inside.

As we were coming out, we met a man whom I recognized as Alfred
Wright, the director of the Northern Union Insurance Company. He
seemed surprised to see us.

“Hullo, Poirot!” he exclaimed. “What are you doing here? I didn’t
know you were on this case.”

“I am,” said Poirot. “The Company asked me to investigate.”

“Well, you won’t find much, I’m afraid. It’s a clear case of
suicide, if you ask me. Maltravers was on the verge of bankruptcy,
and he knew it. He insured his life for fifty thousand pounds and
then blew his brains out.”

“But the doctor says he died of a hæmorrhage,” I put in.

“Doctor!” Wright laughed scornfully. “What do these country
doctors know? He probably didn’t even look at the body properly.
I tell you, it’s suicide.”

“Perhaps you are right,” said Poirot. “But I should like to be
