sure. By the way, Wright, did you know Maltravers well?”

“Oh, I knew him in business, of course. But I didn’t know him
personally. He was a bit of a mystery, you know. Nobody seemed to
know much about him.”

“I see. Well, we must be getting back to the inn. Good-bye,
Wright.”

As we walked away, Poirot was silent for a time. Then he said:

“You know, Hastings, there is one thing that bothers me. Why should
Maltravers have chosen to die in just that way? If he wanted to
commit suicide, why didn’t he use a more certain method? A rook
rifle is not a very reliable weapon for such a purpose.”

“Perhaps he didn’t want it to look like suicide,” I suggested.
“Perhaps he wanted his wife to get the insurance money.”

“That is possible, of course. But even so, it seems a very clumsy
way of doing it. And then there is the question of the blood on
his lips. That doesn’t fit in with a gunshot wound.”

“Unless he shot himself through the mouth,” I said.

“Even then, the doctor would have seen it. No, there is something
here that we haven’t got to the bottom of yet.”

We spent the evening at the inn, and Poirot was very quiet. He
sat in his chair with his eyes closed, and I knew he was thinking.
Suddenly he sat up.

“Hastings! I have it! I know how it was done!”

“How?” I asked eagerly.

“But I must be sure. We will go back to the Manor tomorrow morning,
and then I will tell you.”

The next morning we were back at Marsdon Manor. Mrs. Maltravers
received us in the morning-room. She looked even more beautiful
than before, but she was evidently very nervous.

“I hope you have some good news for me, Monsieur Poirot,” she said.
“The suspense is very trying.”

“I think I can promise you that the matter will be settled today,
madame,” said Poirot gravely. “But first I should like to ask you
a few more questions.”

“Of course. Anything I can tell you.”

“When your husband returned from London on Wednesday morning, did
he tell you anything about his trip?”

“No. He seemed very much upset, as I told you. He wouldn’t talk
about it.”

“I see. And you say he went into his study and stayed there all
the afternoon?”

“Yes.”

“And you were out all the afternoon?”

“Yes, I went down to the village, as I told you.”

“I see. Now, madame, I want you to tell me the truth. Did you see
Captain Black on Tuesday night?”

Mrs. Maltravers started, and her face went pale.

“I—I don’t know what you mean.”

“Come, madame, it is no use denying it. We know that Captain Black
was here on Tuesday night, and that you saw him. Why did you tell
us your husband was away?”

Mrs. Maltravers burst into tears.

“It’s true,” she sobbed. “He was here. But I didn’t want my husband
to know. He was very jealous, you see. And Captain Black—well, he
and I were very old friends. There was nothing wrong, I assure
you. But I knew my husband wouldn’t understand.”

“I see. And where was your husband on Tuesday night?”

“He was in London, as I told you. He went up on Monday and didn’t
come back until Wednesday morning.”

“I see. Now, madame, one more question. Did your husband have any
enemies?”

“Enemies? No, I don’t think so. Why do you ask?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “I don’t think your husband committed
suicide. I think he was murdered.”

Mrs. Maltravers gave a little cry and sank back in her chair.

“Murdered! But who—who could have murdered him?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to find out.”

He turned to me.

“Hastings, will you go and find Dr. Bernard and ask him to come
here at once? And also Mr. Wright, if you can find him.”

I did as I was told, and in about half an hour they were both there.
Poirot was waiting for them in the morning-room.

“Now, gentlemen,” he said, “I have called you here because I believe
I have discovered the truth about Mr. Maltravers’ death. Dr.
Bernard, you said that the cause of death was a hæmorrhage,
probably caused by a gastric ulcer. Mr. Wright, you said it was
suicide. You were both wrong. Mr. Maltravers was murdered.”

There was a moment of stunned silence. Then Dr. Bernard spoke.

“Murdered! But how? There was no sign of any wound.”

“That is where you are wrong, doctor,” said Poirot. “There was a
wound, but it was a very small one. So small that you didn't notice
it.”

“But where?”

“In the roof of the mouth,” said Poirot. “Mr. Maltravers was shot
through the mouth with his own rook rifle.”

“But that would be suicide!” cried Wright.

“Not necessarily,” said Poirot. “It could have been done by someone
else. Someone who knew about his condition—someone who knew that
he was expecting a hæmorrhage. Someone who could make it look like
a natural death.”

“But who?” asked Mrs. Maltravers, her voice trembling.

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am about to show you.”

He went to the door and called the parlourmaid.

“Will you ask Captain Black to come in, please? I believe he is
waiting in the hall.”

Captain Black entered the room, looking rather puzzled.

“You wanted to see me, Monsieur Poirot?”

“Yes, Captain Black. I wanted to ask you one more question. When
you were in the East, did you ever come across a drug called—well,
let us call it ‘the Red Death’?”

Captain Black’s face went white.

“I—I don’t know what you’re talking about.”

“I think you do,” said Poirot. “It is a drug that causes a sudden
and violent hæmorrhage. It is very difficult to detect, but it
leaves a very characteristic stain on the lips. The kind of stain
that Dr. Bernard saw on Mr. Maltravers’ lips.”

“But—but I didn’t give it to him!” cried Captain Black. “I didn’t
even see him!”

“I know you didn’t,” said Poirot. “But someone else did. Someone
who had access to your luggage while you were staying at the Anchor
Inn. Someone who knew that you had brought this drug back from the
East with you.”

“But who?”

Poirot turned to Alfred Wright.

“Mr. Wright, you are a director of the Northern Union Insurance
Company. You knew that Mr. Maltravers had insured his life for fifty
thousand pounds. You also knew that he was on the verge of
bankruptcy. You saw a chance to make a lot of money for your
company—and perhaps for yourself as well. You knew that if Mr.
Maltravers died of a natural cause within a year, the company would
have to pay out. But if he committed suicide, they wouldn't. So
you decided to murder him and make it look like suicide.”

“That’s a lie!” cried Wright. “I didn't even know Maltravers!”

“Oh, yes you did,” said Poirot. “You knew him very well. You were
the man who suggested that he should insure his life. You were the
man who told him that he was going to die soon. You played on his
fears until he was ready to believe anything. And then, on
Wednesday afternoon, you went to see him. You found him in his
study, and you gave him a drink—a drink that you had spiked with
the drug you had stolen from Captain Black’s luggage. Then you took
him out into the garden and staged the whole thing. You even fired
the shots with the rook rifle to make it look like he’d been
shooting rooks. But you made one mistake. You didn’t realize that
the drug would cause such a violent hæmorrhage. You thought it
would look like a natural death. But when you saw the blood on his
lips, you realized that the doctor might suspect something. So
you tried to convince us all that it was suicide.”

Wright was cowering in his chair, his face a mask of terror.

“It’s not true!” he whimpered. “You can't prove anything!”

“I think I can,” said Poirot. “You see, when you were in Captain
Black’s room at the inn, you accidentally dropped something. A
small pill-box with the name of a London chemist on it. I found
it this morning. And I think that when the police check with that
chemist, they will find that you purchased some of this drug quite
recently.”

Wright gave a sudden cry and tried to bolt for the door, but I was
too quick for him. I tackled him and held him until the police
arrived.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we were sitting in the train on our way
back to London. “That was a very clever piece of work. How did you
know it was Wright?”

“It was the discrepancy, Hastings. The discrepancy I mentioned
yesterday. You see, Mrs. Maltravers said her husband had a
premonition of death. But why should a man who has a premonition
of death go and insure his life for such a large sum? It doesn't
make sense. Unless someone else suggested it to him. Someone who
had an interest in his death. And when I saw Wright at the church,
I realized that he was the man. He was so anxious to prove that
it was suicide. And then there was the drug. I knew that Captain
Black had been in the East, and it was a simple matter to search
his room and find the drug. After that, it was only a matter of
putting the pieces together.”

“And the pill-box?” I asked. “Did you really find it?”

Poirot smiled.

“No, Hastings. That was a little bluff. But it worked, did it not?
_L’heureux hasard_, as we say in France.”

I laughed.

“You’re a clever devil, Poirot!”

“No, my friend. I am only Hercule Poirot. And now, I think I will
have a little sleep. It has been a very tiring day.”

“I’ll do anything I can to help you, I’m sure,” replied the young
soldier; “but I’m afraid I didn’t notice anything out of the
ordinary. You see, although Maltravers was an old friend of my
people’s, I didn’t know him very well myself.”

“You came down—when?”

“Tuesday afternoon—for the night. I went back to town Wednesday
morning.”

“And what was his manner—at dinner on Tuesday night?”

“Rather depressed, I should have said. But Mrs. Maltravers tells
me he was in the habit of being depressed, was he not?”

“So it seems. Did he say anything to you on the subject of his
death?”

“No—well, yes. Now I come to think of it, he did say something
rather curious. We were sitting in the library after dinner, and
he had been silent for some time. Then he suddenly said: ‘I
suppose, Black, you’ve seen some pretty queer things out in Africa?
Death, and all that?’ I told him I had seen a good deal of it.
‘There was one fellow,’ I said, ‘who was always in a funk of it.
He used to say that when his time came he’d come back and show us.’
‘And did he?’ asked Maltravers, quite seriously. ‘Well,’ I said,
‘it’s a queer thing, but he did!’ I could see Maltravers was
fearfully interested. He made me tell him all about it—how the
fellow had appeared, and so on. He seemed quite to brood over it.”

“That is very interesting,” said Poirot. “And when did you say
good-bye to him?”

“At the station. He drove me down on Wednesday morning.”

“What time was the train?”

“Ten-twenty.”

“And you have not seen him since?”

“Not till I saw the news of his death in the paper.”

“Thank you, Captain Black. You have been most kind.”

Captain Black took his leave, and Poirot turned to me with a
puzzled frown.

“That is very interesting,” he said again. “It seems that Mr.
Maltravers was much occupied with the idea of death. But why—why
did he ask such a question of a man he hardly knew? It is not
natural, Hastings.”

“I don’t see that,” I argued. “If he were a man of a morbid turn of
mind, it would be the very thing he would do.”

“Perhaps you are right. But, all the same, I am not satisfied.”

“What are you going to do now?”

“I shall go back to the Manor and see Mrs. Maltravers once more.”

“Tuesday afternoon, from town. I stayed over the night, and we
didn’t go into his affairs at all. He seemed just as usual—a
bit quiet, perhaps, but that was all. And he was full of his
intentions of going into the city on Wednesday morning, but changed
his mind at the last minute and stayed at home. I left after
breakfast.”

“I see,” said Poirot, “a very ordinary visit. And yet you say he
seemed a little quiet. Can you account for that at all?”

Captain Black hesitated.

“Well,” he said at last, “I believe he was a little worried about
money matters. I don’t know that for a fact, but I had a sort of
idea. He seemed a little preoccupied, as though he had something
on his mind.”

“I see,” said Poirot again. “And you didn’t notice any sign of
illness?”

“None at all.”

Poirot sat for a few minutes in silence. Then he said:

“Thank you, Captain Black. You have been most helpful.”

When the young soldier had left the room, Poirot turned to me.

“What do you think of that, Hastings?”

“It seems to me to confirm the theory of suicide,” I said.

“Suicide? You still think that?”

“Well, what else could it be?”

“Murder,” said Poirot quietly.

“Murder! But how? There was no sign of violence.”

“Exactly. That is the cleverness of it. But I am convinced that
Maltravers was murdered.”

“By whom?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we have to find out. But I have a
shrewd idea.”

“You mean—the wife?”

“Or her lover. Or both of them. We must not forget that Captain
Black was here on Tuesday night. And he is very devoted to Mrs.
Maltravers.”

“But the doctor’s evidence?”

“Dr. Bernard is an old fool,” said Poirot shortly. “He saw what
he expected to see. He did not look for anything else. But we,
Hastings, we must look for everything. And first of all we must
look for the weapon.”

“The weapon? But there was no weapon.”

“There is always a weapon,” said Poirot. “And in this case it is
a very peculiar one. Come, we will go back to the Manor.”

We found Mrs. Maltravers in the garden. She looked surprised to
see us.

“I thought you had gone,” she said.

“We missed our train,” said Poirot easily. “And as we had a little
time to spare, I thought I would like to have another look at the
spot where your husband was found.”

Mrs. Maltravers led the way to the plantation. It was a lonely
spot, some distance from the house.

“It was just here,” she said, pointing to a patch of long grass.

Poirot knelt down and began to examine the ground. Presently he
gave a little cry of triumph.

“See, Hastings!”

He held up a small, dark object. It was a broken piece of a
hypodermic needle.

“Aha!” said Poirot. “I thought as much. Now we have the weapon.
Mr. Maltravers was not killed by a gastric ulcer. He was killed
by a lethal injection of some powerful poison.”

Mrs. Maltravers gave a piercing scream and fell fainting to the
ground.

“I came down on Tuesday morning,” replied Captain Black. “I went
to London and did some shopping and saw some old friends, then
returned by an early train on Wednesday morning, intending to
catch the mid-day boat for East Africa. But I had a wire from my
lawyers which changed my plans. So I took the afternoon train
straight back here. When I arrived, it was to find the place in
a state of chaos, and poor Maltravers dead.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And as to Mr. Maltravers’ manner on the
Tuesday?”

“He seemed all right—just a bit quiet, you know. He mentioned that
the insurance people were making a lot of trouble about his policy,
and that he’d have to go and see them in London.”

“That would be Alfred Wright, I suppose,” I interposed. “He’s the
manager of the Northern Union.”

“No doubt,” said Captain Black. “But Maltravers didn’t seem
particularly worried. He was more interested in his garden, I
think.”

“Tuesday afternoon, and left again on Wednesday morning.”

“What was Mr. Maltravers like that evening?”

“Oh, quite normal. I didn’t notice anything special about him.
We sat and talked in the smoking-room after dinner, and he told
me some rather good stories—he’d been a bit of a traveller in his
time.”

“He was quite cheerful, then?”

“Oh, yes.”

“And you noticed no sign of that—how do you say—premonition of his?”

“I can’t say I did. To tell you the truth, I’d no idea he had
anything of the sort.”

“He didn’t mention his health, for instance?”

“No. He said he’d never felt better in his life.”

“Indeed. That is very interesting.”

Poirot’s eyes had a far-away look in them.

“Now, about those stories he told you? Can you remember any of
them?”

“Oh, they were just ordinary stories. One was about a man who
lived in a haunted house. It was rather a creepy story, but I
don’t suppose it would interest you.”

“On the contrary, I am immensely interested in ghosts. Do you
remember the details?”

“Well, not all of them. But it was something about a man who saw
a ghost in his bedroom every night, and it turned out to be his
own reflection in a mirror that had been moved.”

“_Tiens_! That is very curious. And did Mr. Maltravers seem to
believe in ghosts himself?”

“He said he didn’t, but he told the story as if it were true.”

“And was that the only story he told you?”

“No, there were one or two others. One was about a man who was
murdered in a very ingenious way—but I forget the details of that
one.”

“A pity,” said Poirot. “I should have liked to hear that one.
However, I must not detain you any longer. Many thanks for your
kindness.”

“Tuesday morning. I stayed for the night and left after lunch the
next day. Of course, the news of the tragedy came as a great blow.”

“Exactly. You were in the house on Wednesday morning. Did you see
nothing, hear nothing, that was at all unusual?”

“Nothing whatever.”

“Mr. Maltravers was in his usual health?”

“Seemed as right as a trivet.”

“He did not mention that he had had a previous hæmorrhage?”

“Not a word.”

“And you were with him—when?”

“From breakfast till about half-past twelve. Then I went for a
stroll by myself, and we met at lunch.”

“And after lunch?”

“I went up to the station. He said he was going to potter about
with his gun. I must say he seemed a bit down in the mouth at
lunch, but I thought it was just the weather—it was a beastly
day.”

“What did you talk about at lunch?”

“Oh, nothing in particular. I was telling him about a chap I knew
in India who had been cursed by a Brahmin.”

“Aha!” Poirot’s face lit up. “Tell me about that.”

Captain Black looked surprised.

“Oh, it wasn’t much of a story. This fellow had lived with a girl,
and then when he was going to marry some one else the girl’s father
cursed him—said that before the new moon he would be dead, and
that he would die of a bleeding mouth. The fellow actually did
die—died of a hæmorrhage! Curious coincidence, wasn’t it? I
remember Maltravers was tremendously interested in the story.”

“I bet he was!” cried Poirot. “And he died on Wednesday. When is
the new moon, Hastings?”

“To-morrow,” I replied.

“_Mon Dieu!_” said Poirot. “This is most interesting.”

He rose and bowed to the Captain.

“A thousand thanks, _monsieur_. You have been of the greatest
assistance to me. I will not detain you any longer.”

The Captain withdrew. I turned to Poirot.

“What on earth is all this about? You don’t mean to say you believe
in that Brahmin’s curse?”

“My friend, I believe in nothing that is not strictly logical.
But let us consider the facts. On Tuesday night this story is
told. On Wednesday Mr. Maltravers dies—of a bleeding mouth! Is
it possible that he was so much impressed that the thing actually
happened? We have heard of such cases of ‘suggestion.’ But no,
that will not do. For, as I have already told you, there was a
slight discrepancy. You noticed it? No? But I will tell it to you.
The blood was on the _lips_ of the dead man. Now a hæmorrhage from
a gastric ulcer would not show itself in that way. The blood would
be swallowed. There might be a little—but the lips would not be
saturated. No, that blood came from the _outside_. Now, how could
it have got there? Only in one way. It was put there!”

“But why?” I cried.

“To make the thing appear a death from hæmorrhage. But, as we have
seen, the blood must have been put there _after_ death. Therefore,
Mr. Maltravers did not die of a hæmorrhage. He died—of what?
And who put the blood on his lips? Not the doctor—for he was not
called until the man was dead. Then it was either the person who
found him, or some one who saw him after he was dead. Now, who
found him?”

“One of the gardeners, I think Mrs. Maltravers said.”

“Quite so. But it might have been Mrs. Maltravers herself. Suppose
she found him—dead? Suppose she had some reason for wanting it to
be thought that he had died of a hæmorrhage?”

“But what reason?”

“The fifty thousand pounds insurance! Remember, if he committed
suicide, the money is lost. But if he died of a hæmorrhage—well,
that is a different matter. Now, we must find out how he died.
And there I confess I am at a loss. There were no signs of
poisoning, and the doctor is quite sure it was not a case of
shooting. So how did he die?”

“Could it have been some very subtle poison?”

“I have thought of that. But it seems unlikely. Now, I have a plan.
It is a very little plan, and I do not know if it will succeed,
but we can but try. We will go back to the Manor.”

Mrs. Maltravers was in the drawing-room. She looked surprised at
seeing us again.

“I must apologize, madame,” said Poirot, “but I have just had a
telegram from my friend, Mr. Alfred Wright, of the Northern Union
Company. He is coming down here this evening, and I should be so
much obliged if you would allow us the use of a room for a small
meeting. Also, would it be possible for you to be present?”

“Certainly, if you wish it.”

“I thank you, madame. And there are two other people I should like
to be present. One is Dr. Bernard, and the other is Captain
Black.”

Mrs. Maltravers looked slightly troubled.

“Of course, if you wish it,” she murmured.

“Then at nine o’clock this evening, if that will suit you?”

“Oh, quite.”

“I thank you, madame.”

We spent the afternoon making several inquiries in the village.
Poirot seemed particularly interested in the local chemist’s shop.
I could not imagine what he was driving at, but I have long ago
learned that it is useless to ask him questions.

At nine o’clock we were all assembled in the morning-room at the
Manor. Mrs. Maltravers, looking very pale and beautiful in her
black dress, sat in a large armchair. Dr. Bernard and Captain
Black were also there, the latter looking somewhat uncomfortable.
And, finally, there was Mr. Alfred Wright, a tall, thin man with
a very sharp nose and a general air of being much more alert than
the others.

Poirot rose and took his place at the head of the table.

“Ladies and gentlemen,” he began, “I have asked you all to meet
me here to-night because I have come to a very strange conclusion.
I was sent here to investigate the death of Mr. Maltravers. At
first it seemed a very simple case. But as I went on, I found
several things that were very difficult to explain. And finally,
I realized that Mr. Maltravers did not die a natural death.”

There was a general stir of surprise. Mrs. Maltravers gasped, and
Dr. Bernard broke in:

“My dear sir, this is preposterous! I examined the body myself——”

“And found blood on the lips,” finished Poirot. “But that blood,
doctor, was put there _after_ death!”

“What!” cried the doctor. “Who by?”

“That is what I am going to tell you,” said Poirot. “But first,
let us see how Mr. Maltravers died. He did not die of a hæmorrhage.
He did not die of poison. He did not die of a bullet wound. How,
then, did he die? I will tell you. He died of _fright_!”

“Fright?” I exclaimed.

“Yes, fright. Now, let us go back to Tuesday night. Captain Black
tells a story of a man who was cursed and died of a bleeding
mouth. Mr. Maltravers is much impressed. He is already in a state
of great nervous tension. He is on the verge of bankruptcy. He
has just insured his life for a large sum. He sees a way out. If
he can make his death appear to be a natural one, his wife will
be provided for. He decides to die of the ‘curse’! He knows that
if he can produce the appearance of a hæmorrhage, no one will
suspect the truth. But how to produce that appearance? He thinks
and thinks. And then he remembers something. He remembers that
he has a little rook rifle. He goes out into the grounds. He
fires two shots—to make it appear that he has been shooting rooks.
And then—he sees something!”

Poirot paused. The room was deathly still.

“He sees something that terrifies him. He sees a figure—a tall,
dark figure—standing among the trees. The figure points a finger
at him. And in a voice that seems to come from the grave, it
cites the curse! ‘Before the new moon, thou shalt die! And thou
shalt die of a bleeding mouth!’”

Mrs. Maltravers gave a little cry and hid her face in her hands.

“Mr. Maltravers is frozen with terror,” continued Poirot. “He
tries to speak, but no words will come. And then, suddenly, he
falls to the ground—dead! The shock has been too much for his
weak heart. He has died of fright!”

“But the blood?” I asked. “You said the blood was put there
afterwards.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “The person who had played the part of
the ‘ghost’—the person who had intended to frighten him, but
certainly not to kill him—was horrified at what had happened.
They saw that their plan had succeeded only too well. But they
also saw that if it were known that Mr. Maltravers had died of
fright, the insurance money might be lost. So they quickly
obtained some blood—perhaps from a bird that had been shot—and
smeared it on the dead man’s lips. Then they stole away,
intending to come back later and ‘discover’ the body. But, as
it happened, one of the gardeners found it first.”

“And who was this person?” asked Mr. Wright, his sharp nose
quivering with excitement.

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am now going to reveal. But first,
I must tell you of a little discovery I made this afternoon. In
the local chemist’s shop, I found that a certain person had
purchased a large quantity of—phosphorus!”

“Phosphorus!” I cried. “What for?”

“To make the ‘ghost’s’ face and hands shine in the dark, of course!”
said Poirot. “And now, I will ask that person to stand up!”

There was a moment of intense silence. Then, slowly, one of the
people in the room rose to their feet. It was—Alfred Wright!

“Yes,” he said, his voice trembling. “I did it! But I didn’t mean
to kill him! I only wanted to frighten him—to make him think he
was going to die, so that he would confess to the frauds he had
been committing against the Company! I never dreamed it would
end like this!”

“So,” said Poirot, “it was you, the director of the Insurance
Company, who played the ghost! It is a strange world, my friends,
a very strange world!”

He turned to Mrs. Maltravers.

“Madame, I have the honour to inform you that your claim will be
paid in full. The Northern Union Company cannot refuse to pay
when one of its own directors was responsible for the death!”

And with a low bow, Hercule Poirot led the way out of the room.

“But Poirot,” I said, as we walked back to the inn, “how did you
know it was Wright? And what about the blood?”

“My friend,” said Poirot, “it was quite simple. Who had the
greatest interest in proving that Maltravers was a fraud? The
Insurance Company, of course. And Wright was the only one who
knew all the facts. As for the blood—well, I must confess that
that was a little ‘suggestion’ of my own! There was no blood on
the lips, Hastings. But I knew that if I said there was, the
guilty person would be sure to betray himself!”

“You old fox!” I said.

Poirot smiled.

“It is the ‘little grey cells’, my friend,” he said. “The ‘little
grey cells’!”

“Tuesday afternoon. I went up to town early Wednesday morning, as
my boat sailed from Tilbury about twelve o’clock. But some news I
got made me alter my plans, as I dare say you heard me explain to
Mrs. Maltravers.”

“You were returning to East Africa, I understand?”

“Yes. I’ve been out there ever since the War—a great country.”

“Exactly. Now what was the talk about at dinner on Tuesday night?”

“Oh, I don’t know. This and that. There was some talk of
blood-poisoning, I remember. A man out there had died of it.”

“How did he get it?”

“Oh, a very simple thing. The man was in the habit of sucking his
pen when he was writing, and one day he must have got a bit of the
metal on his tongue or something. At any rate, he died in about
twenty-four hours.”

“I see. That was interesting.”

“Yes, I told Maltravers about it. He seemed particularly interested.
Is there anything else?”

“I don’t think so. I thank you very much.”

“Oh, that’s all right. Glad to have been of any use.”

Captain Black went out, and Poirot turned to me.

“What do you think of that, Hastings?”

“A very pleasant young fellow,” I said.

“I am not talking about his character, but about what he told us.
You did not see the significance of it? No, I see that you did not.
And yet it was plain enough. Now, I have one more inquiry to make.”

“Where?”

“At the village chemist’s.”

I followed him, somewhat mystified. Poirot’s next proceeding was
even more mystifying. Having first ascertained that the chemist
did a little photography, he requested to be supplied with a
particular kind of chemical. The chemist had not got it in stock,
but promised to get it by the following day.

“That will do,” said Poirot. “I will call for it then.”

“But we are going back to London!” I uttered.

“No, no, my friend. I have changed my mind. We stay at the Anchor
Inn.”

“But what did you want that chemical for?”

“A little experiment, Hastings. A little experiment. And now for
the last and most important of my inquiries. I am going to the
Manor.”

“To see Mrs. Maltravers?”

“No, to see the parlourmaid.”

He was as good as his word. He found the girl at the back door of
the house. A very few minutes sufficed for his questions. Then we
returned to the Inn.

“I have much to think about,” he explained, “and for that, as you
know, silence is necessary. Also a little game of Patience. It
calms the nerves and lets the little grey cells do their work.”

I took the hint and left him. I myself was not a little puzzled.
What could the parlourmaid have told him? What was the meaning of
this chemical? What——but it was no use. I must wait.

Dinner was a somewhat silent meal. Poirot was still deep in thought.
But after the meal his mood changed. He became unusually loquacious,
and told me many of his early experiences in the Belgian police
force. It was not until the following morning that he referred to
the case.

“_Eh bien_, Hastings,” he said, as he sipped his coffee. “I have
thought. I have arranged. This morning we will have a little
theatrical performance. I have already sent a note to Mrs.
Maltravers, to Dr. Bernard, and to Captain Black, and to my friend
Alfred Wright, asking them to be present at the Manor at eleven
o’clock.”

“What are you going to do?”

“I am going to reconstruct the crime.”

“Then it _was_ a crime?”

“We shall see. Let us go.”

On our arrival at the Manor we were shown into the drawing-room.
The four people we had come to see were already there. Mrs.
Maltravers, looking more beautiful than ever in her widow’s weeds,
was sitting on a sofa. Captain Black was standing behind her. Dr.
Bernard was by the window, and Alfred Wright, a thin, nervous-looking
man, was fidgeting with his hands.

Poirot bowed to them all.

“I thank you for coming,” he said. “I have a few words to say to
you. You all know that I have been investigating the death of Mr.
Maltravers on behalf of the Northern Union Insurance Company. At
first I was inclined to think that it was a case of suicide. But
I have changed my mind. I am now convinced that it was a case of
murder.”

A simultaneous cry went up from his audience.

“Murder!” cried Mrs. Maltravers. “But who——”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to show you. But first I
must ask you all to come with me to the spot where the body was
found.”

He led the way out of the house and across the lawn to the little
plantation. When we reached the edge of it, he stopped.

“It was here, I believe, that the body was found?” he said,
addressing the doctor.

“It was,” said Dr. Bernard.

“Now,” said Poirot, “I will ask you all to stand exactly where you
are. I am going to show you how the crime was committed.”

He took from his pocket a small bottle and a piece of cotton-wool.
He soaked the wool in the liquid from the bottle and then, to our
intense surprise, he began to rub it over his own lips. In a
moment they were a bright, vivid red.

“Now,” he said, “I am Mr. Maltravers. I have been out shooting
rooks. I have my little rifle with me.”

He picked up a stick from the ground and held it as though it were
a rifle.

“I am walking along here, at the edge of the wood. Suddenly I feel
a sharp pain in my throat. I put my hand to my mouth. When I take
it away, it is covered with blood. I fall to the ground. I am
dead!”

He suited the action to the word, and fell prone on the grass. For
a moment there was a dead silence. Then Mrs. Maltravers gave a
piercing scream.

“It’s him!” she cried. “It’s him! I can see him! He’s standing there
behind you, Monsieur Poirot! His face—his face—it’s all covered
with blood!”

She sank to the ground in a dead faint.

Poirot sprang to his feet.

“So!” he said. “The experiment has succeeded. Hastings, the
brandy!”

I hurried to the house and returned with some brandy. Mrs.
Maltravers was beginning to come to. Poirot was bending over her.

“It is all right, madame,” he was saying. “It was only a little
theatrical performance. There is no one there—no one at all.”

Mrs. Maltravers opened her eyes and looked round her with a
shudder.

“I saw him,” she whispered. “I saw him as plainly as I see you.”

“I know, I know,” said Poirot soothingly. “But now you are better.
Let us go back to the house.”

We returned to the drawing-room. Mrs. Maltravers was still very
much shaken. Poirot sat down beside her.

“And now, madame,” he said, “I have a few more questions to ask
you.”

“Must you?” she moaned. “I am so tired.”

“Only one or two. On the night before your husband died, did you
not go into his room after he was asleep?”

Mrs. Maltravers hesitated for a moment.

“I—I may have done. I don’t remember.”

“And did you not take something from his bedside table?”

“I don’t know what you mean.”

“I think you do. You took his pen, did you not? The pen he always
used.”

Mrs. Maltravers’ face went deathly white.

“I—I don’t know what you’re talking about,” she gasped.

“I think you do,” said Poirot. “And now I will tell you what
happened. You had heard Captain Black’s story of the man who died
of blood-poisoning through sucking his pen. It gave you an idea.
You wanted your husband’s life insurance money. You knew that he
was on the verge of bankruptcy. You knew that if he died, you
would be a rich woman. So you decided to kill him. You went to
his room that night and you took his pen. You dipped it in a
deadly poison—a poison that would cause an internal hæmorrhage.
Then you put it back. The next day, your husband, as was his
habit, sucked his pen while he was writing. In a few hours he was
dead.”

Mrs. Maltravers gave a low moan and buried her face in her hands.

“It’s a lie!” she cried. “A wicked, cruel lie!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you can explain why you were
so terrified when I did my little ‘theatrical performance’? You
thought you saw your husband’s ghost, did you not? You thought he
had come back to denounce you.”

“I—I——”

“And perhaps you can also explain this.”

Poirot took from his pocket a small object and held it up. It was
a fountain-pen.

“This,” he said, “is the pen your husband was using on the day he
died. I found it in his pocket. I have had it analyzed. It
contains traces of a very deadly and unusual poison.”

Mrs. Maltravers gave a sudden, sharp cry and started to her feet.

“It’s not true!” she screamed. “I didn’t do it! I didn’t!”

And then, with a sudden, convulsive movement, she fell to the
floor.

Dr. Bernard hurried to her side. After a moment he looked up, his
face very grave.

“She is dead,” he said. “Heart failure.”

“So,” said Poirot. “Justice has been done.”

He turned to the rest of us.

“I will now explain,” he said. “I suspected Mrs. Maltravers from
the first. Her story of her husband’s ‘premonition’ was too thin.
And then there was the discrepancy I mentioned. She said she had
been to the village for some stamps. But the parlourmaid told me
that she had not left the house all the afternoon. Why should she
lie about such a small thing? Only because she wanted an alibi
for the time her husband was killed. Then there was Captain
Black’s story. It was clear that it had given her the idea for
the murder. As for the pen—I did not find it in the husband’s
pocket. I found it in Mrs. Maltravers’ own desk. She had forgotten
to destroy it. I had it analyzed this morning, and my suspicions
were confirmed.”

“But the ghost?” I asked. “How did you manage that?”

Poirot smiled.

“A very simple matter, my friend. A little chemical which, when
heated, produces a very realistic imitation of a human figure.
I had some of it in my pocket, and when I fell on the grass I
managed to ignite it. The rest was easy. Mrs. Maltravers’ own
guilty conscience did the rest.”

“And the red on your lips?”

“Red ink, Hastings. Red ink!”

And Poirot, with a twinkle in his eye, began to strap up his small
valise.

“And now, my friend,” he said, “we will catch the afternoon train
back to London. I think my friend Alfred Wright will be satisfied
with the result of my investigations.”

Thus ended the mystery of Marsdon Manor. It was one of Poirot’s
most brilliant cases, though I must confess that for once he had
succeeded in completely hoodwinking me. But then, as he would say
himself, he is a very exceptional man.

“Oh, nothing in particular. Let me see. Maltravers was rather
depressed, I thought, and he had a lot of talk with me about my
prospects. Asked me how much capital I’d got, and what I thought
of the chances for a man who went out there now. He was very
anxious for me to get on. Mrs. Maltravers kept trying to turn the
subject, and we got on to big-game shooting. I told them some of
my experiences, and then, after dinner, Maltravers came out into
the garden with me, and I showed him a few of the latest things
in rifles. He seemed quite keen. He took quite a lot of interest,
and insisted on trying my little Mauser—a very pretty little weapon
it is—and then we had a look at his own little rook rifle. He asked
a lot of questions about it, and seemed quite taken with the idea.”

“Oh, I don’t know. This and that. There was another guest there—a
Mr. Wright—who had some business with Maltravers, I believe.”

“Alfred Wright? A director of the Northern Union?”

“That’s the man. He was staying the night too. We were talking
mostly about my life in Africa. Maltravers was particularly
interested in the superstitions of the natives, and their belief
in magic and all that. He was quite excited, I remember, when I
told him a story of a native who had been cursed by a witch doctor
and who simply lay down and died of no apparent cause.”

“Ah!” Poirot leaned forward. “You told him that story? And did
Mr. Maltravers appear to be in good health at the time?”

“He seemed all right, though he was a bit depressed, I thought.
He kept on saying that he didn’t expect to live much longer.”

“I see. Well, thank you, Captain Black. I think that is all I
wanted to know.”

Captain Black took his leave, and Poirot sat for a long time
in silence. Then he suddenly stood up.

“Hastings, I have it! The missing link!”

“What is it?”

“We must go back to the Manor at once. There is one thing I must
verify.”

“Let me see,” said Captain Black, as he thoughtfully lit a pipe.
“I think we talked about the prospects of a wet season, and some
new sort of tractor that Maltravers was thinking of getting. And
then I remember he asked me some questions about the native
customs, and we talked a bit about that.”

“Specifically what customs?”

“Oh, I think it was the blood-feuds and things of that sort. It’s
all quite interesting, you know. I gave him some rather weird
details, I’m afraid. There’s one tribe, for instance, who have a
most curious way of killing their enemies. They believe that if
they can only get some of their enemy’s blood, they can make him
die. And they have a most uncanny way of doing it, too. They get
hold of a little of the blood, and then they have a ceremony and
the man dies of internal hæmorrhage. It’s a sort of sympathetic
magic, you see.”

“_Tiens_!” said Poirot, with a sudden light in his eyes. “That is
truly remarkable. And did you relate this to Mr. Maltravers?”

“Yes, I believe I did. He seemed quite interested, I remember.”

“And you left for London—when?”

“Early next morning—eight o’clock train.”

“I see. Many thanks to you, Captain Black. You have been most
helpful.”

Captain Black having taken his departure, Poirot turned to me
with a look of triumph.

“You see, Hastings? The internal hæmorrhage! The very thing!”

“But, my dear Poirot, you don’t mean to say you believe in this
mumbo-jumbo?”

“Not for a moment! But what if _someone else_ believed in it? What
if Mr. Maltravers was a very superstitious man, and the suggestion
of such a thing was enough to bring on a fatal attack? It has
happened before now.”

“But the doctor said it was a gastric ulcer.”

“Doctors, my friend, are not infallible. We must see this Alfred
Wright. He may be able to tell us something more about Maltravers’
state of mind.”

“Wait a bit. I don’t know. Oh, I know, I was telling them some
stories of the sort of life one leads out there.”

“Indeed. What sort of stories?”

“Oh, just the ordinary things. About the natives, and so on. They
seemed very interested. Especially Maltravers.”

“He seemed interested, did he? In what, particularly?”

“The farm and the way we lived, and all that. And then I happened
to mention a thing that happened to a fellow I knew out there—a
distressing sort of thing. I don’t know why I should have
remembered it—the sort of thing that gets on one’s nerves, you
know. It had been in the papers, too.”

“What was it?”

“Oh, a very simple thing. A man was out shooting, and he was found
dead. It was supposed that he had had a sudden internal
hæmorrhage. But it turned out—it turned out he’d been murdered.”

Captain Black’s face was very grave.

“Murdered?” I cried. “How?”

“Well, you see,” Captain Black continued, “this fellow was a bit
of a mystery. Nobody knew much about him. And it turned out he’d
been a sort of—well, a sort of international spy. And someone had
managed to—to get at him. They found a tiny little hole—smaller
than a pin’s head—just behind the ear. And in it was a minute
particle of—of some South American poison. It’s a thing the
natives use, you know.”

“Good heavens!” I cried.

“And you say Mr. Maltravers was interested in this story?” asked
Poirot, his eyes fixed on the young man’s face.

“Yes, he seemed very much interested. He asked all sorts of
questions about it.”

“And Mrs. Maltravers?”

“Oh, she was interested, too. She said it was the most
extraordinary thing she’d ever heard. She couldn’t believe it
could be true.”

“And that was on Tuesday night?”

“Yes.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And you left on Wednesday morning?”

“Yes.”

“And on Wednesday afternoon Mr. Maltravers was found dead?”

“Yes. It’s a very strange coincidence, isn’t it?”

“Very strange,” said Poirot. “Very strange indeed.”

He was silent for a moment, then he rose and held out his hand.

“Well, thank you very much, Captain Black. You’ve been most
helpful. We must be getting back to town now. Good-bye.”

When we were once more in the street, I turned to Poirot.

“What do you think of that story?” I asked. “It’s a most
extraordinary thing.”

“It is indeed,” said Poirot. “A very extraordinary thing. And now,
my friend, we must go and see the doctor again.”

“The doctor?”

“Yes. I have a little question to ask him.”

We found Dr. Bernard in his consulting-room. He looked up with some
annoyance as we entered.

“Well, what is it now?” he asked.

“I only wanted to ask you one question, doctor,” said Poirot
mildly. “When you examined the body of Mr. Maltravers, did you
happen to look behind the ear?”

The doctor stared at him.

“Behind the ear? What on earth for?”

“Oh, just a whim of mine,” said Poirot. “Did you?”

“No, I did not,” said the doctor. “Why should I?”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “Why should you? Thank you, doctor. That
is all I wanted to know.”

As we left the house, Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“And now, Hastings, we will go back to Marsdon Manor.”

“But what for?”

“To see Mrs. Maltravers. I have a little experiment I want to
try.”

“An experiment?”

“Yes. A little experiment in—what shall we say?—in psychology.”

When we arrived at the Manor, we were told that Mrs. Maltravers
was in the garden. We found her sitting on a stone seat, looking
out over the fields. She rose as we approached.

“Monsieur Poirot! I thought you had gone back to London.”

“I had intended to do so, madame,” said Poirot. “But a little
thing occurred to me—a little thing that I felt I must speak to
you about. You will forgive me?”

“Of course. What is it?”

“It is about a story that Captain Black was telling us. A very
strange story about a man who was murdered in Africa. You
remember it?”

Mrs. Maltravers’ face went very pale.

“Yes,” she said. “I remember it. Why?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “I have just been talking to Dr. Bernard.
And he tells me that when he examined your husband’s body, he
did not look behind the ear.”

Mrs. Maltravers caught her breath.

“Behind the ear? But why—why should he?”

“Because,” said Poirot, his voice very low and clear, “if he had
looked behind the ear, he might have found—a tiny little hole.
Smaller than a pin’s head.”

Mrs. Maltravers gave a low cry and sank back on to the seat. Her
face was ashen.

“What do you mean?” she gasped. “What are you trying to say?”

“I am trying to say, madame,” said Poirot, “that I believe your
husband was murdered. And I believe I know who murdered him.”

Mrs. Maltravers stared at him, her eyes wide with terror.

“Who?” she whispered. “Who?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to find out. And I think,
if you will allow me, I will stay here for a little while. I
should like to look round the grounds—the place where your
husband was found.”

“Of course,” said Mrs. Maltravers. “Do whatever you like. I—I
feel a little faint. I think I will go into the house.”

She rose and walked slowly away. Poirot watched her go, a strange
expression on his face.

“And now, Hastings,” he said, “to work!”

We spent the next hour or so wandering about the grounds. Poirot
seemed particularly interested in the little plantation where the
body had been found. He poked about among the leaves with his
stick, and examined the ground with a magnifying glass.

“What are you looking for, Poirot?” I asked.

“I am looking for a little piece of evidence, Hastings. A very
little piece of evidence.”

“And have you found it?”

“Not yet. But I am hopeful. Very hopeful.”

Suddenly he stooped and picked something up.

“Ah!” he said. “What have we here?”

He held out his hand. On the palm lay a small, dark object. It
looked like a tiny piece of wood.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is a thorn, Hastings. A very sharp, very poisonous thorn.”

“A thorn? But how——”

“It is the weapon, Hastings. The weapon that killed Mr.
Maltravers.”

“But how could a thorn kill a man?”

“It was not just a thorn, Hastings. It was a thorn that had been
dipped in a very deadly poison. A poison that causes almost
instantaneous death. And when it is injected into the blood
stream—through a tiny hole behind the ear—it leaves no trace. No
trace at all. Except for a little blood on the lips.”

“Good heavens!” I cried. “But who—who could have done such a
thing?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we are going to find out. And I
think I know where to look. Come, Hastings. We must go back to the
house. I have a little surprise for Mrs. Maltravers.”

When we reached the house, Poirot asked to see Mrs. Maltravers.
She was in the drawing-room, looking very pale and agitated.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot?” she asked. “Have you found anything?”

“I have found this, madame,” said Poirot, holding out the thorn.

Mrs. Maltravers stared at it.

“A thorn? What of it?”

“This is no ordinary thorn, madame,” said Poirot. “This is a
poisoned thorn. The weapon that killed your husband.”

Mrs. Maltravers gave a cry and fell back in her chair.

“No!” she gasped. “No! It’s not true!”

“It is perfectly true, madame,” said Poirot. “And I think I know
who used it.”

He turned to the door.

“Come in, if you please, Monsieur Wright.”

Alfred Wright, the director of the Insurance Company, stepped into
the room. He looked very grave.

“Mr. Wright!” cried Mrs. Maltravers. “What are you doing here?”

“I asked Mr. Wright to come down,” said Poirot. “I thought he
might be interested in my discovery. You see, Mr. Wright is a
very clever man. A very clever man indeed. And he has a very
great interest in this case. A fifty-thousand-pound interest, to
be exact.”

Alfred Wright looked at Poirot, his face impassive.

“I don’t understand you, Monsieur Poirot,” he said.

“Don’t you, Monsieur Wright?” said Poirot. “I think you do. I
think you understand me very well. You see, I have been making a
few inquiries. I have found out that you were in a very difficult
financial position. You had been—shall we say?—borrowing money
from the Company. Money that you could not pay back. And you saw
a way out. A way to get fifty thousand pounds.”

“This is preposterous!” cried Wright.

“Is it?” said Poirot. “I don’t think so. You knew that Mr.
Maltravers was in financial difficulties. You knew that he was
anxious to insure his life for his wife’s benefit. And you saw
your opportunity. You went to see him. You told him that you
could arrange the insurance for him. And you did. But you also
did something else. You went to see Captain Black. You knew that
he had just come back from Africa. You knew that he had some very
interesting stories to tell. And you made sure that he told one
of those stories—the story of the man who was murdered with a
poisoned thorn—when Mr. Maltravers was present.”

“And then?” asked Wright, his voice cold.

“And then,” said Poirot, “you waited. You waited until Mr.
Maltravers was out in the grounds, shooting rooks. You followed
him. You crept up behind him. And you used the thorn. It was very
simple. Very simple indeed.”

“And why should I do such a thing?” asked Wright.

“Because,” said Poirot, “you knew that if Mr. Maltravers died,
the Company would have to pay out fifty thousand pounds. And you
had already made arrangements to—shall we say?—intercept that
money. You had forged a document, making the money payable to
you, instead of to Mrs. Maltravers.”

Alfred Wright stared at Poirot for a moment. Then his face
suddenly crumpled.

“It’s true,” he whispered. “It’s true. I did it. I had to. I
was desperate.”

He sank into a chair, his head in his hands.

Mrs. Maltravers looked from Poirot to Wright, her face full of
horror.

“You!” she gasped. “You killed my husband!”

“I am sorry, madame,” said Poirot. “But the truth must be told.
And now, if you will excuse me, I think we have some matters to
attend to.”

He turned to the door, beckoning to me to follow him. As we
walked down the drive, I looked at him in admiration.

“Poirot,” I said, “you are a genius!”

“It is the little grey cells, my friend,” said Poirot, with a
smile. “The little grey cells. They never fail.”

“Oh, I don’t know. The usual odd topics. Maltravers asked after my
people, and then we discussed the question of German reparations,
and then Mrs. Maltravers asked a lot of questions about East
Africa, and I told them one or two yarns, that’s about all, I
think.”

“Thank you.”

“Any story in particular?” Poirot inquired, leaning forward with an air of great interest.

“Oh, just a silly thing about a man who thought he was being followed by a ‘ghoul’—a sort of phantom that causes its victims to bleed from the mouth and die of sheer terror. It’s a common enough superstition in certain parts of the world. I’m afraid I rather piled on the agony for the sake of the story. Mrs. Maltravers didn’t like it much, but Maltravers seemed quite fascinated. He kept asking me if such a thing were really possible—if a man could truly die of fright from seeing such a manifestation.”

“And what were these yarns, if I may ask?” Poirot’s eyes were twinkling with a sudden light.

“Oh, just the usual sort of thing. I told them one story that seemed to interest them particularly—about a man who was told by a native witch-doctor that he would die on a certain day, and he did—just died of sheer fright. It’s a well-known phenomenon in those parts. Mrs. Maltravers seemed quite struck by it.”

“_C’est très intéressant, ça_,” murmured Poirot. “The power of suggestion! It is a formidable thing, is it not?”

Poirot leaned forward, his eyes blinking rapidly. “One or two yarns, you say? Of what nature? Adventure? Sport? Or perhaps—the supernatural?” Captain Black laughed, though he looked a trifle uneasy. “Oh, nothing very sinister, I assure you. Just the usual sort of thing—the dangers of the bush, and a rather gruesome tale of a man who died of a sudden hemorrhage while out in the wilds. Mrs. Maltravers seemed particularly interested in that one. It’s a nasty way to go, you know, and I suppose it stayed in her mind, considering what happened to poor Maltravers the next day.”

“And these stories of yours,” said Poirot, “they were perhaps of
the blood-curdling variety? Tales of the supernatural?”

Captain Black laughed. “Well, I told one about a fellow who was
cursed by a witch-doctor in the Congo. The poor devil was told
he’d die of a hæmorrhage within twenty-four hours—and he did!
Frightened to death, I suppose. Maltravers was particularly
interested in that one—kept asking me questions about how the
man looked and what the symptoms were.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “I see. It is very suggestive. And now,
Captain Black, I will wish you a very good day.”

“Tell me, Captain,” said Poirot, his eyes suddenly narrowing, “did you by any chance mention a certain story—a story of a man who was frightened to death?”

Captain Black looked a little startled. “Why, yes, as a matter of fact, I did. I told them a yarn about a fellow out in Nairobi who died of a heart attack because he thought he’d been shot by a ghost. It was just a bit of camp-fire nonsense, you know. But why do you ask?”

“It is a curious coincidence, that is all,” murmured Poirot. “And after you told this story, what happened? Did Mr. Maltravers seem—how shall I say—upset?”

“Not particularly. He seemed a bit quiet, perhaps. But then, he was a quiet sort of chap anyway. Look here, what are you driving at?”

Poirot was silent for a moment, then he said gently: “With your
permission, I should like to try a little experiment. You have told
us all that your conscious self knows, I want now to question your
subconscious self.”

“Psychoanalysis, what?” said Black, with visible alarm.

“Oh, no,” said Poirot reassuringly. “You see, it is like this, I
give you a word, you answer with another, and so on. Any word, the
first one you think of. Shall we begin?”

“All right,” said Black slowly, but he looked uneasy.

“Note down the words, please, Hastings,” said Poirot. Then he took
from his pocket his big turnip-faced watch and laid it on the table
beside him. “We will commence. Day.”

There was a moment’s pause, and then Black replied:

“_Night_.”

As Poirot proceeded, his answers came quicker.

“Name,” said Poirot.

“_Place_.”

“Bernard.”

“_Shaw_.”

“Tuesday.”

“_Dinner_.”

“Journey.”

“_Ship_.”

“Country.”

“_Uganda_.”

“Story.”

“_Lions_.”

“Rook Rifle.”

“_Farm_.”

“Shot.”

“_Suicide_.”

“Elephant.”

“_Tusks_.”

“Money.”

“_Lawyers_.”

“Thank you, Captain Black. Perhaps you could spare me a few minutes
in about half an hour’s time?”

“Certainly.” The young soldier looked at him curiously and wiped
his brow as he got up.

“And now, Hastings,” said Poirot, smiling at me as the door closed
behind him. “You see it all, do you not?”

“I don’t know what you mean.”

“Does that list of words tell you nothing?”

I scrutinized it, but was forced to shake my head.

“My dear friend, consider the word ‘Shot’. To that, our Captain
replies ‘Suicide’. And to ‘Rook Rifle’, he replies ‘Farm’. Now, why
should he associate these things? It is because on Tuesday night, a
story was told—a story of a man who committed suicide with a rook
rifle on a farm. And who told that story? Why, the person who wished
to put the idea of suicide into the mind of a man already depressed
by financial failure. A man who was ‘pottering about’ with a rook
rifle the very next day!”

“It is simple, Hastings. To the word ‘shot’, he responded ‘suicide’. Now, why should he do that? If Mr. Maltravers died of a sudden hæmorrhage, as the good doctor says, the word ‘shot’ should have evoked ‘rifle’, or ‘rook’, or even ‘accident’. But ‘suicide’—that implies a certain train of thought already present in the mind. On Tuesday night, they were discussing the possibility of a man taking his own life. And yet, Mrs. Maltravers told us her husband had a ‘premonition’ of death by natural causes. There is a discrepancy there, Hastings. And then there is the matter of the blood. I find myself wondering if the good Dr. Bernard is quite as observant as he believes himself to be. It is time for a little experiment—one that will require the presence of all our characters.”

“It tells me everything,” said Poirot. “Consider the word ‘Shot’ and the response ‘Suicide’. Captain Black has suicide in his mind in connection with the death of Mr. Maltravers. Why? Because of the story he told at dinner on Tuesday night. We must hear that story, Hastings. It is the key to the whole mystery. But there is one more thing. Do you remember what Mrs. Maltravers said? That her husband had a premonition of his death? A very convenient premonition, was it not? And the doctor—the good Dr. Bernard—he is very sure, very certain. It is all very interesting, Hastings. Very interesting indeed.”

“My dear Hastings, look at ‘Shot’ and ‘Suicide’. Does that not strike you as significant? The official version of the death is a hæmorrhage, yet to the word ‘Shot’, our friend the Captain instantly replies ‘Suicide’. It suggests, does it not, that he has the idea of a shot and a suicide linked together in his mind? And then ‘Rook Rifle’ and ‘Farm’. What is the connection there? I will tell you. It is the story he told at dinner on Tuesday night—a story of a man who committed suicide on a farm with a rook rifle! It was that story, Hastings, that gave someone an idea. But we must verify my little theory. We will return to the Manor, and I shall require the assistance of our friend the Captain.”

“It is very simple,” said Poirot. “Consider the word ‘Shot.’ To it, Captain Black responded ‘Suicide.’ Why? Because on Tuesday evening, a story was told—a story of a man who committed suicide. And who told that story? Captain Black himself! But there is more. To the word ‘Story,’ he replied ‘Lions.’ He told a tale of the African bush, Hastings, a tale of a man who died in a most peculiar fashion. It was that story, I am convinced, that provided the inspiration for this ‘natural’ death. We must return to the Manor at once. I have a little theatrical performance of my own to stage—one that will make the dead speak!”

“I will assist you. To begin with, Black answered well within the
normal time limit, with no pauses, so we can take it that he
himself has no guilty knowledge to conceal. ‘Day’ to ‘Night’ and
‘Place’ to ‘Name’ are normal associations. I began work with
‘Bernard’ which might have suggested the local doctor had he come
across him at all. Evidently he had not. After our recent
conversation, he gave ‘Dinner’ to my ‘Tuesday,’ but ‘Journey’ and
‘Country’ were answered by ‘Ship’ and ‘Uganda,’ showing clearly
that it was his journey abroad that was important to him and not
the one which brought him down here. ‘Story’ recalls to him one of
the ‘Lion’ stories he told at dinner. I proceed to ‘Rook Rifle’
and he answered with the totally unexpected word ‘Farm.’ When I
say ‘Shot,’ he answers at once ‘Suicide.’ The association seems
clear. A man he knows committed suicide with a rook rifle on a farm
somewhere. Remember, too, that his mind is still on the stories he
told at dinner, and I think you will agree that I shall not be far
from the truth if I recall Captain Black and ask him to repeat the
particular suicide story which he told at the dinner-table on
Tuesday evening.”

Black was straightforward enough over the matter.

“I remember now,” said Black. “It was a story about a man in the Transvaal who found himself in much the same position as Mr. Maltravers—facing bankruptcy, with a large insurance policy. He committed suicide by a very ingenious method. He used a small-bore rifle, such as a rook rifle, and fired it through the roof of his mouth into the brain. It causes an internal hemorrhage and leaves very little trace. Unless a doctor is specifically looking for a bullet wound, he would likely attribute the death to a natural hemorrhage. I happened to mention the story at dinner that night.”

“It was a yarn I heard out in Uganda,” explained Captain Black. “A fellow there was in a bad way—debts, you know—and he wanted his life insurance to go to his wife. He knew that suicide would forfeit the lot. So he hit on a grisly but clever idea. He took a small-bore rifle, put the barrel in his mouth, and fired. It caused an internal hemorrhage that looked exactly like a natural break in a blood vessel. No external wound, you see, just some blood on the lips. The doctor who examined him was easily fooled and called it a natural death. I happened to recount the tale at the dinner table on Tuesday night. Mr. Maltravers seemed quite interested in the details.”

“It was just a yarn I was telling them,” said Captain Black. “A fellow I knew out in Nairobi. He was in a bit of a hole, financially, and he wanted his wife to have his life insurance. But there was a suicide clause. So he hit on a most ingenious, if somewhat unpleasant, idea. He used a small-bore rifle—a rook rifle, in fact—and fired it straight down his throat. It left no mark except a little blood on the lips, and the doctor, a bit of an old fossil, certified it as a natural death from an internal hæmorrhage. The insurance company paid out, and the widow was left a rich woman. I thought it was a pretty clever story, but I’m afraid it rather upset Mrs. Maltravers.”

“It was a yarn I told them at dinner,” Black said, leaning back. “About a fellow I knew out in the Transvaal. He was in a hole, poor devil—debts and all that—and he decided to end it. He used a rook rifle—put the barrel in his mouth and pulled the trigger with his toe. A quick way out, though a bit of a shock for the person who finds the body, I imagine. I'm afraid it was rather a gruesome tale for a dinner table, but Mrs. Maltravers seemed quite interested in the details of how it was done.”

“Yes,” said Captain Black. “I was telling them about a fellow I knew out in the Bush. He wanted to give his wife a fright—thought she didn't care for him enough, or something. He went out, fired a shot from his rifle, and then lay down with a bottle of red ink spilt over his face. When his wife came out and saw him, she let out a piercing shriek, and the poor beggar, who'd had a weak heart, was so startled by her scream that he died on the spot! It was a bit of a grim tale for a dinner table, I suppose, but Mrs. Maltravers seemed quite interested in the details of how he'd managed the 'blood' effect.”

“Yes, I did tell them that story now that I come to think of it.
Chap shot himself on a farm out there. Did it with a rook rifle
through the roof of the mouth, bullet lodged in the brain. Doctors
were no end puzzled over it—there was nothing to show except a
little blood on the lips. But what——”

“What has it got to do with Mr. Maltravers? You did not know, I
see, that he was found with a rook rifle by his side.”

“You mean my story suggested to him—oh, but that is awful!”

“Do not distress yourself—it would have been one way or another.
Well, I must get on the telephone to London.”

“What are you going to do?” I asked.

“I must inform my friend Alfred Wright of my conclusions,” Poirot
replied, his eyes twinkling. “He will be most interested. The
theory of the insurance company was that Maltravers committed
suicide to save his wife from ruin. But if he did so, he would
surely have left some word, some message. He did not. Why?
Because it was not suicide. It was murder.”

“Murder!” I exclaimed. “But the doctor said——”

“The doctor is an old fool,” said Poirot. “He saw blood on the
lips and jump to the conclusion of a hemorrhage. He did not look
for a bullet hole in the roof of the mouth because he did not
expect to find one. But Mrs. Maltravers knew. She heard the story
at dinner. She saw the opportunity. She is a very clever woman,
Hastings.”

“You mean she killed him?”

“Wait and see, my friend. We must now return to Marsdon Manor.”The evening shadows were lengthening as we once more reached the gates of Marsdon Manor. To my surprise, a car was just drawing up, and from it stepped a middle-aged gentleman whom I recognized as Alfred Wright, the director of the Northern Union. Poirot greeted him with a flourish. Our arrival seemed to cast a gloom over the house. Mrs. Maltravers received us in the drawing-room, her face a mask of weary sorrow, while Dr. Bernard stood by the fireplace, looking thoroughly disgruntled at this new intrusion. Captain Black hovered in the background, his bronzed face troubled. Poirot took his stand in the center of the room, the light from the setting sun glinting off his patent leather boots.

“Then you believe it was suicide, after all?” I asked.

“What else can it be? The insurance company would have been
satisfied by any ordinary doctor’s report, but since they have
called me in I must be able to prove my case. A little talk with
Mrs. Maltravers will soon settle the matter.”

“You mean she will tell you?”

“Why not? She must have known, even if she did not suspect it at
first. I am going back to the Manor now.”

“I’ll come with you.”

“As you please.”

But when we reached the house we found that Mrs. Maltravers was
out.

“We will wait,” said Poirot, seating himself in the hall. “I do
not think she will be long.”

For some time we sat in silence. The hall was dimly lit by a single
lamp. On the wall hung a collection of arms, and I was looking at
them when I heard a slight sound. Poirot was sitting with his eyes
half closed, and his face was very pale.

“Hastings,” he whispered. “Look! What do you see there—on the
stairs?”

I looked, and for a moment I could have sworn I saw a dim figure
moving. Then I realized it was only the shadow of a large bronze
statue.

“It is nothing, Poirot,” I said. “Your nerves are on edge.”

“My nerves! No, it is not that. But look—look!”

He was pointing towards the door of the morning-room. It was
opening slowly. As I watched, a man’s hand, a very white hand,
came round the edge of the door. Then a face appeared—a face that
I recognized.

It was the face of the dead man, Mr. Maltravers!

I must have cried out, for the face vanished and the door was
shut. Poirot sprang to his feet and I followed him. We burst into
the room. It was empty!

“He was here,” I cried. “I saw him.”

Poirot did not answer. He was looking at the window, which was
open. We hurried to it and looked out. There was no one to be
seen.

“It was a ghost,” I said, and my voice shook.

“A ghost, or a very substantial man,” said Poirot. “Let us see
if we can find any traces of him.”

But the search was fruitless. We returned to the hall to find Mrs.
Maltravers had just come in. She looked from one to the other of
us in surprise.

“What is the matter?” she asked. “You both look as if you had seen
a ghost.”

“We have,” I said.

She turned very pale.

“A ghost! What do you mean?”

“Madame,” said Poirot, and his voice was very grave. “I have to
tell you that I have seen your husband.”

“My husband! But he is dead—he is in his coffin.”

“I know. But I have seen him—here, in this house.”

Mrs. Maltravers screamed and fell fainting into a chair.

“You should not have told her like that,” I said reproachfully.

“It was the only way,” said Poirot. “Now we must see what we can
find out.”

But at that moment the parlourmaid came running into the hall.

“Oh, if you please, sir,” she cried. “There’s a man in the
garden—I saw him through the kitchen window.”

Poirot was out of the house in a flash, and I followed him. We
searched the garden thoroughly, but there was no sign of anyone.
When we returned to the house we found that Mrs. Maltravers had
recovered, and was being looked after by her maid.

“I think we had better go,” said Poirot. “There is nothing more
we can do here tonight.”

As we walked back to the inn, I asked him what he thought of the
extraordinary occurrence.

“I think, Hastings, that there are more things in heaven and earth
than are dreamt of in your philosophy. But tomorrow we shall see.”

The next morning Poirot was up early.

“I am going to the village,” he said. “I have one or two
inquiries to make. You had better stay here, Hastings, in case
anyone should call.”

He was away for about two hours. When he returned his face was
grave.

“I have seen the doctor,” he said. “And I have seen the
undertaker. It is as I thought.”

“What do you mean?”

“Mr. Maltravers did not die of a hæmorrhage.”

“Then what did he die of?”

“He was murdered!”

“Murdered! But who——”

“That is what we have to find out. But I think I know. We will
go to the Manor.”

When we arrived at the house we were told that Mrs. Maltravers was
in the morning-room. We went in and found her sitting by the
window. She looked very pale and tired.

“I have come to tell you, madame,” said Poirot, “that I have
discovered the truth.”

She looked at him with startled eyes.

“The truth? What do you mean?”

“I mean that your husband did not commit suicide. He was
murdered.”

“Murdered! But who could have murdered him?”

“That is what I am going to tell you.”

Poirot paused for a moment, and then he said:

“He was murdered by someone who knew of the story Captain Black
told at dinner on Tuesday night. Someone who saw in it a way to
kill Mr. Maltravers without leaving any trace of the crime.”

“But who?” gasped Mrs. Maltravers.

“Someone,” continued Poirot, “who knew that Mr. Maltravers was in
financial difficulties, and that his life was insured for a large
sum. Someone who stood to gain by his death.”

He turned to me.

“Hastings, will you go and ask Mr. Wright to come here? He is in
the library.”

I went to the library and found Mr. Wright, the director of the
Insurance Company, who had arrived that morning. He followed me
back to the morning-room.

“Mr. Wright,” said Poirot. “I have been telling Mrs. Maltravers
that her husband was murdered.”

Mr. Wright looked at him in amazement.

“Murdered! But the doctor’s report——”

“The doctor was mistaken,” said Poirot. “Mr. Maltravers was
killed by a very clever and cold-blooded murderer. And I can
prove it.”

He turned to Mrs. Maltravers.

“Madame, I must ask you to be brave. I am going to show you how
your husband was killed.”

He took from his pocket a small object and held it up. It was a
hypodermic syringe.

“This,” he said, “was the weapon used. Your husband was injected
with a deadly poison—a poison that causes all the symptoms of a
hæmorrhage. And the person who did it was——”

He paused, and then he said:

“Dr. Ralph Bernard!”

Mrs. Maltravers gave a cry and fell back in her chair. Mr. Wright
looked at Poirot in horror.

“Dr. Bernard! But why——”

“Because,” said Poirot, “Dr. Bernard was also in financial
difficulties. He had been borrowing money from Mr. Maltravers,
and he knew that if Mr. Maltravers went bankrupt he would never
be repaid. But he also knew about the insurance policy. He saw
a way to get his money and at the same time to rid himself of a
creditor. He killed Mr. Maltravers, and then, as the attending
doctor, he was able to certify the cause of death as a hæmorrhage,
knowing that no one would suspect the truth.”

“But the ghost?” I asked. “What about the ghost we saw last
night?”

“The ghost,” said Poirot with a smile, “was a little device of
my own. I suspected Dr. Bernard, and I wanted to see how he would
react if he thought his victim had returned from the grave. I
arranged for a friend of mine, who is an actor, to personate Mr.
Maltravers. It was he you saw in the morning-room last night.
And Dr. Bernard, who was also in the house, saw him too. His
terror gave him away.”

At that moment the door opened and Dr. Bernard himself walked into
the room. He looked pale and haggard.

“I heard what you said,” he said, his voice shaking. “It is true.
I killed him. I was desperate—I didn’t know what else to do.”

He sank into a chair and buried his face in his hands.

“And now,” said Poirot, “I think we had better send for the
police.”

As we left the house, I turned to Poirot.

“You are a wonderful man, Poirot,” I said.

“_Merci, mon ami_,” he replied. “But it was really very simple.
It was the rook rifle that gave me the clue. You see, a rook rifle
is not a very effective weapon for suicide—unless you know
exactly how to use it. And the only person who would have known
that was someone who had heard Captain Black’s story. Once I
knew that, the rest was easy.”

And so the mystery of Marsdon Manor was solved, and once more
Hercule Poirot had triumphed.

Poirot spent a considerable time in the telephone booth. When he emerged, he looked remarkably satisfied. He informed me that he had been speaking to Alfred Wright, the director of the Northern Union, and had requested that he come down to Marsdon Leigh by the evening train. “He is very anxious about his fifty thousand pounds, our friend Alfred,” Poirot remarked. “He will bring with him a certain assistant from his office whom I require for my little experiment. And now, Hastings, we shall return to the Manor, but we must be careful not to be seen. I wish to examine the plantation where the poor Mr. Maltravers met his end.”

“To the Northern Union, I suppose?” I suggested.

“No,” he replied, with his hand on the receiver. “I am going to
telephone to my friend Alfred Wright. He’s the man who can help
us now. And then we will go back to the Manor.”

“But you said there was no mouse in the mouse-hole.”

“My friend, I have a little plan. I have a feeling that we shall
find what we seek if we look in the right place.”

“And that is?”

“The house of the dead, Hastings! The house of the dead!”

He was in one of his most theatrical moods, and I could get nothing
more out of him. We reached the Manor and were again received by
the widow. Poirot apologized for our return.

“It is a small matter, madame. I have just been having a long talk
with my friend Mr. Wright, whom you may know as a director of the
Insurance Company. He is also a very celebrated occultist. He
thinks it possible that your husband’s spirit may be able to give
us some information. He is coming down here this evening, and we
hope with your permission to hold a small séance.”

Mrs. Maltravers looked at him with some apprehension.

“Oh, but is it—is it quite right? My husband was a Christian
Scientist, you know, and he might not like it.”

“I am sure he would be the first to wish us to know the truth,”
replied Poirot solemnly. “And we can but try. Mr. Wright is most
anxious to do so.”

Mrs. Maltravers reluctantly gave her consent.

“I shall be very glad to see Mr. Wright,” she murmured. “I have
heard his name before. But I cannot say I like the idea of a
séance.”

“It will be quite a small one,” Poirot assured her. “Only ourselves
and—oh, I forgot! We must have one person more. Dr. Bernard,
perhaps?”

“If you wish,” she said, her eyes fixed on him.

“I will go and fetch him,” I offered.

“Do, Hastings, do. And tell him that Mr. Wright is coming down
from London.”

I found the doctor at home, and he was obviously much interested
in the idea.

“Occultism, eh? Very interesting, very interesting. I’ve always
wanted to see something of the kind. I’ll come with pleasure.”

Poirot was away for some time. When he returned, he looked more like a cat who had found the cream than ever. He began to hum a little tune under his breath as he checked his appearance in the mirror. “I have spoken to Alfred Wright,” he announced. “He was most helpful—perhaps a little too helpful. It is interesting, is it not, how people reveal themselves when they think they are most secure? He has agreed to join us at the Manor this evening; he is coming down by the next train. I have also sent a little message to Dr. Bernard and Captain Black, requesting their presence as well. We shall have a most interesting evening, Hastings. The air of Essex is very conducive to the truth, and I have a little experiment in mind that will finally clarify the meaning of that ‘suicide’ story which Captain Black so obligingly provided.”

Poirot had a lengthy conversation over the wire, and came back
thoughtful. He went off by himself in the afternoon, and it was
not till seven o’clock that he announced that he could put it off
no longer, but must break the news to the young widow. My sympathy
had already gone out to her unreservedly. To be left penniless,
and with the knowledge that her husband had killed himself to
assure her future was a hard burden for any woman to bear. I
cherished a secret hope, however, that young Black might prove
capable of consoling her after her first grief had passed. He
evidently admired her enormously.

We were again shown into the morning-room, and after a little
preamble Poirot told her the truth.

“I have no alternative, madame. Your husband committed suicide.
It is my duty to inform the Insurance Company. I am extremely
sorry, but there is no help for it.”

Mrs. Maltravers was naturally very much upset.

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot, it can’t be true. My poor husband—what he
must have suffered. Is it not possible——”

“It is not possible, madame. The evidence is too strong. The
story of the suicide which was told at dinner on Tuesday night,
and the fact that he was found with the rook rifle, all point to
the same thing. And then, there is the fact that his life was
insured for fifty thousand pounds, and his affairs were on the
verge of bankruptcy. I’m afraid you will have to face it.”

She looked at him with her large blue eyes full of tears.

“I suppose you must do your duty, Monsieur Poirot. But it is very
hard.”

“I am glad to see you are so reasonable, madame. And now, I think,
if you have no objection, I should like to ask the servants a few
questions.”

“Certainly. Which of them do you wish to see?”

“The parlourmaid, I think, if you would be so kind.”

Mrs. Maltravers rang the bell, and the parlourmaid appeared.

“This gentleman wishes to ask you a few questions, Jane,” said
Mrs. Maltravers. “I will leave you with him.”

She went out of the room, and Poirot began his questioning.

“You were in the house on Wednesday afternoon, were you not?”

“Yes, sir.”

“You did not go out?”

“No, sir.”

“Did you hear any shots?”

“I think I did hear one or two, sir, but I didn’t think anything
of it. Master was often out with his gun.”

“I see. And you did not see your master after lunch?”

“No, sir.”

“Did you see anyone else?”

“No, sir—at least—I saw a gentleman go into the house about half
past four.”

“A gentleman? Who was he?”

“I don’t know, sir. I’ve never seen him before. He was a tall,
middle-aged gentleman, with a grey beard.”

“I see. And what did he do?”

“He just went into the house, sir. I didn’t see him come out
again.”

“I see. Thank you, Jane. That will do.”

The girl went out, and Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings? A mysterious stranger with a grey beard.
What do you make of that?”

“I don’t know. It’s very extraordinary.”

“It is, is it not? And now, I think we will go and have a little
talk with the gardener who found the body.”

We found the man in the garden, and Poirot questioned him
closely. He had nothing much to add to what he had already told
us. He had found the body at about five o’clock, and had at once
