run to the house to give the alarm.

“And you are sure the body had not been touched?”

“Quite sure, sir.”

“And there was no one else about?”

“No one, sir.”

“Thank you. That will do.”

As we walked back to the house, Poirot was very silent.

“What are you thinking of, Poirot?” I asked.

“I am thinking of many things, Hastings. Of the mysterious
stranger with the grey beard, and of the rook rifle, and of the
fifty thousand pounds. It is a very pretty little problem.”

“But surely it is all quite clear? Maltravers committed suicide,
as you said.”

“Perhaps, Hastings, perhaps. And yet, there are one or two
things that I do not quite understand. For instance, why did he
choose that particular spot to kill himself? And why did he use a
rook rifle? A revolver would have been much more certain.”

“But he hadn’t got a revolver.”

“True, he hadn’t. But he could easily have got one. And then,
there is the mysterious stranger. Who was he, and what was he
doing there? No, Hastings, I am not yet satisfied. I must think,
I must think.”

We reached the house, and Poirot went into the morning-room to
speak to Mrs. Maltravers. I waited for him in the hall. In a few
minutes he came out, looking very grave.

“I have told Mrs. Maltravers that I must go back to London at once.
I have a lot to do, and I must not waste any more time. You will
come with me, Hastings?”

“Of course.”

We went to the station and caught the next train to London.
During the journey Poirot was very silent, and I did not like to
disturb him. When we reached Liverpool Street, he took a taxi to
his rooms, and I went back to my own.

The next morning I received a note from Poirot asking me to come
and see him at eleven o’clock. When I arrived, I found him
sitting at his desk, with a pile of papers in front of him.

“Ah, Hastings, I am glad you have come. I have been very busy
this morning, and I think I have at last solved the mystery of the
death of Mr. Maltravers.”

“You have? Who was it?”

“Wait a moment, my friend. All in good time. First, let us
consider the facts. Mr. Maltravers was on the verge of bankruptcy.
He insured his life for fifty thousand pounds. He was found dead
with a rook rifle by his side. The cause of death was an internal
hæmorrhage. Now, as I told you, a man cannot commit suicide by
swallowing poison that would cause such a hæmorrhage. But there is
another way in which such a hæmorrhage could be caused. Do you
know what it is?”

“No.”

“It could be caused by a blow—a very violent blow on the
stomach. Such a blow would cause an internal hæmorrhage, and
might easily prove fatal. Now, who could have given Mr.
Maltravers such a blow?”

“I don’t know.”

“Think, Hastings, think. Who was there at the time?”

“Well, there was Mrs. Maltravers, and the servants, and the
mysterious stranger.”

“Exactly. The mysterious stranger. Now, who was he?”

“I’ve no idea.”

“I think I can tell you. He was a man named Alfred Wright.”

“Alfred Wright? The director of the Insurance Company?”

“The same. And why was he there? Because he knew that Mr.
Maltravers was going to commit suicide, and he wanted to prevent
him. He had heard the story of the suicide in East Africa, and he
guessed that Mr. Maltravers was going to try the same thing. So
he went down to Marsdon Manor to stop him. He found Mr.
Maltravers in the plantation, and they had a violent quarrel. In
the course of the quarrel, Wright struck Maltravers a blow on the
stomach, which caused the hæmorrhage from which he died. Then,
frightened at what he had done, he fled from the scene, and has
been in hiding ever since.”

“But how do you know all this, Poirot?”

“I have been making inquiries, Hastings. I found out that Wright
had been seen in the neighbourhood of Marsdon Manor on Wednesday
afternoon. And then, I found this.”

He held up a small piece of paper.

“What is it?”

“It is a receipt for a grey beard, which Mr. Wright purchased
at a theatrical costumier’s on Tuesday morning. You see, he wanted
to disguise himself so that he should not be recognized.”

“But why should he want to disguise himself?”

“Because he did not want anyone to know that he was going to
see Mr. Maltravers. He knew that if it were known that a director
of the Insurance Company had been to see him, it would look very
suspicious if Mr. Maltravers were to die shortly afterwards. So
he took every precaution. But, unfortunately for him, he was seen
by the parlourmaid, and his disguise was not as perfect as he
thought.”

“But this is incredible, Poirot. Alfred Wright, a director of the
Northern Union, a murderer!”

“Not a murderer, Hastings. It was an accident. He did not mean
to kill him. But he is responsible for his death, and he must pay
the penalty.”

“And what are you going to do?”

“I have already done it. I have informed the police, and they
are now on their way to arrest Mr. Wright. And now, I think, we
will go and have some lunch. I am very hungry.”

And that was the end of the mystery of the death of Mr. Maltravers.
It was a very sad business, but I suppose justice must be done.
As for Mrs. Maltravers, I hear that she has since married Captain
Black, and I hope they will be very happy together. They
certainly deserve to be, after all they have been through.

When we reached the house we were told that Mrs. Maltravers was
out in the garden. We went in search of her, and found her sitting
on a seat at the edge of the little wood where her husband had
met his death. She was looking very pale and her eyes were large
and frightened.

“I have some very serious news for you, madame,” began Poirot
gently. “It is about the insurance on your husband’s life.”

She began to tremble.

“Is there any difficulty?”

“A very serious difficulty. You see, the Company has discovered
that your husband committed suicide.”

Mrs. Maltravers uttered a stifled cry.

“It is not true! He did not—he did not! How can they prove it?”

“By the story he heard at dinner on Tuesday night,” said Poirot.
“He followed that story to the letter. He killed himself with a
rook rifle—through the roof of his mouth. It was very clever—the
body had to be moved, of course, because of the blood, but that
was easily managed.”

Mrs. Maltravers was shaking with terror.

“But—but—if it is suicide—I shall not get the money?”

“No,” said Poirot, “you will not get the money.”

She looked at him with a strange expression.

“Then I have done it all for nothing!” she cried. “All for
nothing—and I am ruined!”

She sank back on the seat, her face buried in her hands. Poirot
stood watching her for a moment, then he turned away.

“Come, Hastings,” he said. “There is nothing more for us to do
here.”

We walked back to the village in silence. I was feeling very sorry
for the poor girl. It was a tragedy, any way you looked at it.
But Poirot seemed strangely preoccupied.

“What is it?” I asked at last.

“I am wondering, Hastings, whether I have been very clever—or very
stupid. I think—I think—I have been very stupid.”

“In what way?”

“I have a feeling that there is something I have missed—something
that would explain everything.”

He was silent for a while, and then he said suddenly:

“Hastings, I must go back. I must go back to the Manor at once.”

“But why?”

“Because I have just remembered something. Something that Dr.
Bernard said. Something very important.”

He would say no more, and we hurried back to the house. As we
approached, we saw a figure coming towards us. It was Dr. Bernard.

“Ah, doctor,” said Poirot. “The very man I wanted to see. I have
been thinking over what you told me this morning.”

The doctor looked at him suspiciously.

“Well?”

“You said, did you not, that Mr. Maltravers was a Christian
Scientist?”

“I believe so. Why?”

“And yet he was insured for fifty thousand pounds?”

“I don’t see the connection.”

“Do you not? A Christian Scientist does not believe in death—or
disease. Why, then, should he insure his life?”

The doctor stared at him.

“I—I really don’t know.”

“And there is another thing. You said there was blood on his lips.
But if he died of a hæmorrhage, there would be more than that,
would there not?”

“It—it depends,” stammered the doctor.

“Exactly. It depends. And now, Dr. Bernard, I am going to ask you
a very simple question. Who killed Mr. Maltravers?”

The doctor went white to the lips.

“I—I don’t know what you mean.”

“I think you do. You were the only person who saw the body before
it was moved. You were the only person who could have—shall we say—
arranged matters. You see, doctor, I have been making a few
inquiries. I find that you were in very low water financially—that,
in fact, you were on the verge of bankruptcy.”

The doctor made a desperate effort to recover himself.

“It is a lie! A wicked lie!”

“Is it? We shall see. And now, if you will excuse me, I have a
little business to attend to with Mrs. Maltravers.”

He turned and walked towards the house, leaving the doctor standing
speechless in the middle of the road.

“Poirot!” I cried. “What does it mean? Do you really mean that
the doctor——”

“Wait, Hastings, wait. All will be clear in a few minutes.”

We found Mrs. Maltravers in the morning-room. She looked up
fearfully as we entered.

“What is it?” she asked. “Why have you come back?”

“I have come back, madame, to tell you that I know the truth.”

She shrank back in her chair.

“The truth?”

“Yes. I know that your husband did not commit suicide. I know
that he was murdered.”

She gave a low cry.

“Murdered? By whom?”

“By your lover, Captain Black.”

“No, no! It is not true!”

“Is it not? Then perhaps you will tell me who it was that you saw
in the garden on Tuesday night—the man who was with your husband
just before he died?”

She did not answer, but her eyes were fixed on his face in a kind
of horror.

“I will tell you,” said Poirot. “It was Mr. Alfred Wright.”

“Alfred Wright?” I gasped. “But he is the director of the Insurance
Company!”

“Exactly. And he is also, if I am not mistaken, the man who was
having an affair with Mrs. Maltravers.”

The woman gave a scream and fell back in her chair.

“It’s a lie! A wicked lie!”

“Is it? We shall see. And now, Hastings, if you will be so good as
to fetch the constable, I think we shall find Mr. Wright at the
Anchor Inn. He was expecting to hear from Mrs. Maltravers that
all was well, but I think he will find his expectations
disappointed.”

As I went to the door, I saw Poirot looking at the woman with a
look of grim satisfaction.

“_Eh bien_, Hastings,” he said. “It was a very pretty little
plot—but they forgot that Hercule Poirot has a sense of smell!”

And with that he turned and walked out of the room.

The arrest of Alfred Wright followed shortly afterwards. It
appeared that he had been involved in some very shady financial
transactions, and had used the Insurance Company’s money to cover
his losses. When he found that he was about to be discovered, he
conceived the plan of murdering Maltravers and making it look like
suicide, so that the insurance money would cover his defalcations.
He had induced Mrs. Maltravers to help him, promising her a share
of the money. Dr. Bernard had been bribed to give a false death
certificate.

“A very simple case, after all,” said Poirot, as we sat in the
train on our way back to London. “But it shows, Hastings, that
even the most clever criminals make mistakes. They forgot that
a Christian Scientist does not insure his life!”

“But how did you know about Alfred Wright?” I asked.

“My friend, it was the list of words. When I said ‘Money,’ Captain
Black answered ‘Lawyers.’ Now, if he had been the lover of Mrs.
Maltravers, he would have thought of her—or of the money she was
going to get. But he thought of lawyers. That showed me that he
was not interested in the money. And when I said ‘Bernard,’ he
answered ‘Shaw.’ If he had been in league with the doctor, he
would have thought of him. So I knew that the doctor and the
Captain were not working together. And then I remembered that
Alfred Wright was the man who had asked me to investigate the
case. Why should he do that, unless he wanted to make sure that
the insurance company would pay? It was a very clever move—but it
was his undoing.”

“And Mrs. Maltravers?”

“She will be dealt with in due course. A beautiful woman, Hastings,
but a very dangerous one. It is lucky for you that you have me to
look after you!”

And Poirot settled himself back in his seat with a smile of
satisfaction.

The butler (the parlourmaid’s place was taken by a man-servant at
night) showed us into the morning-room. Mrs. Maltravers was
waiting for us.

“You have found out something?” she asked eagerly.

“Madame,” said Poirot, “I have found out—everything. Your husband’s
life is insured for fifty thousand pounds. If it were a case of
suicide that sum would be lost to you.”

She grew very pale.

“It—it was not suicide?”

“Madame, I have reason to believe that it was not.”

“You mean—it was an accident?”

“I do not.”

“Then what do you mean?”

“I mean—murder!”

Mrs. Maltravers sank back in her chair with a little cry.

“Murder? Oh, no!”

“Madame, I must ask you to tell me the truth. Where is the man who
was staying here on Wednesday—the day of your husband’s death?”

“Staying here? There was no one staying here.”

“I think you are mistaken. A man arrived here on Wednesday
afternoon.”

“Oh, you mean the man who came to see my husband about some
business? I don’t know who he was. I only saw him for a minute.
He was a tall man with a beard.”

“I see. And he left—when?”

“Almost immediately, I believe. I was upstairs in my room.”

“I see. And you did not see him again?”

“No.”

“And you have no idea who he was?”

“None whatever.”

“He did not tell you his name?”

“No.”

“And your husband did not mention it?”

“No.”

“I see. Now, I have a little theory. I believe that this man
with the beard was no other than your husband’s murderer.”

“But how—how could he have killed him?”

“That, madame, is what I am going to show you.”

Poirot stepped to the window and threw it open.

“Will you come this way, please?”

He led the way out on to the terrace. I followed, and Mrs.
Maltravers came slowly after us.

“It was just here, was it not, that your husband’s body was found?”

“Yes.”

“And he was lying—how?”

“With his head towards the plantation.”

“I see. And the rook rifle was lying—where?”

“Beside him.”

“I see. Now, I will show you how the murder was committed.”

Poirot took a small object from his pocket. It was a small piece
of wood. He placed it on the ground.

“Now, madame, if you will be so good as to stand just here.”

He indicated a spot a few yards away.

“Now, I am the murderer. I have a rook rifle in my hand. I am
standing here. Your husband is standing where you are. I fire—so!”

He made a gesture as if firing a rifle.

“The bullet enters your husband’s mouth. He falls—so!”

Poirot dropped on to his knees.

“The murderer then runs up to him. He places the rook rifle beside
him. He then runs away. You see how simple it is?”

“But—but there was no bullet wound!”

“Ah, but that is where the murderer was so clever. He used a
bullet made of—ice!”

“Of ice?”

“Precisely. The ice bullet enters the mouth. It melts. There is
no trace of it left. Only a little blood on the lips.”

Mrs. Maltravers stared at him.

“But—but who could have done such a thing?”

“That, madame, is what I am going to tell you. The murderer was—your
husband’s guest, the man with the beard!”

“But who was he?”

“He was—Mr. Alfred Wright!”

“Alfred Wright? But he is a director of the Insurance Company!”

“Exactly. And he is also—your husband’s murderer!”

“But why—why should he kill him?”

“Because, madame, your husband had discovered that Mr. Wright
had been embezzling the Company’s funds. He was going to expose
him. So Mr. Wright decided to kill him. He knew of your husband’s
fears of a second hæmorrhage. He knew of the story Captain Black
had told at dinner. He saw his opportunity. He came here on
Wednesday afternoon. He found your husband alone. He killed him with
the ice bullet. Then he went back to London and sent me here to
investigate the case, thinking that I should find it a case of
suicide and so the Insurance Company would not have to pay the
money. It was a very clever plot, but he forgot one thing.”

“What was that?”

“He forgot—Hercule Poirot!”

Mrs. Maltravers gave a long sigh.

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot, how can I ever thank you?”

“By telling me the truth, madame.”

“The truth?”

“Yes. There was no man with a beard, was there?”

Mrs. Maltravers hesitated for a moment, then she shook her head.

“No,” she whispered.

“I thought not. And your husband did not die of a hæmorrhage,
did he?”

“No.”

“He died—of what?”

“He died—of fright!”

“Of fright?”

“Yes. You see, he was very nervous. He was always imagining things.
And when Captain Black told that story about the man who killed
himself with a rook rifle, it made a great impression on him. He
couldn’t get it out of his mind. And on Wednesday afternoon he
was out with his rook rifle, and he—he began to think about it.
And then—then he saw something.”

“What did he see?”

“He saw—a ghost!”

“A ghost?”

“Yes. He saw the ghost of the man who had killed himself! And it
frightened him so much that he—he died!”

“I see. And who was this ghost?”

“I don’t know. He just said he saw a ghost.”

“I see. Well, madame, I think I can tell you who the ghost was.
It was—Mr. Alfred Wright!”

“Mr. Wright? But he wasn’t here!”

“Oh, yes, he was. He came down here on Wednesday afternoon. He
did not come to the house. He went to the plantation. He knew
your husband would be there. He had dressed himself up to look
like the man in Captain Black’s story. He knew your husband’s
nervous state, and he thought that if he saw the ghost it would
frighten him to death. And it did!”

Mrs. Maltravers looked at him in amazement.

“But how—how do you know all this?”

“Because, madame, I have just had a little talk with Mr. Wright
on the telephone. He has confessed everything!”

“Confessed?”

“Yes. You see, he was not a very strong character. And when I
told him that I had found the ice bullet——”

“The ice bullet? But you said there was no ice bullet!”

“Exactly. But Mr. Wright did not know that. He thought I had
really found it. And so he confessed.”

Mrs. Maltravers sank into a chair.

“Oh, Monsieur Poirot, you are wonderful!”

“It is my business to be wonderful, madame,” said Poirot modestly.

And so the mystery of Marsdon Manor was solved. Mr. Alfred Wright
was arrested and duly punished for his crime. And Mrs. Maltravers,
after a suitable interval, married Captain Black and lived
happily ever after.

As for Poirot, he merely remarked:

“_En vérité_, Hastings, it is a great thing to have the imagination.
Without it, I should never have thought of the ice bullet!”

We found her alone in the morning-room. Poirot told her gently
how he had discovered that her husband’s death was not what it
appeared, but that his investigations into his financial position
showed that he was indeed in a most desperate position.

“But the insurance?” she faltered.

“I regret to have to tell you that there is a suicide clause in
the policy, and that under the circumstances the Company cannot
entertain any claim.”

She sat quite still, her face as white as paper.

“I am very, very sorry, madame,” said Poirot, with a trace of
emotion in his voice.

“Is there no hope?”

“None, I fear.”

She turned to him with a little gesture of despair.

“What am I to do?” she cried. “I have nothing in the world.”

“Madame,” said Poirot, and his eyes were very kind, “I have an
extraordinary proposal to make to you. I am not an old man, and
I have saved some money. If you would honour me by becoming my
wife——”

I could hardly believe my ears. I knew Poirot was an admirer of
beauty, but this—it was incredible! Mrs. Maltravers, however, drew
herself up.

“Monsieur Poirot,” she said, with some dignity, “I can only
attribute your extraordinary proposal to a desire to help me. But
I have a better way than that. I shall go to my husband’s friend,
Mr. Alfred Wright. He is a man of great influence, and I am sure
he will help me to get some of the money.”

Poirot’s face fell.

“Mr. Alfred Wright?” he said. “He is a very hard man, I fear.
Still, if you wish it——”

“I do wish it,” she said firmly.

“Then I will leave you. But I should like to see you again before
I go.”

“Certainly. I shall be here.”

We walked back to the Anchor Inn in silence. I was too disgusted
with Poirot to speak to him. That he should have taken advantage
of a woman’s distress in such a way! It was unlike him.

When we reached the inn, Poirot went straight to the telephone.
After some delay he got through.

“Is that you, Wright? Poirot speaking. Yes, I have some news for
you. I’ll come up by the morning train. Yes, it’s a suicide all
right. No, no doubt about it. I’ve seen the widow. Yes, she’s
coming to see you to-morrow. She wants to see if you can’t get the
Company to pay some of the money. She’s a very beautiful woman,
Wright. Yes. Good-bye.”

He rang off and turned to me.

“And now, Hastings, we will have some dinner.”

I was still feeling very cold and distant towards him, but he
seemed not to notice it. He was in the highest of spirits. After
dinner he suggested that we should go up to the Manor again.

“To see Mrs. Maltravers?” I asked, with a sneer.

“No, to see the doctor.”

“Dr. Bernard?”

“Yes.”

We found the doctor at home, and Poirot spent some time with him.
When we came out, he was more cheerful than ever.

“And now,” he said, “we will go to the Manor.”

“To see Mrs. Maltravers this time?”

“Precisely.”

We were shown into the morning-room as before. Mrs. Maltravers
was there, but she was not alone. Captain Black was with her.

“I am glad you have come,” she said, “for I wanted to tell you
that I have changed my mind. I shall not go to Mr. Wright. Captain
Black has been so kind as to offer to help me.”

Poirot’s face fell.

“I see,” he said. “Captain Black is a very lucky man.”

“I don’t know about that,” said the Captain, blushing. “But I’m
going to do my best.”

“I’m sure you are,” said Poirot. “And now, if you will excuse me,
I have a little business to attend to.”

He left the room, and I followed him. He went straight to the
library, and I heard him turn the key in the lock.

“What are you doing?” I asked.

“I am going to look for something,” he said.

He was busy for some time, and when he came out he was carrying a
small object in his hand.

“What is it?” I asked.

“A piece of paper,” he said.

He led the way back to the morning-room.

“Mrs. Maltravers,” he said, “I have something to show you.”

He held out the piece of paper. She took it, and as she read it
her face changed.

“Where did you find this?” she gasped.

“In the library,” said Poirot. “It is a letter from your husband’s
lawyers, is it not? It tells him that his financial position is
not so bad as he thought, and that he will be able to pay all his
debts and have a comfortable income left.”

Mrs. Maltravers looked as if she were going to faint.

“But—but—then he didn’t commit suicide?” she gasped.

“On the contrary,” said Poirot, “he was murdered.”

“Murdered!” We all three cried the word together.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “He was murdered by the person who knew of
this letter, and who wanted the insurance money.”

“But who?” cried Mrs. Maltravers.

“That,” said Poirot, “I am going to show you.”

He went to the door and called:

“Come in, please.”

The door opened, and a man entered the room. It was Alfred Wright.

“Mr. Wright!” cried Mrs. Maltravers.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “Mr. Wright is the man who murdered your
husband.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Wright. “I wasn’t even here when he died.”

“That is true,” said Poirot. “But you were here the day before.
And you were the person who suggested the idea of suicide to him.
You knew of his financial difficulties, and you knew of the large
insurance he had just taken out. You also knew that if he committed
suicide the money would be forfeited. But you had a plan. You told
him the story of the man who killed himself with a rook rifle in
such a way that it looked like a natural death. You knew that he
was a man of weak character, and that he would be likely to take
the suggestion. But you did more than that. You saw that he got
the rook rifle, and you even went so far as to load it for him.
But you made one mistake, Mr. Wright. You did not know that the
lawyers’ letter had arrived, telling him that his affairs were
not so bad after all. When he read that letter, he changed his
mind about suicide. But it was too late. You had already arranged
everything. You had even gone so far as to tell Mrs. Maltravers
about the suicide story, so that she would be prepared for it.
And when you heard that he was dead, you were sure that your plan
had succeeded. But you were wrong. Mr. Maltravers did not commit
suicide. He was murdered by you.”

“It’s a lie, I tell you!” cried Wright. “How could I have murdered
him when I wasn’t here?”

“You murdered him,” said Poirot, “by means of a very simple
device. You knew that he was in the habit of shooting rooks in
the afternoon. You also knew the exact spot where he usually stood.
You arranged a mechanical device by which the rook rifle would be
fired at a certain time. It was a very simple device—just a piece
of string and a clock. You set the clock for the time when you
knew he would be there, and then you went away. It was a very
clever plan, Mr. Wright, but it failed because you did not know
about the lawyers’ letter.”

Wright’s face was ghastly. He made a sudden dash for the door, but
Poirot was too quick for him. In a moment he was struggling in
the hands of the two village constables whom Poirot had brought
with him.

“And now, madame,” said Poirot, turning to Mrs. Maltravers, “I
think you will find that the Insurance Company will be only too
pleased to pay the money. And I think,” he added, with a glance
at Captain Black, “that you will not be in need of my assistance
any longer.”

He bowed and led the way out of the room.

“Poirot,” I said, as we walked back to the inn, “you are a wonderful
man.”

“_Mon ami_,” he said, “it was very simple. The discrepancy I spoke
of was the fact that the rook rifle had been fired twice. If a man
wishes to commit suicide, he does not usually fire a preliminary
shot to see if the gun is working properly! And then there was the
lawyers’ letter. I found that in the library, as I told you. It
had been opened, but not read by Mr. Maltravers. It was Mr. Wright
who had opened it, and who had then hidden it, thinking that no
one would find it. But he forgot that Hercule Poirot has eyes that
see everything!”

“And the proposal of marriage?” I asked.

Poirot chuckled.

“That, my friend, was what you call a ‘bluff.’ I wanted to see
what Mrs. Maltravers would do. If she had accepted me, I should
have known that she was not in love with Captain Black. But as
she refused me, I knew that my little plan was succeeding. You
see, Hastings, even Hercule Poirot can be a matchmaker sometimes!”

And he laughed his little bird-like laugh.

“_Eh bien_,” said Poirot, returning after his visit to the Manor,
“I have told her. She was deeply moved—_terriblement_! And she
prayed me to let her see her husband’s body. She had not had the
courage to look on it before, and now she felt it was a duty to
do so.”

“But the body is buried by now!” I exclaimed.

“_Certainement_. So we are to go to the churchyard to-morrow. The
rector is an old friend of Dr. Bernard’s, so he will doubtless
assist us.”

I was somewhat surprised. I did not see what good could result from
the exhumation of the poor man’s remains. But Poirot had his own
way of doing things.

Our interview with the lady was painful. She refused vehemently to
believe the facts that Poirot advanced, and when she was at last
convinced broke down into bitter weeping. An examination of the
body turned our suspicions into certainty. Poirot was very sorry
for the poor lady, but, after all, he was employed by the Insurance
Company, and what could he do? As he was preparing to leave he said
gently to Mrs. Maltravers:

“Madame, you of all people should know that there are no dead!”

“What do you mean?” she faltered, her eyes growing wide.

“Have you never taken part in any spiritualistic séances? You are
mediumistic, you know.”

“I have been told so. But you do not believe in Spiritualism,
surely?”

“Madame, I have seen some strange things. You know that they say
in the village that this house is haunted?”

She nodded, and at that moment the parlourmaid announced that
dinner was ready.

“Won’t you just stay and have something to eat?”

We accepted gratefully, and I felt that our presence could not but
help distract her a little from her own griefs.

We had just finished our soup, when there was a scream outside the
door, and the sound of breaking crockery. We jumped up. The
parlourmaid appeared, her hand to her heart.

“It was a man—standing in the passage.”

Poirot rushed out, returning quickly.

“There is no one there.”

“Isn’t there, sir?” said the parlourmaid weakly. “Oh, it did give
me a start!”

“But why?”

She dropped her voice to a whisper.

“I thought—I thought it was the master—it looked like ’im.”

Mrs. Maltravers gasped, her face turning a sickly, translucent white. “It is the house!” she cried. “I knew it was haunted! Ever since—ever since Wednesday—I have felt it!” Poirot leaned forward, his eyes suddenly glowing with a strange, cat-like green light. “Is it the house, Madame? Or is it the conscience? The spirits of the dead are sometimes permitted to return when they have been—shall we say—dismissed from this life with undue haste. They seek the truth, and they seek the one who sent them into the shadows.” He spoke with a quiet, terrifying authority that held us all spellbound. I felt a cold prickle of apprehension crawl down my spine, and even the shadows in the corners of the room seemed to take on a sinister, shifting life of their own.

“Nonsense,” I cried. “The poor girl is upset, that is all. A shadow, perhaps—” but Mrs. Maltravers had risen from her seat, her face a mask of frozen terror. Her eyes were fixed upon the darkened hallway beyond the dining-room door. “He has come back,” she whispered, her voice barely audible. “I knew he would. He will never rest.” Poirot, however, remained strangely calm, his eyes shining with that peculiar green light that always betokened his intense mental activity. He leaned forward, his voice low and compelling. “Calm yourself, madame. If the dead return, it is because they have a message for the living. Perhaps your husband has something he wishes to say—something that was left unsaid in life. Shall we not see if we can help him find the truth?”

Mrs. Maltravers uttered a stifled cry, her hands clutching the edge of the table until the knuckles showed white. “My husband?” she whispered, her voice trembling with a terror that seemed all too real. “But he is dead—I saw him—we both saw him!” Poirot leaned forward, his eyes shining with a strange green light that I had learned to associate with his moments of most intense focus. “The dead do not always rest, Madame, when the cause of their departure remains shrouded in the mists of deception. Perhaps he has a message for those he left behind—or perhaps he seeks justice for a life cut short.” I felt a sudden, icy chill permeate the room, and even the flicker of the candles seemed to dance with a ghostly rhythm as we sat in a silence that was heavy with the unseen.

Mrs. Maltravers uttered a stifled cry, her hand flying to her throat. The colour, which had begun to return to her cheeks, ebbed away, leaving her deathly pale. Poirot, however, remained singularly unmoved. He leaned forward, his eyes fixed upon the terrified girl, and then turned his gaze slowly towards our hostess. The silence in the room was heavy, broken only by the ticking of the great grandfather clock in the hall. It was as if the very air had grown thick with an unseen presence, a cold breath from the world beyond that chilled the marrow of one's bones.

“Calm yourself, my child,” said Poirot, patting the girl’s arm. “It is the nerves, nothing more. Or stay—is it perhaps something more? Madame,” he turned to Mrs. Maltravers, his voice dropping to a low, persuasive tone, “I have a suggestion. The air in this house is heavy with the unspoken. Why do we not seek the truth from the only one who knows it? Let us hold a séance here, now, in the very room where the master of the house so lately sat.”

I saw Mrs. Maltravers give a terrified start, and my mind flew to
the old superstition that a suicide cannot rest. She thought of it
too, I am sure, for a minute later, she caught Poirot’s arm with
a scream.

“Didn’t you hear that? Those three taps on the window? That’s how
_he_ always used to tap when he passed round the house.”

“The ivy,” I cried. “It was the ivy against the pane.”

“No, it was more like a human hand. Oh, it’s horrible—horrible!”

Poirot moved to the window and threw it open. There was no one
outside.

“It was just a bird, madame,” he said soothingly.

Mrs. Maltravers went back to her seat, but her hand shook so she
could hardly hold her fork. She looked as if she were seeing
ghosts.

“I believe it’s true, what they say in the village,” she whispered.
“I believe this house is haunted.”

“Well, let us see if we can’t get some news of this ghost. Shall
we have a little séance?”

“A séance? Here? Now?”

“Why not? It’s a very good time. We’ll just put out the lights and
sit round the table and see what happens.”

“Oh, I couldn’t!”

“Courage, madame, courage! There is nothing to fear. We are all
friends. You yourself are mediumistic, I’m sure.”

“I’m terrified! I’m terrified!”

“Come, come. Just sit round the table and join hands.”

We did so, and I could feel the poor lady’s hand shaking in mine.
The room was in total darkness, save for a faint glimmer from the
hall.

“Now, let us think of nothing in particular. Just wait. Are you
there, spirit? Give us a sign if you are.”

For some minutes nothing happened, then I heard a faint sound—a
tapping on the table.

“_One, two, three._”

“Is that you, Roger?” gasped Mrs. Maltravers.

“_One, two, three._”

The tapping continued, and suddenly it seemed to me that a faint
phosphorescent light was beginning to show in the corner of the
room.

Mrs. Maltravers gave a low moan.

“It’s Roger! I know it’s Roger! Oh, what does he want? What does
he want?”

“Ask him!” said Poirot.

“Roger—Roger—is that you?”

The tapping was very loud now.

“_Yes._”

“What do you want to tell us?”

The tapping stopped, and for a minute there was a dead silence.
Then a voice, thin and high-pitched, seemed to come from the very
far distance.

“_I want—justice—justice._”

Mrs. Maltravers gave a long, low cry.

“Roger—Roger—forgive me!”

“_Justice_,” came the voice again. “_Tell them—tell them the
truth._”

With a sudden, sharp cry, Mrs. Maltravers fell forward on the
table. Poirot sprang to his feet and turned on the light.

“_Vite, vite_, Hastings! Water—brandy!”

He was bending over the unconscious woman.

“She’s fainted. It was too much for her.”

We worked over her for some minutes, but it was not until we had
given her some brandy that she showed signs of returning
consciousness. Then she opened her eyes and looked round her
with a terrified expression.

“Where is he? Where is he?”

“He has gone, madame. He will not trouble you again.”

“But he said—he said——”

“He said you were to tell the truth. That is it, is it not?”

She looked at him with a wild, hunted expression.

“I will tell you—I will tell you everything. It was I—I did it.”

“You killed your husband?”

“Yes.”

“But how? He died of a hæmorrhage.”

She shook her head.

“No, no. I—I shot him.”

“Shot him?”

“Yes, with the rook rifle. I knew about that story Captain Black
told. I—I thought it would be quite safe. I waited till he was out
in the garden, and then I went out and shot him through the mouth.”

“But the doctor? He said——”

“The doctor is a fool. He saw what I wanted him to see. He only
looked at the blood on the lips and jumped to his own conclusion.”

“And the motive?”

“We were ruined. I didn’t know it till a few days ago. He had
insured his life for fifty thousand pounds. I thought—I thought
it would be so easy. And then—then when you came—and that Captain
Black——”

She broke down into a fit of sobbing.

Poirot patted her hand.

“There, there, madame. Do not distress yourself. It is better to
have told the truth.”

He turned to me.

“Hastings, will you go and fetch Dr. Bernard? He must be informed
of these new developments.”

I went off on my errand, my head in a whirl. When I returned with
the doctor, I found Poirot alone in the morning-room.

“Where is Mrs. Maltravers?” I asked.

“She has gone to her room. She is very much upset, naturally.”

“And what are you going to do?”

“My friend, I have already done it. I have telephoned to the
police.”

“The police!”

“But certainly. What did you expect? A murder has been committed.”

“But I thought—I thought you were acting for the Insurance
Company?”

“So I am. And they will be very much interested to hear that Mr.
Maltravers did not commit suicide, but was murdered by his wife.”

“But the séance—the ghost——”

Poirot chuckled.

“A little arrangement of my own, Hastings. A few simple
mechanical devices—and a little ventriloquism. It is often useful
to play upon the nerves of the guilty.”

“Then it wasn’t a real ghost after all?”

“My dear Hastings! You, a man of the twentieth century! No, it was
not a real ghost. But it served its purpose.”

“And Mrs. Maltravers will be hanged?”

“I should imagine so. She is a very cold-blooded murderess.”

I sighed. It seemed a pity that such a beautiful woman should
come to such an end. But, as Poirot said, she was a murderess.

“But what about the discrepancy you mentioned?” I asked. “The one
you noticed when we were at the house before?”

“Ah, that! It was very simple. Mrs. Maltravers told us that she
had been to the village to get some stamps. But when I looked at
the letters on the hall table, I saw that they were all stamped
with stamps of an old issue—stamps that had been in the house for
some time. So I knew that she was lying. And when a woman lies
about a small thing like that, it is usually because she has
something much bigger to conceal.”

“You are a wonderful man, Poirot,” I said admiringly.

“I am a very simple one, Hastings. I only use my eyes—and my little
grey cells.”

She shook her head. “No, no, I know it wasn’t. He is here, he’s
in this house!”

“Madame!” Poirot spoke firmly. “I do not think you need be
afraid—if you have done no harm. But it is true, there is a strange
influence at work here. I feel it myself. And there is a presence
here—a presence that has something to tell us. The spirit of the
man who has just passed away is here, and he wants us to know the
truth. Madame, if you will only do as I tell you, we may find out
what it is.”

“What can I do?”

“We will have a séance. We will put out the lights and join hands
round the table. And we will ask the dead man to tell us what he
will. It is the only way.”

I felt that Poirot was taking a very strange course, but then he
was always a little unconventional.

Mrs. Maltravers was trembling all over.

“Oh, I don’t think I could—I’m so frightened.”

“Courage, Madame! I will be beside you.”

“And Captain Black? He—he was there, too.”

“By all means, let us have the Captain. He will be at the inn, I
expect.”

“Yes, I believe he is.”

“Then we will send for him.”

Ten minutes later Captain Black arrived, and Poirot explained his
purpose. The young man looked a little doubtful.

“I don’t know that I care for that sort of thing,” he said
hesitantly. “Seems a bit—ghastly, don’t you know?”

“No, no, it is for the best. Mrs. Maltravers wishes it.”

“Oh, in that case, of course——”

We adjourned to the morning-room, and there the lights were put
out and we sat in a circle round the table. Poirot’s voice came
to us out of the darkness.

“Is there any one here?”

There was no answer.

“Is there any one here?” he asked again.

Still no answer.

“We will wait a little.”

We waited in silence for what seemed a long time. Then, suddenly,
a cold breath of air seemed to pass through the room. Mrs.
Maltravers gave a little stifled cry.

“He is here,” whispered Poirot. “I feel him. Now, speak! Who is
it? Is it the spirit of the man who died on Wednesday?”

A low, moaning sound came from somewhere.

“Speak! Tell us what it is you want us to know. Was it suicide?”

“No.” The word seemed to be breathed rather than spoken.

“Then what was it? Was it—murder?”

There was a sudden, sharp cry from Mrs. Maltravers.

“No, no, don’t say that! It wasn’t murder! It was an accident!
He—he did it himself!”

“Then why are you here?” Poirot’s voice was stern. “Why do you
haunt this house?”

“Because—because I cannot rest. I want the truth to be known.”

“Then tell us the truth. Who killed you?”

There was a long silence. Then, suddenly, a light appeared in the
corner of the room. It was a faint, greenish glow, and in the
middle of it we saw—or thought we saw—the face of the dead man!

It was a terrifying sight. Mrs. Maltravers shrieked and fell
forward on the table. Captain Black sprang to his feet, and Poirot
turned on the lights.

Mrs. Maltravers was in a dead faint. Poirot and I carried her to
a sofa, and then Poirot turned to Captain Black.

“You see, _mon ami_, how it is? The dead do not rest when they
have been foully murdered.”

“Murdered?” Black gasped. “But you said just now——”

“I said many things. Now, I will tell you the truth.”

Mrs. Maltravers was shaking with terror, and when she got up and
suggested our moving into the drawing-room for coffee we followed
her with alacrity. I could see that the house was getting on her
nerves. Poirot looked around the room as we entered.

“A beautiful room, madame, but do you not feel it is a little
chilly?”

“I do feel cold.” She shivered.

“And what is that I see there?”

Poirot pointed to a small table on which stood a bowl of roses.

“Those flowers—they are quite dead.”

Mrs. Maltravers looked at them.

“They were quite fresh this afternoon. I—I don’t understand.”

“They have been blighted—by some evil influence,” said Poirot
gravely. “Madame, I believe your husband’s spirit is in this room.”

She looked at him with an expression of such mortal terror that
I felt for her with all my heart.

“I—I cannot bear it,” she cried. “Let us go into the hall—anywhere.”

“No, madame,” said Poirot firmly. “You must stay here. Your husband
has something to say to you. I can feel him near us.”

Suddenly, the lights went out. I heard a low moan from Mrs.
Maltravers, and Poirot’s voice calling to me to be silent.

Then, out of the darkness, a voice spoke. It was a man’s voice,
low and very clear.

“_Jane_,” it said. “_Jane, I am here_.”

Mrs. Maltravers gave a stifled scream.

“_Jane, why did you do it?_”

“Oh!” she cried. “I—I—mercy—mercy!”

“_Jane, tell them everything—it is the only way for me to rest._”

“I will—I will!” she gasped.

Suddenly the lights went up. Mrs. Maltravers was lying on the floor
in a dead faint. Poirot was standing by the switch.

“Hastings, quickly. Get me some water.”

I ran into the dining-room and brought back a carafe. Mrs.
Maltravers was just beginning to come to. Poirot was bending over
her.

“There, there, madame. It is all over. You will feel better now.”

“What was it?” she whispered. “Did he—did he really speak?”

“He did,” said Poirot. “And now you must tell us everything, as
he said.”

She looked at him for a moment and then buried her face in her
hands.

“I will. It’s better than this awful fear. I—I didn’t mean to do
it. But he wouldn’t give me any money, and I wanted it so badly.
And then he insured his life, and I thought—if only he were dead!
And then that young man came and told us about the man who killed
himself with the rook rifle, and I thought how easy it would be.
So when he was out in the garden I went out and spoke to him. He
was just going to shoot at a rook, and I said, ‘Let me see if I
can do it.’ He laughed and gave me the rifle. I told him to shut
his eyes and open his mouth, and then—I shot him. Oh, it was
horrible—horrible! But I didn’t think anyone would ever know.”

She broke into a passion of sobbing.

Poirot turned to me.

“Hastings, if you would go and fetch the doctor.”

I went, and when I returned with Dr. Bernard, Mrs. Maltravers had
been taken upstairs.

“A most painful business,” said the doctor. “A most painful
business. I could never have believed it of such a charming lady.”

“No,” said Poirot dryly. “But then, you see, you are a man,
doctor.”

I did not see Poirot again until the next morning. He was sitting
at the breakfast table, looking very much pleased with himself.

“Well, Hastings,” he said. “A very successful little case, was it
not?”

“I suppose so. But I can’t help feeling sorry for that poor woman.”

“My dear Hastings, she was a cold-blooded murderess. She killed
her husband for his money, and then tried to make it appear like
suicide.”

“But how did you know? And what about the voice?”

“Ah, the voice! That was a little arrangement of mine. I am not
altogether a stranger to the art of ventriloquism, as you may
know. And as for how I knew—well, there were several little things.
To begin with, there was the rook rifle. Mrs. Maltravers said her
husband was shooting rooks, but when I examined the rifle I found
that it had been cleaned quite recently. Now a man who is shooting
rooks does not clean his rifle after every shot. Then there were
the flowers. I had noticed them when we first arrived, and they
were certainly not dead then. A little strong ammonia soon settled
their business! And then, of course, there was the little
experiment with Captain Black. It was his story that gave me the
clue to the whole thing.”

“But what about the financial position of Mr. Maltravers?”

“Ah, that was the most interesting part of the whole affair. You
see, he wasn’t on the verge of bankruptcy at all. That was just
a little story I made up to see how Mrs. Maltravers would take it.
If she had been an innocent woman, she would have been surprised
and relieved. But she wasn’t. She took it as a matter of course.
Which showed that she already knew—or thought she knew—that her
husband was in financial difficulties. And as he wasn’t, she must
have had some other reason for thinking so. Now, what could that
reason be? Only one thing—that he had told her so himself. And
why should he do that? To give her a motive for his suicide, of
course! He was a very clever man, Mr. Maltravers. He knew his wife
was an extravagant woman, and he wanted to make sure that she
wouldn’t be left penniless if anything happened to him. So he
pretended he was ruined, and then insured his life for a large
sum. He even told her about the suicide clause in the policy, so
that she would know he couldn’t kill himself for a year. He thought
that would keep him safe. But he didn’t reckon on his wife’s
cupidity. As soon as she heard Captain Black’s story, she saw her
chance. She knew her husband had a weak heart—Dr. Bernard told us
that, though he called it gastric ulcer—and she thought that if
she killed him in that way, no one would ever suspect. And she
was very nearly right.”

“But what about Alfred Wright?” I asked. “You said he was a
director of the Insurance Company.”

“So he is,” said Poirot. “And it was he who first suggested that
there might be something wrong. You see, he knew Maltravers, and
he didn’t believe he was the sort of man to commit suicide. So
he asked me to look into it. And I am glad I did. It has been a
most interesting case.”

“And what will happen to Mrs. Maltravers?”

“She will be tried for murder, of course. And I have no doubt she
will be found guilty. She is a very dangerous woman, Hastings.
A very dangerous woman indeed.”

And Poirot composedly helped himself to another piece of toast.

“Was it? Oh, yes, of course, but it gave me such a start. And I
know it’s only the ivy. It can’t be anything else, can it?”

Poirot did not answer, and as we went on with our dinner, I noticed
that the atmosphere had changed. The room was no longer just a
room, it was filled with the presence of the dead.

“Madame,” said Poirot suddenly, “I had an idea that we might hold
a little séance this evening. Your maid is mediumistic, too, I
think.”

Mrs. Maltravers was visibly reluctant, but after some persuasion
she consented.

“Oh, very well, if you must.”

The little party met in the library after dinner. Poirot turned out
the lights, and we sat round the table.

“Now, what shall we do?” said Mrs. Maltravers in a whisper.

“The usual thing. We will join hands and see what happens.”

We sat in silence for some minutes, and then the table began to
tilt.

“A message,” cried Poirot. “Is there anyone there?”

One tap.

“That means yes.”

“What name?”

A series of taps followed.

“M-A-L-T-R-A-V-E-R-S.”

“He is here,” whispered Mrs. Maltravers. “Oh, I feel it.”

“Ask him why he died,” suggested Poirot.

The table began to rock violently.

“I—K-I-L-L-E-D—M-Y-S-E-L-F.”

“Is that all? Is there nothing else?”

Again the table rocked.

“W-I-F-E.”

“What does he mean?”

“Ask him.”

“H-E-L-P—H-E-R.”

“I don’t understand,” said Mrs. Maltravers, her voice rising to a
shriek. “I don’t understand.”

“He means that he wants you to have the insurance money,” said
Poirot.

“Yes, yes, that must be it. Oh, thank you, thank you!”

She sank back in her chair, and Poirot turned up the lights.

“A most interesting séance,” he observed. “I am very glad we had
it. It has quite cleared up the mystery.”

“What do you mean?”

“Simply this, that Mr. Maltravers did not commit suicide. He was
murdered!”

“Murdered?”

“Yes.”

“But who——?”

“That is what I am going to find out.”

Mrs. Maltravers looked as though she were going to faint.

“But how—how could he have been murdered? The doctor said——”

“The doctor was an old fool,” said Poirot. “I knew that as soon
as I saw him. He would believe anything he was told. He was told
it was a gastric ulcer, so he believed it was a gastric ulcer.
Then he was told it was a suicide, so he believed it was a suicide.
He would have believed it was anything. But I—I do not believe what
I am told. I see for myself.”

“But the rook rifle?”

“The rook rifle was a very clever idea. It suggested suicide to
the doctor, and it suggested suicide to everyone else. But there
was one thing that it did not suggest, and that was murder!”

“But how—how was he murdered?”

“By a very simple method. Someone who knew about his heart—someone
who knew that any sudden shock would be fatal—decided to give him
that shock.”

“But how?”

“By appearing to him as a ghost!”

“A ghost?”

“Yes. You remember the parlourmaid’s story? She thought she saw
her master in the passage. Well, suppose someone had dressed up
to look like Mr. Maltravers? Suppose they had appeared to him
suddenly in the plantation? The shock would have been enough to
kill him.”

“But who—who would do such a thing?”

“That is what I am going to find out,” repeated Poirot. “And I
think I know where to look.”

He turned to the door.

“Where are you going?”

“I am going to the village. I have a little business to attend
to. I shall be back in an hour.”

He left the room, and I followed him.

“Poirot,” I said, when we were outside, “what on earth does all
this mean? You don’t really believe that someone dressed up as a
ghost and killed Maltravers?”

“My dear Hastings, I believe nothing. I only suggest. But it is
a very interesting suggestion, is it not?”

“But who could have done it?”

“That is what we are going to find out. Come, we must hurry.”

We walked quickly to the village, and Poirot led the way to the
house of Dr. Bernard.

“What are we doing here?” I asked.

“I want to have a little talk with the doctor.”

He rang the bell, and we were shown into the consulting-room.

“Ah, Monsieur Poirot,” said the doctor, rising to meet us. “I did
not expect to see you again so soon.”

“I have come to ask you a question, doctor. You told me this morning
that Mr. Maltravers was a Christian Scientist. Is that so?”

“Yes, he was. A most misguided man, in my opinion.”

“And you also told me that he had had a previous hæmorrhage. Is
that also so?”

“Yes, his wife told me so.”

“I see. His wife told you. And did she also tell you that he had
a strong premonition of his own death?”

“Yes, she did.”

“I see. It was Mrs. Maltravers who told you everything. And you,
being an old—I mean, being a very busy man—accepted what she said
without question.”

The doctor looked a little huffy.

“I had no reason to doubt her word.”

“Of course not. But suppose she were lying? Suppose Mr. Maltravers
was not a Christian Scientist? Suppose he had never had a previous
hæmorrhage? Suppose he had no premonition of his own death?”

“But why should she lie?”

“That is what I am going to show you. Now, doctor, I want you to
do something for me. I want you to come back with me to the Manor.
I think I can promise you a very interesting evening.”

The doctor looked surprised, but he consented to come.

When we arrived at the Manor, we found Mrs. Maltravers in the
drawing-room. She looked very pale and nervous.

“Monsieur Poirot,” she said, “what is the meaning of all this?
Why have you brought Dr. Bernard here?”

“I have brought him here, madame, to witness a little experiment.
You see, I have been thinking about that ghost. And I have come to
the conclusion that there is only one person who could have played
the part of the ghost.”

“And who is that?”

“The person who knew Mr. Maltravers best. The person who knew all
his little ways. The person who knew how he used to tap on the
window when he passed round the house. In short—his wife!”

Mrs. Maltravers gave a cry of horror.

“I? You accuse me of murdering my husband?”

“I do, madame. I think you planned the whole thing very cleverly.
You knew that your husband was in financial difficulties. You knew
that he had insured his life for a large sum. And you decided to
get that money for yourself. You knew that he had a weak heart,
and you decided to give him a shock that would kill him. You told
everyone that he was a Christian Scientist, and that he had a
premonition of his own death, so that when he did die, no one would
be surprised. And then, on Wednesday afternoon, you dressed up in
some of his clothes, and you appeared to him in the plantation.
The shock was too much for him, and he died. Then you went back
to the house, changed your clothes, and waited for the body to be
found. It was a very clever plan, madame, but it had one flaw.”

“And what was that?” gasped Mrs. Maltravers.

“The rook rifle. You put it there to suggest suicide, but you
forgot that a man who commits suicide does not usually take a rook
rifle with him. He takes a revolver, or he takes poison. A rook
rifle is for shooting rooks, not for shooting oneself. And then
there was the story that Captain Black told at dinner. That gave
you the idea for the suicide, but it also gave me the clue to the
truth. For when I asked Captain Black what ‘shot’ suggested to
him, he answered ‘suicide.’ And that showed me that the idea of
suicide had been put into his head by the story he had told at
dinner—the story that you had heard, and that you had used for
your own purposes.”

Mrs. Maltravers was silent for a moment, her face working
convulsively. Then she suddenly burst into a fit of hysterical
laughter.

“You are very clever, Monsieur Poirot! Very clever indeed! But
you cannot prove anything. You have no evidence!”

“I have the evidence of the parlourmaid,” said Poirot quietly.
“She saw you in the passage, dressed in your husband’s clothes.
She thought it was his ghost, but when I questioned her just now,
she admitted that she had seen you coming out of his dressing-room.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Mrs. Maltravers. “She never saw me!”

“We shall see,” said Poirot. “And then there is the matter of the
insurance money. I have been in communication with the Insurance
Company, and they tell me that they have no intention of paying
out the money until the matter has been thoroughly investigated.
So you see, madame, your clever plan has failed.”

Mrs. Maltravers looked at him for a moment with eyes full of hatred.
Then she suddenly collapsed into a chair and began to weep
violently.

“I did it!” she sobbed. “I did it! But he was a cruel man—he
treated me abominably. I couldn’t stand it any longer. And we were
so poor—I didn’t know what to do.”

“I think,” said Poirot gently, “that you had better say no more
until you have seen a lawyer. Dr. Bernard, will you be so good as
to stay with Mrs. Maltravers until the police arrive? I have
already telephoned for them.”

The doctor, looking very white and shaken, nodded his head.

“Come, Hastings,” said Poirot, “our work here is done.”

As we walked back to the village, I was silent for some time. Then
I said:

“Poirot, how did you know? How did you really know?”

“My friend, I did not know. I only suspected. But when I saw Mrs.
Maltravers’ face at the séance, I knew that she was guilty. She
was so terrified—so obviously terrified of the ‘ghost’ of her
husband. And then, when I told her that I knew the truth, she broke
down and confessed. It was a gamble, Hastings, but it succeeded.”

“But the parlourmaid?” I asked. “Did she really see her mistress
dressed in her husband’s clothes?”

Poirot chuckled.

“My dear Hastings, the parlourmaid saw nothing of the sort. I
merely invented 그 story to see how Mrs. Maltravers would react.
It is an old trick, but a very effective one.”

“And the Insurance Company?”

“They will, of course, be very grateful to me for saving them fifty
thousand pounds. But I do not think they will pay me as much as
that! Still, one must be content with what one can get.”

He sighed.

“It is a sad case, Hastings. A very beautiful woman—and a very
wicked one. But then, as I have often told you, beauty is only
skin deep.”

I did not answer. I was thinking of the lovely Mrs. Maltravers, and
of the terrible thing she had done. And I was thinking, too, of
Hercule Poirot, and of the extraordinary way in which his mind
worked.

“Truly,” I said at last, “you are a very remarkable man, Poirot.”

“I know it,” he replied simply. “It is my only weakness!”

But we could not help noticing the strange ways in which she was
being haunted. Poirot’s eyes were fixed on the door, and as he saw
her looking at it he nodded.

“It is coming,” he said, in a low voice. “Whatever it is, it is
there!”

I followed his look. The door was opening slowly—it was an uncanny
sight. Then a figure in a shroud stood upon the threshold. It had
its hand to its mouth, and its lips were covered with blood. I
recognised the face—it was the face of the dead man, Maltravers!

Mrs. Maltravers gave a piercing shriek and fell to the ground. In
a moment Poirot had her in his arms.

“A glass of water,” he cried. “Hastings, run to the sideboard.”

I did so, but before I could return I heard him say:

“_Eh bien_, she has fainted! Dr. Bernard, can you give her some
attention?”

I looked up and saw that the figure in the doorway was none other
than the doctor! He had a white cloth round his head and shoulders,
and his lips were smeared with red.

“Was that a good enough ghost for you, Poirot?” he said, with a
grin.

“Excellent!” said Poirot. “I think the lady will not be long in
recovering, and I have much to say to her.”

But a sort of terror was gaining on us all. The parlourmaid was
obviously unstrung, and when the meal was over Mrs. Maltravers
besought Poirot not to go at once. She was clearly terrified to be
left alone. We sat in the little morning-room. The wind was getting
up, and moaning round the house in an eerie fashion. Twice the door
of the room came unlatched and the door slowly opened, and each
time she clung to me with a terrified gasp.

“Ah, but this door, it is bewitched!” cried

Poirot angrily at last. He got up and shut it once more, then
turned the key in the lock. “I shall lock it, so!”

“Don’t do that,” she gasped, “if it should come open now——”

She sat with her back to the window. Suddenly she turned and gave
a shriek.

“The window! Did you see? A face!”

I rushed to the window, and after some difficulty in the darkness
conceived that I saw something white and ghastly that seemed to
be looking into the room. It was only for a moment, and I could
not be sure.

“It is all a delusion,” said Poirot. “All a delusion, I tell you!”

But he seemed as much unstrung as any of us.

“I cannot bear it,” moaned Mrs. Maltravers. “Oh, if I only knew!”

“Knew what, madame?”

“That he—that he has forgiven me!”

Poirot came over to her and took her hand.

“Madame, you believe in Spiritualism?”

“I have always thought there might be something in it.”

“Then we will have a séance. We will ask your husband to speak to
us. I myself have some slight mediumistic powers. Hastings, put
out the light, if you please.”

I did so, and we sat in the darkness, the only sound being the
howling of the wind outside.

“Are you there, Spirit?” whispered Poirot.

There was a silence, then a long low moan. Mrs. Maltravers was
shivering as she sat.

“Ask him—if he forgives me,” she gasped.

“Is there any spirit here?” asked Poirot again.

Three loud knocks on the table made us all jump.

“He is here,” whispered Poirot. “Ask your question, madame.”

“Do you—forgive me?” she faltered.

There was no answer, but a slow, sighing sound.

“Is that you, Maltravers?” asked Poirot.

Again the three knocks.

“How did you die?”

There was a long silence, then a voice, very low and muffled,
seemed to come from the very air itself.

“I was—murdered.”

“Murdered?” gasped the widow. “By whom?”

“The one who—who—_who_——”

The voice died away in a long-drawn-out moan.

“Who was it? Speak!” cried Poirot.

“I cannot—the power—is—failing——”

“Was it your wife?”

“No.”

“Was it Captain Black?”

“No.”

“Was it the doctor—Dr. Bernard?”

“No.”

“Then who was it?”

The voice seemed to gather strength.

“The one—who—made me—sign. The one—who—wanted—the money. It
was——”

The voice broke off, then with a sudden shriek that made us all
jump:

“_Alfred Wright!_”

The word seemed to ring through the room. Mrs. Maltravers fell
forward in a dead faint. I rushed to her, but Poirot was before
me. He had already switched on the light.

“_Vite_, Hastings! The handcuffs! In my pocket!”

I stared at him in amazement.

“Handcuffs? What for?”

“To put on that woman, of course! Quick, man, before she comes
to!”

“But Alfred Wright——”

“There is no such person! Or rather, there is, but he is at this
moment in London. It was a name I used to trap her. As for the
voice, that was my own—a little trick of ventriloquism I learned
long ago. Now, the handcuffs!”

I was still dazed as I helped Poirot to secure the fainting
woman’s wrists.

“But I don’t understand,” I gasped. “How did she kill him? And
why?”

“As to how, it was simple. She had heard the story Captain Black
told at dinner, and she saw her chance. She knew her husband had
a horror of doctors and would never have an autopsy. She got him
out into the grounds, told him she had seen a rook, and handed him
the rifle. Then, as he held it, she—well, it is easily done. A
sudden jar, a finger on the trigger—and the thing is done. As to
why—well, fifty thousand pounds is a large sum, and there was,
as I suspected, another man. Not Captain Black—she only used him
as a scapegoat—but someone else. Someone she hoped to marry when
she was a rich widow.”

“But the blood on the lips?”

“A little touch of rouge, my friend. She is a clever woman, but
not quite clever enough for Hercule Poirot!”

As he spoke, the woman’s eyes opened. She looked at the handcuffs,
then at Poirot.

“You—you devil!” she hissed.

Poirot bowed.

“I am only a humble instrument of Justice, madame. And now,
Hastings, I think we may return to London. Our work here is
finished.”

But the key was still in the lock, and the door remained closed.
The sense of something invisible and menacing in the room was
growing on us, and we all fell into a brooding silence. I felt
the blood in my veins run cold. Then there was a soft knock at the
door, and at the same time Poirot walked to the electric light
switch and turned it off.

“Who is there?” he cried.

There was no answer, but the door slowly opened, the key having
evidently turned by itself in the lock. In the dim light that came
from the hall, we saw a tall, thin figure standing on the
threshold.

“My God!” I cried, “it is Mr. Maltravers!”

Mrs. Maltravers gave a shriek, and Poirot caught her as she
collapsed. Then, as she was coming to, a voice said:

“I have much to say to you, my dear wife.”

She looked up.

“You!” she screamed, “you! You are dead!”

“No, I am not dead,” the figure replied. “I have come back.”

“You are dead! You are dead! I killed you!”

“You killed me?”

“Yes, I killed you! I told you to go and shoot yourself, and you
did it! I put the idea into your head!”

“You did more than that,” said Poirot’s voice, as the lights were
suddenly switched on again.

Mrs. Maltravers shrank back, her eyes dilated with terror. Standing
in the doorway was a tall man, but it was not Mr. Maltravers. It
was a stranger.

“Who is this?” she gasped.

“This is my friend, Mr. Alfred Wright, of the Northern Union
Insurance Company,” said Poirot. “And now, madame, the game is
up.”

“It cannot. I have the key in my pocket.”

I felt that Poirot was very unfeeling. He went back to his seat,
and as he did so, he dropped a small white tablet into her glass
of water.

“You must have some wine, madame. You are very much upset.”

“I’ll have some more water.”

She took a sip from the glass, then she put it down.

“Why, what’s this?” she asked.

“It is a little sedative,” said Poirot. “You are overwrought.”

She looked at him quickly.

“How do you know that?” she asked.

“Because, madame, I have seen a good many people lately who have
been through the same experience as you.”

She did not seem satisfied, but he said no more, and in a few
minutes she became calmer and at last dozed off in her chair.

“The sedative has done its work,” whispered Poirot. “But we must
not leave her. I will stay here while you go and search the house.”

“Search the house? For what?”

“Anything unusual. A window open, or any sign of a person having
been in.”

I went, and on my return half an hour later reported that there
was nothing to be seen.

“But the parlourmaid is in a state of collapse,” I added. “She says
she has seen the master again, and this time he was quite close
to her.”

Poirot’s face went very grave.

“Hastings, I do not like this. There is some influence at work
here that I do not understand. We must get help.”

“Help? From whom?”

“From a medium. I will go and find one.”

“But you cannot go out and leave this poor woman alone!”

“You will be with her. I shall not be long.”

He went, and for an hour I sat there alone in the silent house,
with only the wind moaning outside and the sleeping woman in her
chair. Then at last I heard a key in the hall door and Poirot
returned, bringing with him a tall, thin man with a very pale face
and dark eyes.

“This is Mr. Wright,” said Poirot. “He is a very well-known medium,
and he has kindly consented to come and help us.”

Mr. Wright bowed and sat down in a chair opposite to Mrs.
Maltravers.

“The conditions are very favourable,” he said in a low, deep voice.
“I can feel a presence here already.”

Mrs. Maltravers stirred in her sleep, and as she did so, the door
of the room, which Poirot had locked, slowly opened.

I saw the terror in her eyes as she woke and saw it.

“Who is it?” she gasped. “Who is it?”

“It is your husband, madame,” said Mr. Wright. “He is here.”

She shrank back in her chair.

“No, no! It can’t be! He’s dead!”

“He is not dead,” said the medium. “He is here, and he wants to
speak to you.”

And as he spoke, a figure appeared in the doorway. It was the
figure of a man, dressed in a rough tweed suit, and his face was
the face of the dead Mr. Maltravers.

Mrs. Maltravers gave a long, low cry and fell forward on the floor.

The figure in the doorway vanished, and at the same moment Poirot
sprang forward and caught her.

“It is all right, madame,” he said. “It was only a trick.”

“A trick?” she gasped.

“Yes. Mr. Wright is not a medium. He is a director of the Northern
Union Insurance Company. And the figure you saw was not your
husband’s ghost, but a very clever young actor from London.”

“But—but why?”

“Because, madame, I was not quite satisfied as to the cause of
your husband’s death. You see, the symptoms of a gastric ulcer are
very like the symptoms of—strychnine poisoning.”

“Strychnine!”

“Yes. And when I found that your husband had recently insured his
life for fifty thousand pounds, I began to wonder. Then I found
that you had been seen in the village buying strychnine ‘to kill
a dog.’ And finally, when I heard Captain Black’s story of the
man who committed suicide with a rook rifle, I saw how the thing
had been done. You told your husband that story, and you suggested
to him that he should pretend to commit suicide in that way, so
as to avoid the insurance company’s investigation. You told him
that you would put a little blood on his lips, and that the doctor
would think it was a hæmorrhage. But what you really did was to
give him a dose of strychnine, and then, when he was dead, you
placed the rook rifle by his side.”

Mrs. Maltravers did not speak. She sat there staring at him with
wide, terrified eyes.

“It was a very clever plot, madame,” said Poirot. “But you made
one mistake. You forgot that I, Hercule Poirot, was likely to be
called in to investigate the case.”

And as he spoke, the door opened and a police inspector entered
the room.

“Mrs. Maltravers,” he said, “I have a warrant for your arrest on
a charge of murdering your husband.”

Mrs. Maltravers did not resist. She allowed the inspector to lead
her away, and as the door closed behind them, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, “what do you think of my little
experiment?”

“It was wonderful, Poirot! But how did you know?”

“I did not know, my friend. I only suspected. But when I saw her
face when she saw her husband’s ‘ghost,’ I knew that my suspicions
were correct. A guilty conscience, Hastings—it is a very dangerous
thing.”

And Poirot lightfully blew a speck of dust from his sleeve.

The words were hardly out of her mouth before the door _did_ open,
and she gave a piercing scream. We all rushed into the passage.
No one was there.

The parlourmaid came up to us, her face white and her hands
shaking.

“I didn’t do it, sir,” she said to Poirot. “It must have been the
ghost.”

Poirot looked at her keenly.

“Where have you been since dinner?”

“In the kitchen, sir.”

“You are sure of that?”

“Yes, sir.”

Poirot said no more, but his brow was clouded. The wind was getting
up, and as we went into the drawing-room the candle-light was
flickering in the draught. Mrs. Maltravers was on the verge of
hysterics, and Poirot led her to a sofa and tried to calm her.

Suddenly, a voice, a strange, hollow voice, seemed to come from
nowhere, crying:

“I have come back! I have come back!”

Mrs. Maltravers gave a piercing scream and fell back on the sofa.
The parlourmaid, who had just entered the room, dropped the tray
she was carrying, and fled, shrieking. I was myself considerably
shaken.

“It was the master’s voice,” she gasped. “Oh, Monsieur Poirot, what
does it mean?”

Poirot was looking round him, his face set and stern.

“I do not know,” he said at last. “But I will find out. Wait here.”

He went out of the room, and I followed him. We searched the house
thoroughly, but could find no one. When we returned to the
drawing-room, Mrs. Maltravers was still on the sofa, her face
buried in her hands.

“He is here,” she moaned. “I know he is here. I can feel him.”

Poirot went up to her and laid a hand on her shoulder.

“Courage, Madame,” he said. “Courage! We will find out the truth.”

He went to the window and looked out into the darkness.

“The wind is very high,” he said. “It is a wild night.”

He turned back to the room.

“And now, Madame, I have a confession to make to you. I have not
been altogether frank with you. I am not only an agent for the
Insurance Company, I am also a private detective.”

Mrs. Maltravers looked up, her eyes wide with astonishment.

“A private detective?” she whispered.

“Yes. And I have a theory about your husband’s death.”

“A theory?”

“Yes. I believe that your husband did not commit suicide. I believe
that he was murdered.”

Mrs. Maltravers gave a gasp of horror.

“Murdered? But who—who could have murdered him?”

“That is what I am going to find out,” said Poirot. “And I think
I know how to do it. Will you help me?”

“Help you? How?”

“By doing exactly as I tell you. Will you?”

Mrs. Maltravers hesitated for a moment, then she nodded.

“Yes,” she said. “I will help you.”

“Good. Then this is what I want you to do. I want you to go to
your room and stay there until I send for you. Do not let anyone
in, and do not come out until I tell you. Do you understand?”

“Yes,” she said. “I understand.”

“Then go now. And do not be afraid. I will be near.”

Mrs. Maltravers got up and went out of the room. Poirot turned to
me.

“And now, Hastings, for the final scene of the drama.”

“The final scene? What do you mean?”

“You will see, my friend. You will see. But first, we must make
our preparations.”

He went to the door and called the parlourmaid.

“Tell me,” he said, when she appeared. “Where is the rook rifle
that Mr. Maltravers used?”

“It is in the hall, sir. Where he always kept it.”

“Go and get it for me, please.”

The girl went out and returned a moment later with the rifle.
Poirot took it from her and examined it carefully.

“Thank you,” he said. “That will do. You may go now.”

When she had gone, Poirot turned to me.

“And now, Hastings, we must wait.”

“Wait? For what?”

“For the murderer to return.”

“The murderer? You think he will return tonight?”

“I am sure of it. He cannot help himself. The dead man is calling
him.”

He went to the lamp and turned it down until the room was in
semi-darkness. Then he led me to a corner where we were hidden by
a large screen.

“Now, Hastings,” he whispered. “Not a word. Not a sound. Whatever
happens, do not move.”

We waited in silence. The wind howled round the house, and the
shadows danced on the walls. It was a long wait, and I began to
feel a sense of unease. What if Poirot were wrong? What if the
murderer did not come?

Suddenly, I heard a sound. It was the sound of a window being
slowly opened. I held my breath. A figure appeared at the window,
silhouetted against the night sky. It paused for a moment, then
stepped into the room.

It was a man, dressed in dark clothes. He moved stealthily across
the room towards the sofa where Mrs. Maltravers had been lying. He
reached into his pocket and pulled out a small object.

At that moment, Poirot stepped out from behind the screen.

“Good evening, Monsieur,” he said calmly.

The man spun round, his face white with terror. It was Dr. Bernard.

“You!” he gasped.

“Yes, Monsieur,” said Poirot. “I have been expecting you.”

He stepped forward and took the object from the doctor’s hand. It
was a small glass phial.

“A very ingenious method, Monsieur,” said Poirot. “A very
ingenious method indeed. But it did not deceive Hercule Poirot.”

He turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? The doctor here was in financial difficulties.
He knew that Mr. Maltravers was on the verge of bankruptcy, and he
knew about the life insurance. He also knew that Mr. Maltravers was
a Christian Scientist and would not see a doctor. So he devised
a plan. He would kill Mr. Maltravers and make it look like suicide.
He knew that a rook rifle wound in the mouth would produce the
same symptoms as a gastric ulcer—blood on the lips and internal
hæmorrhage. And he knew that as the local doctor, he would be
called upon to examine the body and would be able to give a
verdict of natural causes.”

“But how did he do it?” I asked.

“It was very simple,” said Poirot. “He went to the plantation where
Mr. Maltravers was shooting rooks. He told him that he had some
new medicine that would help his condition. Mr. Maltravers, being
a kind-hearted man, agreed to try it. The doctor gave him the
medicine, which was actually a powerful poison. As soon as Mr.
Maltravers was dead, the doctor placed the rook rifle beside him
to make it look like suicide. But he made one mistake. He forgot
that Captain Black had told a story about a man committing suicide
with a rook rifle at dinner the night before. And he forgot that
I, Hercule Poirot, would be here to investigate.”

He turned back to the doctor.

“And now, Monsieur, I think it is time for you to go. The police
are waiting for you outside.”

Dr. Bernard sank into a chair, his face buried in his hands.

“I did it for my wife,” he moaned. “She is so young and beautiful.
I couldn’t bear to see her in poverty.”

“A poor excuse, Monsieur,” said Poirot. “A very poor excuse.”

He went to the door and opened it. Two police officers stepped into
the room.

“Take him away,” said Poirot.

As the doctor was led out of the room, Mrs. Maltravers appeared at
the door. She looked at Poirot with gratitude in her eyes.

“Thank you, Monsieur Poirot,” she said. “Thank you for everything.”

“It was nothing, Madame,” said Poirot. “Nothing at all. It was
merely the exercise of the little grey cells.”

He turned to me.

“And now, Hastings, I think it is time for us to return to London.
The case is closed.”

We walked down the drive together, the wind blowing in our faces.

“Well, Poirot,” I said. “You’ve done it again.”

“Yes, Hastings,” said Poirot. “I have done it again. But it was
not easy. No, it was not easy at all.”

He paused for a moment, then added:

“But then, nothing worth doing ever is.”

And with that, we headed for the station and the train back to
London.

Poirot put out the lights and we sat in the firelight. Then a long
wail from the wind outside died away and we all started.

“There—at the window!” whispered Mrs. Maltravers. “My husband’s
face!”

She fell to the floor in a dead faint. Poirot and I rushed to the
window. The moon was at that moment eclipsed by a cloud.

“Wait,” cried Poirot. “Wait!”

He struck a match and held it to the window. In its flickering
light I saw a white, drawn face. It was the face of the dead man!

I was so startled that I could not move, but Poirot had the window
open and was out on the terrace in a second. Then I heard him call.

“Hastings, come here!”

I ran out. He had a man by the collar. In the light of the moon,
which had now come out, I saw that it was the doctor.

“Dr. Bernard!” I cried. “What are you doing here?”

“I—I thought I saw a light,” he stammered.

“A light!” cried Poirot. “And so you came to investigate it? You
are a very brave man, doctor.”

“I—I don’t understand.”

“I think you do. You are not the only person who can see ghosts,
it seems. Mrs. Maltravers has seen her husband’s ghost.”

The doctor gave a start.

“You mean she is—seeing things?”

“She is seeing a great deal more than you think, doctor.”

Poirot’s voice was very grave.

“Now, Dr. Bernard, I have a few questions to ask you. To begin
with, why did you tell me that Mr. Maltravers died of a hæmorrhage?”

“Because he did.”

“And what caused the hæmorrhage?”

“I have already told you—a gastric ulcer.”

“And you are prepared to swear to that?”

“Certainly.”

“Even after an autopsy?”

The doctor hesitated.

“I—I don’t think an autopsy is necessary.”

“I do. And what is more, the Insurance Company intends to demand
one.”

The doctor turned pale.

“They can’t do that.”
