“Oh, yes, they can. And I think they will find some very interesting
things. For instance, they might find that Mr. Maltravers did not
die of a hæmorrhage at all.”

“Then what did he die of?”

“That is what I am going to ask you, doctor. You were the only
person who saw the body before it was moved. You were the person
who signed the death certificate. If there was anything wrong,
you were the person who must have known it.”

The doctor was silent.

“Now, Dr. Bernard, I will be frank with you. I know that Mr.
Maltravers did not die of a gastric ulcer. I know that he was
murdered. And I think I know who murdered him.”

The doctor looked up quickly.

“You know?”

“Yes. And I think you know too. You were a friend of Mrs.
Maltravers, were you not?”

“I—I have known her for some time.”

“Exactly. And you were very sorry for her when her husband died?”

“I was. She is a very beautiful woman.”

“She is. And a very clever one. She knew that her husband was on
the verge of bankruptcy. She knew that if he died, she would be
left penniless. But she also knew that if he died within a year
of insuring his life, she would get fifty thousand pounds. Unless,
of course, he committed suicide.”

“But he didn’t commit suicide.”

“No, he didn’t. But she wanted it to look as if he had. That was
why she got Captain Black to tell that story at dinner. She knew
her husband was a nervous man, and she thought the suggestion
might work. But it didn’t. Mr. Maltravers had no intention of
committing suicide. So she had to kill him herself.”

“That’s a lie!” cried a voice from the window.

It was Mrs. Maltravers. She was standing there, her eyes flashing.

“How dare you say such a thing? My husband died of a hæmorrhage.
The doctor said so.”

“The doctor said what you told him to say, madame,” said Poirot
sternly. “He was in love with you, and he wanted to protect you.
But he didn’t know that you had already planned everything. You
knew that Captain Black was going to East Africa. You knew that
he would be away for a long time. So you thought you could safely
use his story. But you didn’t know that he would come back. That
was your first mistake.”

“It’s not true!” she cried. “I didn’t kill him!”

“Then how did he die, madame? He was found with a rook rifle by
his side. There was blood on his lips. It looked like the suicide
Captain Black had described. But there was one thing you forgot.
A rook rifle makes a noise. And no one heard a shot.”

“I heard one,” she said quickly. “I told you I heard one or two
shots in the distance.”

“Yes, you told me so. But no one else heard them. And the gardeners
were working quite near. If a shot had been fired, they would have
heard it. No, madame, no shot was fired. Mr. Maltravers was killed
in a much more silent way.”

“How?” I asked, leaning forward.

“He was poisoned,” said Poirot. “Poisoned with a very rare and
deadly poison which causes internal hæmorrhage. A poison that is
very difficult to detect, unless you know what to look for. And
there is only one person who could have had access to such a
poison.”

He turned to the doctor.

“Dr. Bernard, I think you have something to tell us.”

The doctor looked from Poirot to Mrs. Maltravers. Then he bowed
his head.

“It’s true,” he whispered. “She asked me for it. She said she
wanted it for—for some experiments she was doing. I didn’t know
what she wanted it for. I swear I didn’t!”

“You lie!” shrieked Mrs. Maltravers. “You gave it to me because
you wanted him out of the way! You wanted me for yourself!”

“Madame,” said Poirot, “it is no use. The truth is out. And now,
if you will excuse me, I have a telephone call to make. I think
the police will be interested in what we have discovered.”

He turned to me.

“Come, Hastings. We have finished here.”

As we walked down the drive, I turned to Poirot.

“But Poirot, how did you know? And what about the ghost?”

Poirot chuckled.

“The ghost, my friend, was a little invention of my own. I saw
that Mrs. Maltravers was a very nervous woman, and I thought I
would play upon her fears. I knew that if she thought she was
being haunted, she would soon break down. As for the face at the
window—well, that was our friend the doctor. I had told him that
I suspected him, and he was naturally anxious to know what we were
doing. So he followed us and looked in at the window. It was the
flickering light of the match that made him look like a ghost.”

“And the poison?”

“Ah, the poison! That was a little piece of bluff, Hastings. I
did not know that he had been poisoned. But I did know that if
he had been, the doctor must have known it. And when I saw the
doctor’s face when I mentioned an autopsy, I knew I was on the
right track.”

“But who was the culprit, Poirot? You said it was one of four.”

“And so it was, my friend. Mrs. Maltravers was the one who
conceived the plan and carried it out. But she could not have
done it without the help of the doctor. And then there was
Captain Black, whose story gave her the idea. And finally, there
was our friend Alfred Wright.”

“Alfred Wright!” I cried. “But what had he to do with it?”

“He was the one who asked me to investigate the case, Hastings.
If he had not done so, the murder might never have been
discovered. So you see, he also played his part.”

“But you haven't told me who the true culprit is yet!” I
exclaimed.

Poirot smiled.

“The true culprit, Hastings? Why, it was the person who actually
administered the poison, of course.”

“And who was that?”

“Mrs. Maltravers, my friend. She put it in her husband’s tea.
And then, when he was dead, she carried him out to the plantation
and put the rook rifle by his side. It was a very clever plan,
but she forgot one thing.”

“What was that?”

“She forgot Hercule Poirot!”

And with a little laugh, my friend stepped into the waiting taxi.

And even as she spoke the impossible happened. The locked door
slowly swung open. I could not see into the passage from where I
sat, but she and Poirot were facing it. She gave one long shriek
as she turned to him.

“You saw him—there in the passage?” she cried.

He was staring down at her with a puzzled face, then shook his
head.

“I saw him—my husband—you must have seen him too?”

“Madame, I saw nothing. You are not well—unstrung——”

“I am perfectly well, I——Oh, God!”

Suddenly, without any warning, the lights quivered and went out.
Out of the darkness came three loud raps. I could hear Mrs.
Maltravers moaning.

And then—I saw!

A white figure was standing in the doorway—the figure of a man
with a white face and blood upon his lips. I could see him
distinctly, for he was luminous!

Mrs. Maltravers gave a long, shuddering sigh, and then—her voice
rang out with a scream of terror.

“It was you—you—I killed you. I—I didn’t want to, but I did. I—I
did it with the little rifle. I——”

Her voice failed her, and she fell in a heap.

At that moment the lights went on. Poirot was standing by the
switch, and there was no luminous figure in the doorway.

“_Eh bien_, Hastings,” he said, and I saw that he was smiling. “I
think you have heard her confession? A little theatrical,
certainly, but then I have always been a devotee of the drama.”

A figure, tall and dark, appeared in the doorway, its face
white—the dead man!

Mrs. Maltravers was now a heap on the floor, her face buried in
her hands, but the figure in the doorway moved towards her.

“I have come back,” it said in a hollow voice. “You killed me!”

“Oh, have mercy—have mercy!” she screamed. “I didn’t mean to do
it—I only meant to suggest it to you. I didn’t think you’d really
do it!”

Then she sank down in a dead faint.

The lights went on again. I looked up. It was Poirot who had
switched them on. And the figure in the doorway?

I rubbed my eyes. It was not the dead man at all, but a tall,
rather elderly man, with a pleasant vagueness of manner.

“Dr. Bernard!” I gasped.

The doctor smiled.

“I am a good actor, am I not?” he asked. “I am glad my little
theatrical display was so successful.”

“But what does it mean?” I asked Poirot. “I don’t understand.”

“Wait,” he said. “We have first to deal with Mrs. Maltravers.”

It was some time before she was restored to consciousness, and
when she realized that she had been trapped she became like a wild
thing. But she soon saw that it was useless to deny the truth.
She had already confessed, and Poirot’s witness, the doctor, had
heard it all.

“I will go now,” said Dr. Bernard. “I think you can manage without
me.”

“One moment, doctor,” said Poirot. “I should like to ask you one
or more questions. You see, it was your behaviour this morning
that first put me on the right scent.”

“My behaviour?” said the doctor, looking surprised.

“Yes. You were so very positive as to the cause of death. Now, in
my experience, a doctor is never quite so sure as that—unless he
has some reason for it. And then you were so very anxious to avoid
an autopsy. That, too, was suspicious. Why should you be so anxious
to avoid an autopsy? There could be only one reason—because you
knew what an autopsy would reveal.”

“I don’t understand,” said the doctor. “I did not know what an
autopsy would reveal. I was merely anxious to spare the widow’s
feelings.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “But why should you be so anxious to spare
the widow’s feelings? You hardly knew her. She had only been in the
place a few months. No, there must be some other reason. And then
I remembered what you had said about her being so beautiful and
charming. You were, in fact, a little bit in love with her, were
you not, doctor?”

The doctor flushed.

“I—I——” he stammered.

“It is nothing to be ashamed of,” said Poirot kindly. “She is a
very beautiful woman. But it was that which made you so anxious
to shield her. You suspected that she had had something to do with
her husband’s death, and you wanted to protect her. Is that not
so?”

The doctor bowed his head.

“Yes, it is true. I did suspect it. But I had no proof.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And so you were willing to sign a death
certificate which you knew to be false, in order to save her. A
very noble sentiment, no doubt, but not very legal, doctor.
However, we will say no more about that. The important thing is
that it was your behaviour which first made me realize that Mrs.
Maltravers was not the innocent victim I had at first supposed her
to be.”

“But how did she kill him?” I asked. “She wasn’t even there when
he died.”

“She did not kill him in the ordinary sense of the word,” said
Poirot. “She killed him by suggestion. You remember the story
Captain Black told at dinner? She knew her husband was in
financial difficulties, and she knew he had a premonition of death.
She saw her chance. She suggested to him that he should commit
suicide in the way Captain Black had described. She played on his
fears and his anxieties, until at last he did exactly what she
wanted him to do. It was a very clever and a very cruel murder.”

“But the insurance money?” I asked.

“Ah, that was the motive, of course. She knew that if he committed
suicide the insurance money would be forfeited. But she also knew
that if the cause of death was not discovered, the Company would
have to pay. And she counted on the doctor’s help to see that the
cause of death was not discovered. As we have seen, she was not
disappointed.”

“And what about the ghost?” I asked. “How did you manage that?”

Poirot smiled.

“That was very simple. A little phosphoresent paint on the
doctor’s face, a few well-timed noises, and the thing was done.
I knew that if I could work upon her fears, she would betray
herself. And she did.”

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we walked back to the inn, “I must
congratulate you. It was a very clever piece of work.”

“It was nothing, my friend,” said Poirot modestly. “A little
psychology, a little theatricality—that is all. But I am glad to
have been of service to my friend Alfred Wright. He is a good man,
and I should not like to see him cheated by such a woman as Mrs.
Maltravers.”

We reached the inn and went in to bed. It had been a long and
tiring day, and I was glad to get some sleep. But as I lay in the
dark, I couldn’t help thinking of the beautiful Mrs. Maltravers,
and the cruel way in which she had driven her husband to his
death. It was a strange world, I thought, and there were many
strange things in it. But at least I had the satisfaction of
knowing that justice had been done.

The next morning we returned to London. Poirot was in high spirits,
and talked incessantly all the way. But I was quiet and thoughtful.
I couldn’t get the image of Mrs. Maltravers out of my mind. She
was so beautiful, and yet so wicked. It was a combination that
I found hard to understand.

But as Poirot would say, it is the psychology that matters. And
in the end, it was the psychology that had tripped her up.

So ended the case of the Marsdon Manor. It was one of the most
interesting cases that Poirot and I had ever been involved in,
and I shall always remember it as a classic example of Poirot’s
brilliant methods.

A ghostly figure, the very image of the dead man, stood in the
doorway. He was pointing a finger at his wife, and as I watched
his lips seemed to move.

Mrs. Maltravers shrank back with a shriek of terror.

“Oh, my God! I did it—I did it! I killed him! But I never thought
you would come back—like this! Oh, have mercy—have mercy!”

She fell on the floor in a dead faint.

The lights went up as suddenly as they had gone out, and I saw
Poirot standing by the switch. But the ghost had vanished.

“What does it all mean?” I gasped. “What did she say?”

“She confessed to the murder of her husband, Hastings. A very
neatly planned and executed murder, too. It was she who suggested
the idea of suicide to him, after hearing Captain Black’s story.
She even went so far as to provide the rook rifle, and then, while
he was in the plantation, she joined him and persuaded him to
re-enact the scene of the suicide—only, instead of his pulling
the trigger, she did it for him.”

“But the ghost?”

“The ghost, my friend, was an actor—a very clever actor whom I
had sent for from London. He was made up to resemble the dead man,
and I arranged for the lights to go out at the psychological
moment. A little melodrama, perhaps, but it was necessary to
frighten her into a confession.”

“And the door opening?”

“A very simple matter of a piece of black silk thread. I had one
end in my pocket, and the other was attached to the handle of the
door. As for the three taps—well, I think I may claim the credit
for those myself.”

He smiled at me, his eyes twinkling.

“You see, Hastings, the Northern Union will be very much indebted
to me. They will not have to pay out that fifty thousand pounds.”

“But how did you know she was guilty?” I asked. “What was the
discrepancy you noticed?”

“Ah, that! It was very simple. Mrs. Maltravers told us that she
went to the village to get some stamps. But when I examined her
husband’s desk, I found a book of stamps in the drawer—and it was
full. Why should she go to the village for stamps when there were
plenty in the house? It was a small point, perhaps, but it was
enough to set me thinking. And then there was the matter of the
two shots fired from the rook rifle—why two shots, if it was a
case of suicide? No, my friend, it was a very clever murder, but
not quite clever enough for Hercule Poirot.”

He took a sip of his tea and sighed with satisfaction.

“And now, Hastings, if you have finished your packing, we will
take the next train back to London. I think we have earned a little
rest.”

The door of the room was wide open, and in the passage stood a
figure—a tall, grey-haired man, with a face like a mask. His hands
were held out before him, and he seemed to be looking through us
all. Mrs. Maltravers was on her knees, her hands before her face.

“_Speak_,” she cried. “What do you want?”

The figure did not move, but its lips parted, and a low, gutteral
voice came from them.

“Tell—tell the truth.”

“I will—I will tell everything.”

The voice seemed to die away.

“Speak,” she cried again. “Wait—don’t go. I tell you—I did it.
Only don’t—don’t look at me like that.”

She sank down on the floor in a huddled heap.

The lights went up as suddenly as they had gone out. Poirot was
standing by the switch, and the figure in the passage had
vanished.

Mrs. Maltravers was still on the floor, but as the light came she
struggled to her feet.

“What was it?” she gasped. “Where is he?”

“Madame,” said Poirot gravely, “you have confessed. It only
remains for me to send for the police.”

“Confessed? What do you mean?”

“You said you did it.”

“I didn’t know what I was saying. I was terrified. It was a vision
—a ghost.”

“No, madame, it was no ghost. It was a very clever piece of acting
on the part of my friend, Mr. Alfred Wright, the director of the
Insurance Company. He is a very good amateur actor, and with a
little make-up——”

“You—you dared!”

The woman was transformed. She looked like a tiger-cat.

“Madame,” said Poirot, “it was necessary. I knew you had killed
your husband. I knew how you had done it. You saw him sitting in
his chair, sleeping after his lunch, and you remembered the story
Captain Black had told at dinner the night before. You took the
little rook rifle, you put the muzzle of it into his mouth and
pulled the trigger. The little bullet entered the brain, and
there was nothing to show but a few drops of blood on the lips.
And then you took the body and the gun out into the grounds and
left them there. You were very clever, but not quite clever enough.
You did not know that the Northern Union would send Hercule
Poirot to investigate.”

High up in the air, a face, or what looked like a face, was
hovering. It was a ghastly white face, with a long white beard.
The lips were moving and a voice was speaking.

“I am coming for you—coming for you——”

And then Mrs. Maltravers cried out in an agony of terror:

“Oh, God, save me! I didn’t mean to do it. It was Ralph—he told
me how to do it. He said you would never know.”

She fell in a heap at our feet.

“Lights! Hastings, lights!” cried Poirot.

I stumbled to the door and found the switch. The room was flooded
with light. Mrs. Maltravers was lying on the floor. Poirot was
standing by her, and beside him was a tall figure with a long
white beard.

“Good heavens!” I cried. “It’s Mr. Maltravers!”

The figure laughed and tore off the white beard.

“No, Hastings, it is our friend Alfred Wright, who is a bit of
an actor in his spare time. I see you are surprised. I will
explain.”

The man I had seen on the bed upstairs stood there facing us,
gleaming with a faint ghostly light. There was blood on his lips,
and he held his right hand out, pointing. Suddenly a brilliant
light seemed to proceed from it. It passed over Poirot and me, and
fell on Mrs. Maltravers. I saw her white terrified face, and
something else!

“My God, Poirot!” I cried. “Look at her hand, her right hand. It’s
all red!”

Her own eyes fell on it, and she collapsed in a heap on the floor.

“Blood,” she cried hysterically. “Yes, it’s blood. I killed him.
I did it. He was showing me, and then I put my hand on the trigger
and pressed. Save me from him—save me! he’s come back!”

Her voice died away in a gurgle.

“Lights,” said Poirot briskly.

The lights went on as if by magic.

The “ghost” stepped forward, and I saw with amazement that it was no spirit, but a living man—the young clerk from the village whom Poirot had been seen conversing with earlier that afternoon. Mrs. Maltravers, seeing that she had been duped, let out a low, hissing breath of fury, all her previous terror replaced by a cold, hard mask of hatred. Poirot looked down at her with a certain pitying triumph. The “blood” on her hand, which had seemed so supernatural, was a simple chemical reaction; Poirot had managed to apply a certain reagent to her palm during his earlier expressions of sympathy, a substance that turned a vivid red when struck by the particular light of the lamp the “ghost” had carried.

The figure in the passage stepped forward into the room, and I saw with amazement that it was a living man. He was tall and slight, and as he wiped the phosphoric preparation from his face, I realized he was a stranger to me—a young actor Poirot had presumably engaged for the evening's performance. Poirot turned to the prostrate woman with a look of cold triumph, while I remained rooted to the spot, my brain whirling at this sudden transition from the supernatural to the mundane. The "ghost" had played his part to perfection, driven by the psychological pressure Poirot had so carefully built up throughout the evening.

The “ghost” stepped forward into the circle of light, and I saw that he was a young man of slight build, his face cleverly made up with greasepaint and phosphorus to resemble the features of the late Mr. Maltravers. From the shadows of the hallway, a tall, grave man emerged, his eyes fixed upon the collapsed woman. It was Alfred Wright, the director of the Northern Union, who had come down from London at Poirot’s express request to witness the success of his “little idea.” “My friend Alfred Wright,” said Poirot, “I believe you have heard the lady’s confession?”

Poirot stepped forward and calmly took a small electric torch from the hand of the “spirit.” The ghostly figure, now revealed in the returning light, was a young man from the village whom Poirot had recruited for this piece of theatricality, his face expertly whitened with flour and his clothes dusted with phosphorus. As for the “blood” on Mrs. Maltravers’ hand, it was a simple trick of chemistry—a colorless liquid Poirot had surreptitiously applied to her fingers when he had gallantly pressed her hand earlier, which turned a vivid crimson upon contact with the specially treated surface of the door handle.

Poirot stood over the prostrate woman, his face unusually stern. The “ghostly” figure of Mr. Maltravers stepped forward into the light, revealing itself to be a young man I did not recognize, who was now busily wiping luminous paint from his forehead. With a curt nod of thanks, Poirot dismissed him, and he vanished into the shadows of the hall.

“A little theatricality, Hastings,” Poirot remarked, as we moved to lift Mrs. Maltravers onto a settee. “The dead do not return, but a guilty conscience is a powerful medium. I had a young man I know—a very clever actor—play the part of the deceased.”

I stared at the woman’s right hand, which still glowed with that sinister crimson hue. “But the blood, Poirot! How did you manage that?”

“That’s it,” he continued. “You heard, Hastings? And you, Everett?
Oh, by the way, this is Mr. Everett, rather a fine member of the
theatrical profession. I ’phoned to him this afternoon. His make-up
is good, isn’t it? Quite like the dead man, and with a pocket torch
and the necessary phosphorescence he made the proper impression.
I shouldn’t touch her right hand if I were you, Hastings. Red paint
marks so. When the lights went out I clasped her hand, you see. By
the way, we mustn’t miss our train. Inspector Japp is outside the
window. A bad night—but he has been able to while away the time by
tapping on the window every now and then.”

“Then you suspected her all along?” I asked, as we were being
whirled back to London.

“_Mais oui_! She was too beautiful, and too distressed, and she
told me she knew nothing of her husband’s affairs. But I found out
from the insurance office that she had been there herself three
weeks ago, making inquiries. And then, there was the discrepancy.
She told me she had been to the village for some stamps. I
happened to notice that the only stamps in her desk were of the
old issue. They hadn’t any of the new ones in the village, I
found.”

“But how did you know about the rook rifle story? You didn’t even
know Captain Black was here.”

“The gardener told me—and I remembered the case of the man who
shot himself that way in the papers a few months ago. It seemed
to me more than a coincidence that Captain Black should have been
here. Then, when I gave him the word ‘Shot,’ he answered
‘Suicide’ at once. I knew then that he had told them that story.
Mrs. Maltravers must have been very quick to see the possibility
of it. It was a clever murder, Hastings, but she made the mistake
of being a little too beautiful, and a little too unstrung. I
distrust the ‘unstrung’ woman, always. She has too many nerves for
my liking.”

And Poirot leaned back in his seat and closed his eyes.

“What a mind!” I said to myself. “What a mind!”

“But I don’t understand, Poirot. Was she the culprit, then?”

“_Mais oui_, my friend. You see, I was quite sure from the first
that it was not suicide. It was that little rook rifle. Do you
remember my asking her where it was? And she told me that her
husband had it with him, and that she had heard him fire two
shots? Well, when I examined the rifle there were indeed two spent
cartridges in it. But, my friend, the little rook rifle is a
single-shot weapon! You have to open it and take out the old
cartridge and put in a new one before you can fire again. Now, a
man who is going to commit suicide does not fire a shot at a bird,
then reload his rifle, and then fire a second shot into his own
mouth! It was a very simple little point, but it was enough to
show that her story was false. And if her story was false, then
she must have had a hand in it.”

“But how did she do it?”

“Ah, that I cannot tell you for certain. But I can make a very good
guess. I think she must have asked him to show her how the man in
Captain Black’s story had committed suicide. He would naturally
be interested, and would put the barrel of the rifle into his
mouth to show her. And then—a touch on the trigger, and it was
done! A very clever and cold-blooded murder. She had it all
planned, you see. The story of his premonitions of death, the
insuring of his life—it was all part of her scheme.”

“You mean,” I said, as we stood on the platform at Marsdon Leigh
half an hour later, “that Mrs. Maltravers killed her husband?”

“Precisely. She heard the story that Captain Black told at dinner
and saw a way of getting the insurance money—for which she had
already persuaded her husband to apply. She got him to show her
just how the man in the story did it, and then, as he put the rifle
into his mouth, she put her hand on his and—_voilà_! A clever
woman, Hastings, but she had not the necessary _sang-froid_ to
withstand my little theatrical display. She was, as the doctor
rightly said, a ‘mass of nerves.’”

“And Dr. Bernard?”

“A very foolish old man, Hastings. He was so anxious to avoid
giving pain to a beautiful woman that he failed to perform his
duty. A medical man should always be suspicious, but he was
blinded by a pretty face and a few tears.”

“Then she killed him?” I said, as we were being whirled along to
London. “And all this time I have been feeling so sorry for the
poor little woman!”

“Yes, she killed him. You see, she was in love with that young
Black, and no doubt expected to marry him later on. Maltravers’
financial position gave her the excuse. She had no doubt been
worrying him to insure his life for some time. Then this Captain
Black comes along with his story of the suicide in East Africa.
The very thing! He tells it at dinner. Mrs. Maltravers thinks it
over. The next day she gets her husband to go out with her, takes
the rook rifle, and asks him to show her how the man did it. He
puts the barrel in his mouth—she puts her hand on his—the rifle
goes off. That was why she was so upset when Black appeared. She
was afraid he might mention the story to the doctor, and the doctor
might see the coincidence. I had a little talk with the doctor this
afternoon—he’s not such an old ass as he looks, Hastings. I told
him what I suspected, and he was able to tell me that the wound
had certain features which were quite consistent with my theory.
So we arranged our little theatricals. The parlourmaid was in the
plot, of course. We had to prepare the atmosphere, you see.”

“And what about the door?” I asked. “How did it open when it was
locked?”

“Ah, that was my own little invention. A piece of silk thread, my
friend, a piece of silk thread! One should always be prepared for
emergencies. I felt that the open door would be the finishing
touch.”

And Poirot smiled at me with his own inimitable smile.

“But what about the culprit?” I asked. “You told me it had to be
one of the four suspects.”

“And it was, Hastings. Mrs. Maltravers was the hand that held the
weapon, but there was another who stood to gain, and whose shadow
loomed over the tragedy.”

We had a few minutes to wait for our train, and I asked Poirot
the question that was burning in my mind.

“What was it that first made you suspicious?”

“My friend, I told you. There was a discrepancy. The doctor said
Maltravers was a Christian Scientist and therefore did not see a
doctor. The wife said he had already had a hæmorrhage and was
expecting another. If he were a Christian Scientist he would not
believe in hæmorrhages, and if he had had one he would have called
in a doctor. Then, again, there were those two shots from the rook
rifle. If a man wants to commit suicide, one shot is usually
enough. The first shot was a trial one, to see if the rifle would
work. It did not go off—it missed fire. Then he tried again. But
if he were a suicide, he would not have tried again. It was the
wife who was holding the rifle, and it was she who had heard the
story of the suicide on the African farm and had thought of a way
to rid herself of an elderly and possibly bankrupt husband and
realize fifty thousand pounds in the process. She had no idea that
the Insurance Company would investigate—she thought it would be
all quite simple. She is a very beautiful woman, but her brain is
perhaps not quite so good as it might be. She should have
remembered that Hercules Poirot is not easily deceived.”

And Poirot, with a little sigh, climbed into the carriage and
composed himself to sleep.

“You see,” continued Poirot, as we walked briskly through the wind
and rain, “there was a little discrepancy. The doctor seemed to
think the deceased was a Christian Scientist, and who could have
given him that impression but Mrs. Maltravers? But to us she
represented him as being in a grave state of apprehension about
his own health. Again, why was she so taken aback by the reappearance
of young Black? And lastly, although I know that convention decrees
that a woman must make a decent pretence of mourning for her
husband, I do not care for such heavily-rouged eyelids! You did
not observe them, Hastings? No? As I always tell you, you see
nothing!”

"But the blood, Poirot! The hemorrhage?" I exclaimed, still trying to reconcile the medical facts. "Dr. Bernard was quite certain of his diagnosis. Even if he is, as you say, 'an old ass,' he could surely not mistake a gunshot wound for a gastric ulcer!"

Poirot stopped and looked at me, his eyes twinkling in the dark.

"Precisely, my friend. He did not mistake it. He *ignored* it. You recall my little mention of the doctor who once gave a verdict of heart failure until a constable pointed out the bullet? Dr. Bernard was of the same school of thought. He told us himself: 'In my profession we see no need to distress unduly the relatives of a dead patient.' He had been the family physician to the Maltravers for years. When he found the master of the house dead with a little blood on his lips, he chose the most 'natural' cause that would spare the beautiful widow a scandal. He is not a villain, Hastings, merely a man who prefers a quiet life and a tidy death certificate to the rigors of an inquest."

“But how did she do it?” I asked.

“She knew of the story Captain Black had told at dinner. After her
husband’s death, she gave the doctor to understand that Maltravers
had been a Christian Scientist, and she probably told her husband
something of the same kind. On Wednesday morning they went out
together, and she suggested he should show her how the man in the
story had killed himself. He probably didn’t know she was
meddling with the trigger. A very simple crime, and it would
undoubtedly have succeeded had it not been for the Insurance
Company’s suspicions and my own little ‘experiment’ with Captain
Black.”

“And what about Alfred Wright?” I asked, remembering the name Poirot
had mentioned earlier. “You said he was a director of the Northern
Union and had asked you to investigate.”

“But I don’t understand,” I said. “How did she do it? You say
she killed him. Did she—murder him, then?”

“Precisely. She heard the story that Captain Black told at dinner,
and the idea occurred to her. She would make her husband—poor
unfortunate man—act it for her. I should imagine that she
pretended to be interested, and asked him to show her exactly how
it was done. He, no doubt, was only too pleased to please his
charming young wife. He would place the muzzle of the rifle in
his mouth, and she, no doubt, would lean over him and playfully
press the trigger. It was a risk, but a risk worth taking for
fifty thousand pounds. And then she would dispose of the rifle,
and—_voilà_!”

“But how did you know it was she?”

“My friend, it was a process of elimination. Captain Black was
obviously innocent. Dr. Ralph Bernard, though perhaps a little
careless, had no motive. Alfred Wright, our friend at the insurance
company, was the one who sent me—hardly likely to be the culprit.
That left only the beautiful Mrs. Maltravers.”

“But how did she do it?” I asked.

“My dear Hastings, I told you that there was a discrepancy. The
rook rifle was not in the hall, she had it in her hand. He thought
she was going to shoot a bird. She did—but not a bird. She asked
him to show her how to use it, and then—_bang_! The bullet went
through the roof of his mouth. Then she wiped his mouth, and left
him there. It was all so simple that no one thought of anything
but suicide. But, you see, she had not the luck. Black told his
story on Tuesday evening—the very story she needed to help her
carry out her plan. It was too much of a coincidence, Hastings.
My mind began to work from then on.”

“But the motive?” I said, as we stepped out on the platform.

“Ah, Hastings, you are always so practical. Money, of course.
Maltravers had indeed been on the verge of bankruptcy, but he was
also an old-fashioned man with a great deal of pride. He had
confided his troubles to his wife, but not to his doctor. Mrs.
Maltravers, however, saw an opportunity. If her husband were to
die, the insurance money would save her from the poverty she so
dreaded. She had heard Captain Black’s story of the suicide in
East Africa, and it gave her a wicked idea. She persuaded her
husband to pose for a photograph, or perhaps simply to show her
how the unfortunate man in the story had held the rifle. While
he had the barrel in his mouth, she simply stepped forward and
pressed the trigger.”

“Well, there it was. There were the two possibilities. Did Black’s
story suggest an ingenious method of committing suicide to Mr.
Maltravers, or did his other listener, the wife, see an equally
ingenious method of committing murder? I inclined to the latter
view. To shoot himself in the way indicated, he would probably have
had to pull the trigger with his toe—or at least so I imagine.
Now if Maltravers had been found with one boot off, we should
almost certainly have heard of it from some one. An odd detail like
that would have been remembered.

“As for the rest, there was no suicide. The insurance was a
desperate gamble to provide for his wife, and she, knowing the
truth of his financial ruin and having perhaps a more than passing
interest in Captain Black, decided to hasten the end. She used
the very story Black told to stage a ‘natural’ death, knowing the
old doctor would be easily fooled. But she forgot that Hercule
Poirot has eyes that see beyond the rouge on a widow's cheek.”

“And then, my friend, there was the little matter of the
Northern Union. You recall I mentioned my friend Alfred Wright,
a director of that company? It was he who first brought the
suspicious nature of the case to my attention. He had noted the
closeness of the insurance to the death, but more than that, he
had noted the specific beneficiaries. Mrs. Maltravers was to
receive the entirety, but the paperwork had been handled with a
singularly cold-blooded haste that did not sit well with the
image of a grieving widow. Alfred Wright is a man of business,
Hastings; he sees the figures, and the figures told a story of
greed, not of a man seeking to protect his beloved from ruin.”

“But why did she do it?” I asked.

“My dear Hastings! Did you not hear of the large sum for which his
life was insured? Fifty thousand pounds! And she is a young and
beautiful woman, with a life before her—and perhaps a new husband
already in view. She knew he was on the verge of bankruptcy, and
that this was her only chance of a fortune. She is a woman of
resource, as she showed by her quickness in catching at the idea
of the rook rifle and the ‘Christian Scientist’ story to explain
the lack of a doctor. But she could not foresee that I, Hercule
Poirot, would be sent to investigate! Or that I should have the
good fortune to encounter Captain Black and his ‘lion story’ which
provided the very inspiration for her crime.”

“So the murder theory was my choice. And when I found that
Maltravers was on the verge of bankruptcy, I saw the motive for
it. He had, as I suspected, got together all the money he could
to pay the premiums on a life insurance for his wife’s benefit,
and she, no doubt, had been the moving spirit in the whole affair.
But when I was talking to the doctor I saw that he was a man who
did not like to be told that his diagnosis was wrong. I knew that
if I suggested murder he would only have stuck to his gastric
ulcer. No, I had to find some other way. Then it occurred to me
that if I could only play upon the guilty woman’s nerves—and I had
noted her extremely nervous state—she might be frightened into a
confession. Hence my little theatrical display! I must admit that
I did not expect her to give herself away quite so easily as she
did. However, I am glad it is over, and we can get back to town
to-night. What do you say, Hastings? Shall we go to the ‘Palais’
this evening? I believe there is a very good show.”

“I have no doubt she got him to show her how this suicide out in
the East was supposed to have been done. Then, when he was
off-guard, she pressed the trigger. After that she probably
substituted the little rook rifle for the larger one, and wiped
it. It must have been a little larger, you see, to produce that
hæmorrhage. But, as I told you, I knew she had something to
conceal. That was why I did not tell her that we should stay at
the Anchor. But, my friend, what a night!”

We reached the station just as the last train for London was
steaming in. It had been a long and tiring day. I was quite glad
to sink back into the corner of our first-class carriage.

“No, as I say, I inclined to the view that it was a case of murder,
not suicide, but I realized that I had not a shadow of proof in
support of my theory. Hence the elaborate little comedy you saw
played to-night.”

“Even now I don’t quite see all the details of the crime?” I said.

“It is simple, my friend. She asked him to show her exactly how the man in Captain Black’s story had committed the deed. The poor man, suspecting no evil from the wife he loved, placed the barrel of the rifle in his own mouth to demonstrate. Then—she simply reached out and pressed the trigger. A cold-blooded and calculated crime, Hastings, but one that did not account for the ‘little grey cells’ of Hercule Poirot. Alfred Wright and the Northern Union will be most gratified to keep their fifty thousand pounds. And now, let us hasten to the station; this night air is of a dampness most injurious to the moustaches!”

“It is quite simple, Hastings. She heard the story from Captain Black and saw her opportunity. She probably made a game of it, coaxing her husband to demonstrate the ‘impossible’ feat described at dinner. When he placed the barrel of the rook rifle in his mouth to show her, she reached out and pressed the trigger. A cold-blooded calculation, hidden behind the mask of a grieving widow. But she forgot that while the dead may not speak, they can be made to point a finger—with a little help from the stage and the ‘spirit’ of Monsieur Everett! And so, my friend Alfred Wright will be satisfied, the Insurance Company is saved its fifty thousand pounds, and we—we have time for a very good supper in London. The little grey cells, Hastings, they have triumphed once more over the theatricals of a beautiful woman.”

“It is simple, my friend. She saw in Captain Black’s story an ingenious way to rid herself of an aging husband while securing a fortune for herself and, perhaps, a younger lover. She persuaded Maltravers to re-enact the tale he had heard at dinner, perhaps under the guise of a macabre joke or simple curiosity, and when he placed the barrel of the rifle in his mouth, she reached out and pulled the trigger. The lack of an external wound and the doctor’s own incompetence did the rest. She was a clever woman, Hastings, but she did not account for the fact that while the dead do not speak, the guilty conscience is a loud and treacherous thing when confronted by the 'spirits.' And now, let us hasten; the night air is damp, and I fear for the equilibrium of my moustaches!”

“My dear Hastings, it is simple. She persuaded her husband to show her how the man in Captain Black’s story had killed himself—perhaps as a macabre jest. He, unsuspecting, placed the barrel of the rook rifle in his mouth. Then, a quick pressure on the trigger, and the fifty thousand pounds was hers—or so she thought. She played the part of the grieving, penniless widow to perfection, even deceiving you, my friend! But she did not count on the ‘little grey cells’—or the fact that a ghost, even a theatrical one, can be a most effective detective. And now, let us hurry, or we shall indeed miss our train to London.”

“It is simple, Hastings. She persuaded him to show her exactly how the man in the story had done it—and as the barrel was in his mouth, she herself reached out and pressed the trigger. A cold-blooded and calculated murder, staged to look like the suicide she had heard described, all for the sake of that fifty thousand pounds insurance. My friend Alfred Wright and the Northern Union will be most relieved to have escaped so heavy a claim. But for me, Hastings, I have the greater satisfaction. I have seen through the rouge on the eyelids and the ‘mediumistic’ terrors of Mrs. Maltravers. Even the most beautiful face, my friend, cannot hide the darkness of a criminal heart from the ‘little grey cells’ of Hercule Poirot!”

“Let us start from the beginning. Here is a shrewd and scheming
woman who, knowing of her husband’s financial _débâcle_ and tired
of the elderly mate she has only married for his money, induces
him to insure his life for a large sum, and then seeks for the
means to accomplish her purpose. An accident gives her that—the
young soldier’s strange story. The next afternoon when _monsieur
le capitaine_, as she thinks, is on the high seas, she and her
husband are strolling round the grounds. ‘What a curious story that
was last night!’ she observes. ‘Could a man shoot himself in such
a way? Do show me if it is possible!’ The poor fool—he shows her.
He places the end of the rifle in his mouth. She stoops down, and
puts her finger on the trigger, laughing up at him. ‘And now, sir,’
she says saucily, ‘supposing I pull the trigger?’

“And then—and then, Hastings—she pulls it!”
